E_wrong=(1)/(|W|)∑_c^′∈WE(A_c^′→B_c),E_copy=∑ₜ₌₁^T-H(∑ₚmₜ(p) \lVertbₜ(p)-b_t+H(p)\rVert²)/(∑ₚmₜ(p)),

where W is the set of other actions of A. This set is fixed for each source and is the same for every method. E_self uses B’s own action, Eₜᵣ uses A’s correct action, E_wrong uses A’s other actions, and E_copy predicts each frame by the frame H steps earlier. All four use the same mask and the same averaging. The usual transfer gain compares the transferred action with copying,

G=(E_copy-Eₜᵣ)/(E_copy-E_self).

(4)

If a model ignores its action, then Eₜᵣ=E_self and G=1, a perfect score. We compare the correct action with wrong actions instead,

S=(E_wrong-Eₜᵣ)/(E_wrong-E_self).

(5)

S=1 means the transferred action predicts B as well as B’s own action. S=0 means it is no better than the wrong actions on average, and S<0 means it is worse. S can also exceed 1 when the transferred action predicts B better than its own action, and we do not clip it. S is a relative score computed from prediction errors. A value of 0.46 means that the transferred action closes 46% of the error gap between wrong actions and the target’s own action. It does not mean that 46% of the motion was copied. S measures how much better the correct action predicts the target than wrong actions do. It is a measure of action-specific prediction, not a direct measure of how well limbs, contact or deformation are reproduced.

A simple example shows the difference between the two scores. For a model with E_self=0.010, Eₜᵣ=0.014, E_wrong=0.020 and E_copy=0.030, the correct action is better than the wrong ones but worse than B’s own action, which gives S=0.6 and G=0.8. A model that ignores its action gives the same error for every action, for example E_self=Eₜᵣ=E_wrong=0.012. It receives G=1.0, a higher score than the first model, although it transfers nothing. Its S is undefined, because the actions give no difference to measure. In a separate check, models trained for only one epoch get G=1.00 and S≈0.

We compute S only when E_wrong-E_self>10⁻⁶, that is, when B’s own action is better than the wrong actions. S is therefore a conditional score over the pairs that pass this rule. We report how many pairs it removes wherever the errors of single pairs were stored (Section 6.2). We also report two further measures. Wrong-action accuracy is the share of all pairs in which the correct action beats every wrong action, with a chance level of 1/(1+|W|). Action sensitivity is the median of E(B^′→B)/E(B→B), where B^′ is one test clip drawn at random for each target from all test clips, whatever its action class or character. The draw uses a fixed seed, so every method is tested with the same clips. A sensitivity close to 1 suggests that the model makes little use of its action, and in that case we do not interpret its transfer scores.

3.5 Body-plan gap

To separate the body from other changes, we take actions from a character of a held-out family and transfer them to three kinds of target. These are another character of the same family, a character of another animal family, and a human. All are drawn in the same style. We compute two differences,

Δₐₙᵢₘₐₗ=S_same_family-S_other_family, Δₕᵤₘₐₙ=S_same_family-Sₕᵤₘₐₙ.

(6)

A positive value means that transfer is better within the same family. We give 95% intervals by resampling target characters, because the frames and pairs of one character are not independent. Each resample draws whole target characters with replacement and keeps all of their pairs. It is not stratified by source family, and source characters are not resampled, so the intervals may be somewhat narrow.

4 Benchmarks

We use three sources of video. The synthetic benchmark changes only the body, Sprites changes only the appearance, and the animator-made animations provide motion that was not generated by our own code. Table 1 gives an overview.

4.1 Synthetic benchmark

We propose a new synthetic benchmark for this study, and its availability is described in the Data and code availability section. It has 36 characters. There are six body plans (quadruped, biped, blob, limbless, multi-limbed and disjointed), three shapes for each body plan and two colour schemes. Every character performs five actions (run, jump, fall over, turn and crouch) under 20 intents. An intent fixes the effort, direction, start position and start time of an action. The same intent is used for every action and every character. Because of this, every transfer has a correct answer. If character A jumps under intent k, the transferred jump on character B should look like B’s own jump under intent k. In addition, every clip starts with one to four frames of the character standing still. These frames are the same for all five actions, so the first frame does not give the action away. Fig. 4 shows one jump on all six body plans. The quadruped and the biped push off with their legs. The blob squashes and stretches, the limbless body arches, and the parts of the disjointed body fly apart.

Each run holds out one of three body plans, the blob, the biped or the limbless body, and trains on the other five. Training uses intents 0 to 15 of the first two shapes of these five body plans. Testing uses intents 16 to 19, with targets drawn from the third shape, which is never seen, and from the held-out body plan. We train three seeds for each held-out body plan, which gives nine runs per method. The quadruped, multi-limbed and disjointed body plans are always used for training and are never held out.

4.2 Sprites, a same-body control

Sprites [13] has 1,296 characters. They all share one body and differ in skin, top, bottom and hairstyle (Fig. 5). Each character performs walk, spellcard and slash in three directions. We add one to four standing frames before each action, as in the synthetic benchmark, and use the standard train and test split. Because every character has the same body, Sprites tests transfer across appearance only. It therefore checks that the models can transfer actions at all before the body is changed.

4.3 Animator-made animation

DeformingThings4D [12] provides 3D animations of animals and humans. The animal animations were designed by CG artists, and the human animations come from Adobe Mixamo, where they were recorded with motion capture. We render these animations as flat 2D side views so that they can be used with our image-based models. Each character is viewed from the side, drawn in one colour with three shades and a dark outline, and turned to face right (Fig. 6). All characters share one visual style, but their body shapes and movements still differ.

We render every animation with two cameras. The fixed camera uses one view for the whole animation. Its frame covers the 0.5th to 99.5th percentile of the character’s positions over all frames, with a margin of 12%, so that nearly all of the motion stays in view. The body camera recentres every frame on the middle of the character’s bounding box and keeps one scale for the whole animation. It removes the movement of the character across the image, but changes in size, rotation and shape remain. On the synthetic benchmark, the body camera instead shifts every frame so that the centre of the character’s pixels sits in the middle of the image. Neither procedure removes rotation or changes of shape, so we refer to the resulting view as body-centred motion and not as pure body motion.

Our selected subset contains 431 animations. Of these, 169 are labelled animations of 32 animal characters, each with at least four of six action classes. These classes are walk, run, jump, fall, attack and idle. The animals form five families, which are bears, deer, dogs and foxes, rabbits, and a group of cats, raccoons and a hog. A further 235 animations have no usable action label and are used only for training. They include further animations of the 32 labelled animals and animations of 21 other species, such as dragons, birds and a whale. The remaining 27 animations are labelled clips of 24 human characters, which are used only as transfer targets and never in training.

All five labelled animal families walk on four legs. Holding out one family therefore tests transfer to new animal characters with the same broad body plan. Transfer to humans tests a new body plan, although it also brings other differences, such as proportions and clothing. From each animation we sample three clips of 16 evenly spaced frames. One covers the full animation, and the other two cover its first and last three quarters, so they overlap. The two shorter clips are used only for training, and all evaluation uses the full-length clip. Each run holds out one animal family and all humans, and we repeat this for every family. A held-out family is removed from training completely, including its unlabelled animations.

The 21 other species are used only for training and are never held out. However, eight of their animations show felids or a pig (a cat, a leopard, lionesses and a pig), which are related to the cat, raccoon and hog family. This family is held out less strictly than the other four. To test the effect of this overlap, we repeated the main analysis without this family. Every main score, probe and leak value changed by at most 0.03, the order of the methods stayed the same, and the gain of M4 over M2 changed from 0.073 to 0.072. This overlap therefore has little effect on the main comparisons.

5 Model and Objectives

5.1 Model

All methods use the same model (Table 2). The inverse model takes two frames that are H=3 steps apart, together with their difference, and maps them to an action vector with four strided convolutions and two linear layers. The action is normalised with batch normalisation without a learned scale. In M2 to M5 we also apply \tanh to the action and add Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of 0.1 during training. The control models in Section 5.2 switch both on or off together. This limits how much the action can store. The forward model is a U-Net with four levels. The action changes its features through FiLM [22] at the bottleneck and at three decoder levels. The model has 1.85 million parameters with an 8-dimensional action and 1.97 million with a 128-dimensional action.

5.2 Objectives

We compare five model configurations that differ in action size, noise and the losses used to train the action.

M1 uses a 128-dimensional action and only the prediction loss. It is the wide baseline.

M2 uses an 8-dimensional action with noise. M3, M4 and M5 add one loss each to M2.

M3 is a simplified form of CLAW [8]. In place of a second pass of the world model, a small head tries to rebuild a 16×16 copy of the future frame from the action alone. Gradient reversal, which grows to a weight of 0.3 during training, pushes this information out of the action.

M4 is a simplified form of Olaf-World [10]. It aligns the action with the feature change between two frames, whereas Olaf-World aligns actions averaged over a whole clip. A projection of the action must point in the same direction as the change in frozen ImageNet ResNet-18 features between the two frames. We use a cosine loss with weight 0.5.

M5 is a simplified form of DiLA [9]. The action only drives a prediction of the character’s silhouette, which is trained with a mask loss. A second network, which never sees the action, paints the appearance onto this silhouette.

M3 to M5 are simplified adaptations of the published methods, not reproductions. Results for M3 to M5 therefore describe these objectives in our setting and not the published systems.

Three control models separate the parts of these objectives. M1 differs from M2 in action size and in noise, so we also train M2 without noise and M1 with noise. M4 adds a loss and also brings in ImageNet features, so we also train M4 with a frozen ResNet-18 that keeps its random initial weights. The two encoders differ only in their weights. Both resize the frames to 112×112, use the same ImageNet normalisation and give the same 512 features after global average pooling. The loss and its weight are also the same. In all models, noise and \tanh go together. A model with noise applies \tanh to the action and then adds noise, and a model without noise uses neither. As a result, M2 without noise differs from M1 only in action size, and M1 with noise differs from M2 only in action size. All other settings are unchanged.

5.3 Displacement baseline

The baseline has no learned parameters. It moves the target character’s pixels by the same amount as the source character’s centre moves over the same three frames, and leaves all other pixels unchanged. In this way, it transfers the movement of the source across the screen but not the motion of its body. For this reason, a learned model that does not score higher than this baseline transfers only position.

6 Training and Evaluation

6.1 Training

All models in the main experiments are trained for 20 epochs with AdamW, a weight decay of 10⁻⁴ and a one-cycle learning rate schedule with a peak of 10⁻³. Each batch holds 128 pairs of frames, taken from all start positions in all training clips. The loss is the squared error of the predicted frame, and character pixels count ten times more than background pixels. All models were trained on one GPU on Kaggle, and one model takes a few minutes to train. Table 2 lists every setting.

6.2 Evaluation

For each run we report the median of S over the transfer pairs that pass the rule of Section 3.4, together with G, wrong-action accuracy and action sensitivity. Each source animal has two to five other actions, so the chance level of wrong-action accuracy is between 0.17 and 0.33, and the same wrong actions are used for every method. Two linear probes read the action vectors, using their mean and spread over time. The first probe learns the action class from clips of training bodies and is tested on clips of held-out bodies. It measures whether the action class transfers. The second probe predicts the body plan or family of clips from training bodies. It measures how much the action says about its source body, which we call body leak. Both probes are logistic regressions on standardised features with C=0.5. On the animator-made animations the action probe uses balanced accuracy, because the classes have different sizes. On the synthetic benchmark it uses plain accuracy. Family leak uses plain accuracy on both benchmarks.

However, probes read the action and not the motion the model makes. To check the generated motion directly, we train a separate convolutional classifier on real clips of the training families. We then drive each held-out animal from one fixed starting pose with the actions of every training animal for five steps, and the classifier labels the result. The starting pose is the same for every action, so only the action can change the label. Its accuracy on real clips of the same animals gives a reference for this test.

S is defined only when E_wrong-E_self is above a small threshold. On the animator-made animations we stored the errors of every pair for every model and checked three thresholds, 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻³. No pair of any learned model was removed at any of them. For the baseline, at most 0.7% of pairs were removed. So the scores of the learned models cover all pairs. The denominator is also far from zero. For every learned model, E_wrong-E_self is at least 20% of E_self in 95% of pairs, and its median is between 79% and 398%. For the baseline, the 5th percentile is 6%. The synthetic and Sprites runs used the same threshold of 10⁻⁶, but stored only the median per run, so we cannot give the count there.

Clips of one action class cover the same part of each animation, but two characters may not be at the same point of the action at the same time. For example, the take-off of one jump may be compared with the landing of another. We test the effect of this with a best-shift check. We shift the source action in time by up to three steps in either direction and keep the shift with the lowest error on the target. The shift is chosen with the target’s real frames, so this is a diagnostic that gives an upper bound on what timing alignment could add, not a method a model could use. We do this separately for the correct action and for each wrong action, so the correct action gets no advantage. We run this check for M2 and M4 with seed 0 on up to 150 pairs of each kind and family.

The main comparison of all five methods on the animator-made animations uses one seed per held-out family (Sections 7.4 and 7.7). The comparison across the same family, other families and humans (Section 7.5) uses two further seeds of M2 and M4 with all transfer pairs, which gives 10 runs per model. The test of M4 against M2 adds the main seed to these runs, which gives 15 runs. The control models (Section 7.7) use two seeds per family, compared with M2 and M4 trained with the same two seeds, and M1 uses one seed.

7 Results

7.1 The usual gain rewards ignoring the action

Fig. 7 compares G and S on the synthetic benchmark. A model that ignores its action gets G=1.00, higher than every trained model, and its S is undefined. Across the five objectives, G for seen to held-out bodies has a correlation of r=-0.97 with action sensitivity under the fixed camera. That is, a model that relies less on its action gets a higher G. With the body camera, G is also unstable. M5 gets G=-0.76±1.50 over nine runs, because the body moves little and the difference E_copy-E_self becomes small, and its S is 0.41±0.13. We therefore use S for all other results.

7.2 Transfer works when the body is the same

On Sprites, every learned model reaches S between 0.98 and 1.00 on new characters (Table 3). It also finds the correct action class in 100% of test clips. S stays at 0.97 or higher even when the source and target differ in all four parts of their appearance. This shows that the models learn useful actions, and that a change of appearance alone does not break transfer. The baseline also gets S=1.00, but this value is not informative. Every Sprites character performs an action with the same frames, so the correct source moves its centre almost exactly as the target does, and Eₜᵣ is almost equal to E_self. The baseline still predicts worse than copying the frame, with a self-gain of -0.27.

7.3 With a fixed camera, much of the transfer is position

On the synthetic benchmark with a fixed camera, the baseline gets S=0.75±0.06 for seen to held-out body plans (Fig. 8, Table 4). In comparison, M2, M3 and M5 score about the same, between 0.72 and 0.74. Only M4 is higher, at 0.86, and M1 is lowest, at 0.40. The animator-made animations show a similar pattern. The baseline gets 0.71 for seen to held-out families, and the learned models get between 0.35 and 0.79 (Fig. 9, Table 5). A method that only copies movement matches most learned models. Consequently, under a fixed camera, movement across the screen accounts for much of the measured transfer.

7.4 Body motion transfers weakly

With the body camera, the baseline has no movement to copy, and its score on the synthetic benchmark falls to 0.20. The learned models also fall, to between 0.18 (M1) and 0.42 (M4) for seen to held-out body plans. On the animator-made animations, the best model reaches 0.46 for a held-out animal family, and every model scores at most 0.20 from seen bodies to humans (Fig. 9). Without the less strictly held-out cat, raccoon and hog family, these values are 0.47 and 0.20. For sources from the seen families, changing the target from a held-out animal family to a human lowers the score of M2 to M5 by 0.26 to 0.27. Because some human clips were drawn from the front in a first run, we redrew all humans from the side, facing right like the animals, and trained and tested every model again. The human scores with the body camera changed by at most 0.01, so the drop to humans does not come from the viewpoint.

The result also depends on the action. With the body camera on the synthetic benchmark, the baseline gets 0.81 for turn and 0.54 for crouch, which mostly change the outline. In contrast, it gets -0.19 for run and -0.22 for jump, which need the legs or the whole body to move in a way that depends on the body. The learned models, on the other hand, get 0.10 to 0.25 on run and 0.15 to 0.34 on jump.

7.5 Same family, other families and humans

To separate the body from the drawing style, we compare transfer from a character of the held-out family to three kinds of target, drawn in the same style. The target is another character of the same family, a character of another animal family, or a human (Table 6, Fig. 10). Transfer decreases as the target becomes less similar to the source. For M4, it falls from 0.55 within a family to 0.35 for another animal family and 0.20 for humans. Similarly, for M2 it falls from 0.49 to 0.33 and 0.12. The advantage of the same family over other animal families, and over humans, is positive in all 10 runs of both models. The baseline also does better within a family (0.45) than across families (0.27), so part of the benefit of a similar body comes from a similar outline. The learned models add 0.04 to 0.12 over the baseline in every case. The gap from the same family to humans, however, is the same for all three methods (0.38 to 0.39). M4 raises every score but does not shrink the gap to a different body plan.

A simple offset in time does not explain the gap (Table 7). Even when the best shift is chosen with the target’s real frames, transfer from the held-out family to humans rises from 0.10 to 0.17 for M2 and from 0.20 to 0.28 for M4. Humans gain more from the shift than animals do, so differences in timing explain part of the low human scores. The gap from the same family to humans changes only from 0.42 to 0.39 for M2 and from 0.39 to 0.35 for M4.

7.6 What transfers, but not how

A linear classifier still identifies the action class from the actions of unseen bodies. With the body camera on the animator-made animations, a linear probe trained on the actions of the training families identifies the action of a held-out family with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy, where chance is 17%. However, for the same models, body-centred transfer is only 0.11 to 0.46 (Fig. 11). With the body camera on the synthetic benchmark, the probe reaches 48% to 62% plain accuracy, where chance is 20%, and transfer is 0.18 to 0.42. The action class can still be identified from the actions of unseen bodies, but this does not mean that the model can reproduce how those bodies perform the action.

We also use the separate classifier to check the generated motion. When a held-out animal is driven by another animal’s action, the classifier finds the intended action in 52% (M2) and 45% (M4) of cases. These rates are close to those when the animal is driven by its own action (49% and 41%). On real clips of the same held-out families, it recognises 81%, where chance is 17%. Because the classifier was trained only on animals, it recognises only 31% of real human clips, so we do not use it for humans.

Fig. 12 shows the same gap in examples. When the models get a deer’s jump, they keep the bear’s shape and colour, but they predict a blurred bear instead of a bear leaving the ground. With the same jump, the human target is partly redrawn as a four-legged shape, most clearly by M1 and M5. The transferred action carries part of the shape of the source body.

7.7 Less body in the action, better transfer

The largest difference between the models is the amount of body information in their actions. With the body camera, a classifier identifies the training body plan from the 128-dimensional action of M1 in 99% of synthetic clips and the body family in 95% of animator-made clips, and M1 transfers worst of all learned models on every benchmark. The 8-dimensional action of M2, which also adds noise, lowers family leak to 47% and raises body-centred transfer over M1 by 0.27 on average (paired over the five held-out families), and in every family. The control models show that the size of the action causes most of this (Table 8). Without noise on either model, the 8-dimensional action scores 0.23 higher than the 128-dimensional one, in all 5 families. With noise on both, it scores 0.24 higher, in all 10 runs. Over the paired runs, noise adds on average only 0.05 at 8 dimensions and 0.03 at 128 dimensions. In the action-size controls, family leak follows the size as well, 94% to 95% with 128 dimensions and 49% to 57% with 8. Among the five main objectives, M3 and M4 have the lowest family leak, both 38%, and M4 has the highest transfer. However, on the synthetic benchmark M3 has lower body leak than M4 (73% against 81%), so low leak alone does not explain the transfer of M4. Over the 25 animator-made runs, family leak and body-centred transfer have a correlation of r=-0.91 (Fig. 13). These runs share methods, folds and training data, so they are not independent, and the correlation does not establish a cause. On the synthetic benchmark, though, the correlation is weaker, r=-0.35 over 45 runs, because all models except M3 still tell the body plan in 79% to 99% of clips.

On the animator-made animations, M4 gives the highest body-centred transfer scores S of the five objectives. For seen to held-out bodies with the body camera on the animator-made animations, M4 scores higher than M2 in all 15 paired runs (3 seeds and 5 families). The mean gain is 0.073, and single runs range from 0.028 to 0.120. Averaged per family, the gain is 0.052 for bears, 0.064 for dogs and foxes, 0.079 for rabbits, 0.079 for cats, raccoons and the hog, and 0.091 for deer. A t interval over the five family means gives [0.054,0.092]. Only the five families are independent groups, and they share part of their training data, so this shows a consistent gain in our experiments and not a general advantage of M4. A paired test over the five family means gives t(4)=10.6. On the synthetic benchmark, M4 scores 0.072 higher in 8 of 9 runs (t(8)=2.82, p=0.023, d_z=0.94). In contrast, for seen to held-out transfer on the animator-made animations, neither M3 nor M5 scores higher than M2. With the body camera, M4 also has the lowest action sensitivity, 1.5 against 1.9 for M2 (Table 5), and the lowest class probe accuracy of the 8-dimensional models. So its gain does not come from a more detailed action.

To find out whether the gain comes from the extra loss or from the ImageNet features, we replace the frozen encoder with a ResNet-18 that has random weights (Table 8). The result differs between animal and human targets. For seen to held-out animal families, the random encoder adds only 0.01 over M2 (bootstrap interval over the 10 runs, [-0.004,0.025]). Across the 10 paired runs, the ImageNet encoder scores on average 0.066 higher than the random encoder, and it is higher in every run. For humans, the random encoder does as well as the ImageNet encoder, 0.20 for both, and both are 0.08 above M2 in all 10 runs. The random encoder also gives the lowest family leak, 36%, but transfers worse to animals than M4. For new animal families, M4 with the ImageNet encoder scores 0.075 above M2, and M4 with the random encoder only 0.01. This suggests that the pretrained features help, although we did not test why. For humans, the gain comes from the extra loss itself. A random convolutional network still gives features that change when the image changes, mostly with coarse shape and colour. The loss encourages a projection of the action to align with this change, so the action may capture the overall change of the frame. This may favour coarse changes that many bodies share over details of the source body.

8 Discussion

8.1 Three parts of an action

The usual score combines three parts of an action. Our tests separate them for the models and data we use. A baseline that copies only the movement across the screen scores as high as most learned models, so a high score with a fixed camera does not show that an action was learned. The action class can still be read from the actions of unseen bodies. However, the body-centred score of M4 drops from 0.55 within a family to 0.20 for humans. A latent action learned from pixels can therefore keep the action class without giving the forward model enough information to reproduce the motion of the target body. Garrido et al. [11] also found that actions learned without a shared body can become tied to the camera. Our baseline is a related test, because it measures how much transfer can be achieved through movement on the screen alone.

8.2 Should an action be free of the body?

The link between body leak and transfer suggests that reducing body information in the action can improve transfer. The control models support this for action size, since a smaller action both leaks less and transfers better. However, low body leak does not explain the result by itself, because M4 with a random encoder leaks the least and still transfers worse to animals than M4. The gain of M4 also comes from different sources for the two kinds of target. For new animal families the ImageNet features matter, which suggests that pretrained knowledge of how animals look helps when the target is also an animal. For human targets the random encoder does as well, so pretrained features add nothing there, and the gain comes from the extra loss. Still, the gap to humans is the same for M2, M4 and the baseline. The best model closes 46% of the error gap between wrong actions and the target’s own action for a new animal family, and at most 20% for humans. An action with less information about the source body may still indicate that a jump is happening. The forward model must then work out how the new body jumps, although it has only seen the training bodies jump. We have not tested this idea, but a future model could describe the target body separately from the action and write motion on a new body as

x_t+H=f(xₜ, a, body),

(7)

with the action a and the body as separate inputs. In current latent-action models, by contrast, the body is only hidden inside xₜ. One option is a model that describes the structure of the target directly, for example as parts learned from its own video [21], and applies the action to these parts. In such a model, the action would say which parts move and in which direction, for example that the support parts push down so that the whole body rises. The body description would then say which parts of the new character play these roles. Transfer would then require matching parts between bodies. This is hard for a blob without legs, and our benchmark can test it.

8.3 What this means for evaluation

We recommend that work on transfer across bodies includes a baseline that copies only the movement on the screen and a score that compares the correct action with wrong ones. The usual gain can rank models in the reverse order of how much they use the action. Transfer between bodies with a similar structure, such as two robot arms, is not evidence of transfer between different body plans, because the body-specific motion is the part that transfers least in our tests.

9 Limitations

We use small models at 64×64 pixels, all with the same training settings. Between M2 and M3 to M5 only the objective changes. M1 also differs in action size and noise, and we use the control models to separate these two factors. Larger models trained on more varied video may transfer better, so this needs to be tested before our results are applied to large world models. M3 to M5 are adaptations of published methods to our model and may behave differently from the original systems. We also do not compare with skeleton-based motion retargeting [15, 16], because it needs a rig for every character, and most 2D footage does not have one. Our best-shift check only shifts whole action sequences in time. It does not handle actions that are faster or slower on one body than on another. There are only 32 labelled animal characters and 24 human characters. In addition, S measures the inverse and forward models together, so a low score can come from a forward model that cannot draw the new body as well as from the action. The body-centred view still uses pixel error and does not measure joints, contact or body parts directly. The synthetic and Sprites runs stored only the median score per run, so we cannot report how many pairs the condition on S removed there. The synthetic characters move by hand-set rules. The animator-made animations fix this, but they come from 3D meshes drawn in a flat style, without the squash, stretch and smear of hand-drawn cartoons. On the animator-made animations, M2 and M4 use three seeds per held-out family, the control models use two, and M1, M3 and M5 use one. The 24 human characters differ from the animals in more than the body plan, for example in proportions and clothing. Their motion was also recorded with motion capture, whereas the animal motion was made by artists. The human test therefore measures a change of body plan together with these differences. A small test on 43 clips from public-domain cartoons of 1914 to 1916, all checked by the author, gave no clear result. No method distinguished walking, running and falling better than chance, including a frozen ImageNet encoder and a motion baseline. We attribute this to the poor image quality and the small number of clips.

10 Conclusion

In the settings we test, a linear classifier still identifies the action class from the latent actions of unseen animal families and held-out synthetic body plans, but the transferred action closes only part of the prediction error gap on these bodies. On synthetic characters with six body plans and on animator-made animations of five animal families and humans, a baseline that only copies movement matches most learned models under a fixed camera. Body-centred transfer reaches at most 0.46 for a new animal family and at most 0.20 for humans, or 0.31 from seen bodies to humans when the best time shift is chosen with the target’s frames (Table 7). In our experiments, transfer is better when the action has fewer dimensions and holds less information about the source body. Neither a better objective nor allowing for differences in timing closes the gap to human targets, which differ from the animals in body plan, proportions, clothing and the way their motion was made. For this reason, transfer should be measured with a movement baseline and with a score that compares the correct action against wrong ones, rather than with the usual gain alone. Good transfer between similar bodies also did not carry over to bodies with a different structure. Future models could describe the target body separately from the transferred action, and testing whether this closes the gap is a natural next step.

item.title: 语言指令驱动的世界模型各说各话：Tiresias 先统一成「看一帧 + 一句指令 → 输出动作序列」这一件事 ｜ Tiresias: Towards Language-Conditioned World Models
item.description:
一句话：世界模型能做内部推演，语言是最好用的任务描述；但两边的动作空间、数据集与评测协议全都不通。

要点：

  • 价值主张：世界模型通过内部模拟支持规划，而自然语言是最直观的任务指定方式——两者本该结合
  • 现实是碎的：语言条件化的世界建模分散在各领域，动作空间、数据集与评测协议彼此不通
  • Tiresias 提出一个共享任务 LCWM：输入初始视角观测 + 一句语言指令，输出能完成该指令的动作序列

为什么值得看：把「语言 → 动作序列」定为统一任务，等于给语言条件世界模型一个可比的共同底座。对做 AI 驱动 NPC 或自然语言操控的团队，这个任务定义本身就是可用的接口形态。

中文摘要：世界模型能通过内部模拟来支持规划，自然语言则是最直观的任务指定方式，两者结合显然是方向；但现实是语言条件化的世界建模被切碎在各领域，动作空间、数据集与评测协议互不兼容。Tiresias 提出一个共享任务 LCWM：给定智能体的初始视角观测与一句语言指令，输出一段能完成该指令的动作序列。把任务收紧成这个形式，一方面让不同来源的方法可以在同一口径下比较，另一方面也给出了「语言操控世界模型」在接口层应该长什么样。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

Tiresias: Towards Language-Conditioned
World Models

Abstract

World models enable planning through internal simulation, while natural language provides intuitive task specification. Yet, language-conditioned world modeling remains fragmented across domains with disparate action spaces, datasets, and evaluation protocols. We introduce LCWM, a shared task that maps an initial agent-view observation and a language instruction to an action sequence that fulfills the instruction. Its accompanying benchmark, LCWM-Bench, integrates 15 datasets across navigation, robotics, 3D gaming, and driving under a shared action interface and evaluation protocol, pairing 142,987 episodes with 428,961 instructions in three styles. We further propose Tiresias, an agent that plans via selective imagination: a language-conditioned diffusion policy generates candidate trajectories, a trajectory ranker shortlists them, and a video-pretrained world model imagines their visual consequences. A visual ranker evaluates these rollouts, complementing trajectory scores to select the final plan. Tiresias achieves competitive planning and imagination performance on LCWM-Bench. 1 Introduction

“The blind seer, whose mind abides steadfast.”

    3 LCWM-Bench

    3.1 Task Formulation

    We formulate language-conditioned world modeling (LCWM) as follows. Given an initial agent-view RGB observation oₛ and a natural-language instruction I, an agent must predict an action sequence Â_T that fulfills the instruction. We denote the instruction and action sequence by:

    I=⟨w₁,…,wₙ⟩, Â_T=⟨â₁,…,â_T⟩.

    		(1)

    Each action âₜ is a control command with a base parameterization (uₜ,φₜ) shared across all domains, where uₜ∈ℝ² is a planar displacement covering forward, backward, and lateral motions, and φₜ∈ℝ is a yaw rotation. Actions are executed sequentially, with a null action signaling episode termination. The LCWM task spans four domains, D={Navigation,Robotics,3D Gaming,Driving}, which share the base parameterization but incorporate additional domain-specific control channels: 3D gaming adds a vertical displacement zₜ∈ℝ; driving introduces a scalar velocity vₜ∈ℝ; and robotics, controlling an end-effector, appends the vertical displacement zₜ alongside roll, pitch, and a gripper command (ρₜ,ϑₜ,gₜ). The raw controls from all sources are normalized into this shared parameterization (Sec. 3.2).

    3.2 Benchmark Construction

    Instantiating LCWM requires episodes sharing a shared action interface across diverse domains. We build LCWM-Bench in three stages (Fig. 2a).

    Dataset Collection. LCWM-Bench integrates 15 datasets across four domains, mixing real and simulated sources for scene diversity and metric actions (Fig. 2b). Navigation: GoStanford [(Hirose et al., 2018)], RECON [(Shah et al., 2021)], SCAND [(Karnan et al., 2022)], HuRoN [(Hirose et al., 2023)], and TartanDrive [(Triest et al., 2022)] cover indoor, outdoor, social, and off-road ground-robot traversal. Robotics: BridgeData V2 [(Walke et al., 2023)], DROID [(Khazatsky et al., 2024)], RT-1 [(Brohan et al., 2022)], and LIBERO [(Liu et al., 2023a)] provide 6-DoF gripper control across household and office scenes. 3D Gaming: Minecraft [(Lian et al., 2025)] contributes open worlds, while CS:GO [(Pearce and Zhu, 2022)] adds fast-paced human matches. Driving: nuScenes [(Caesar et al., 2020)], KITTI-360 [(Liao et al., 2022)], Waymo [(Sun et al., 2020)], and DrivingDojo [(Wang et al., 2024)] span urban to suburban traffic, representing the benchmark’s highest speeds.

    Shared Action and Observation Spaces. We standardize heterogeneous raw controls (e.g., wheel odometry, end-effector poses) via a shared pipeline. Episodes are converted into per-step motion increments in the local frame (x forward, y left, yaw counter-clockwise, z up), derived from consecutive pose differences when explicit actions are absent. Following [Dong et al. (2026b)], displacements are normalized by each source’s average step size to unify magnitudes. Agent-view frames are resized to 256×256. We then filter out backward, near-static, or overly short clips, segmenting the remainder into semantically coherent episodes following [Bar et al. (2025); Dong et al. (2026b)].

    Instruction Styles. We augment each episode with language instructions in three styles, probing grounding at varying depths: Concise (essential directional cues); Intricate (rich descriptions of objects, layouts, and motion); and Landmark-based (anchoring maneuvers to salient landmarks, e.g., “pass the parked van, then stop at the white door”). Instructions are generated via a coarse-to-fine pipeline. In the coarse stage, Qwen3.6-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026)] generates all three styles from sampled frames, supplemented by trajectory metadata and (for manipulation) native annotations. In the fine stage, these machine-generated instructions are manually verified against the videos for correctness and naturalness. Each episode yields one evaluation sample per style.

    Evaluation Protocol and Metrics. Each domain is partitioned at the source level into train, val seen (held-out episodes from training sources), val unseen (sources completely excluded from training), and test (a mixture of both for future leaderboards). For instance, in navigation, TartanDrive is reserved for val unseen to evaluate generalization against significant visual domain shifts. To assess goal completion and trajectory quality, we report four metrics: SR (Success Rate) requires the terminal position error to be within one average step [(Dong et al., 2026b)], plus a matching terminal gripper state for robotics; nDTW[(Ilharco et al., 2019)] measures path fidelity via order-preserving soft alignment; ATE and RPE[(Sturm et al., 2012)] compute the RMSE of absolute and relative position errors to capture global drift and local accuracy, respectively. The overall LCWM-Bench score is the macro-average of SR and nDTW across the four domains.

    3.3 Benchmark Statistics

    Fig. 2(b–d) summarizes LCWM-Bench. The benchmark comprises 142,987 episodes (≈4.4M frames) from 15 datasets (12 real, 3 simulated), which the three-style annotation expands into 428,961 evaluation samples, partitioned into training (300,276), val seen (38,607), val unseen (34,317), and test (55,761). Robotics contributes the largest share of samples (40%), followed by navigation (29%), gaming (21%), and driving (10%), and the split proportions are preserved within every domain. The domains complement one another in temporal structure (Fig. 2c): robotics episodes are the longest (43.1 steps on average) while navigation ones are the shortest (17.6), and the three instruction styles occupy separated verbosity bands in every domain (Fig. 2d), from 14–23 words for Concise to 57–73 for Intricate.

    4 Tiresias: Planning with a Language-Conditioned World Model

    We propose Tiresias to solve LCWM through selective imagination, combining language-guided trajectory proposals with scene-conditioned evaluation of their imagined consequences (Fig. 3). A language-conditioned diffusion policy (LDP) proposes trajectories, and a trajectory ranker (Tr-Ranker) shortlists them using language and motion alone. A language-conditioned world model imagines the retained candidates, whose rollouts are scored by a visual ranker (V-Ranker). The two ranker scores are fused to select the final plan.

    4.1 Language-Conditioned Diffusion Policy

    The LDP (Fig. 3a) is a DiT-based [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)] diffusion policy [(Chi et al., 2025)] that denoises action sequences under language guidance. Aside from diffusion timestep, conditioning is derived entirely from language, utilizing frozen umT5 [(Chung et al., 2023)] instruction embeddings processed via multi-head cross-attention within every DiT block. Trained to denoise expert trajectories, the LDP learns the distribution of motions corresponding to an instruction, allowing independent noise seeds at inference to yield diverse candidates for subsequent trajectory ranking and visual verification. By design, the LDP is scene-agnostic: its samples span language-permitted possibilities, leaving scene-dependent selection to the world model.

    4.2 Language-Conditioned World Model

    The language-conditioned world model of Tiresias (Fig. 3b) is a multimodal diffusion Transformer that adapts the pretrained Wan2.2 video backbone [(Wan et al., 2025)] to predict futures under trajectory, scene, and language conditions while preserving its native interfaces. Video frames follow the backbone’s original visual pathway, encoded by the frozen VAE [(Wan et al., 2025)], noised, and denoised as video tokens. Two conditioning routes steer this denoising process. First, the candidate trajectory, embedded via a lightweight MLP, directly conditions the denoiser to dictate embodiment motion. Second, cross-attention concatenates the initial frame’s DINOv3 [(Siméoni et al., 2025)] features with the umT5 instruction embedding and a per-domain prompt, supplying critical context: scene content, intended behavior, and embodiment specifics. Formally:

    X̂=(x̂₁,…,x̂_H)∼p_θ(·|xₛ, [fₛ; e_I], Â),

    		(2)

    where X̂ denotes imagined video latents over horizon H; xₛ and fₛ are the VAE latent and DINOv3 features of initial observation oₛ; e_I is the prompted umT5 instruction embedding; and Â is the conditioning trajectory.

    The initial frame thus enters twice: its VAE latent anchors visual appearance, while its DINOv3 features supply high-level semantics often lacking in generative latents, complementing the backbone’s motion and scene priors. Training optimizes the flow-matching objective:

    L(θ)=𝔼_X, c, ε, τ ∥u_θ(X_τ,τ,c)-(ε-X)∥₂²,

    		(3)

    where X denotes the VAE latents of the ground-truth future frames, X_τ=(1-τ)X+τε represents their interpolation toward Gaussian noise ε at flow time τ, u_θ is the denoiser predicting velocity ε-X, and c encapsulates the conditions in Eq. (2).

    4.3 Trajectory and Visual Rankers

    The Tr-Ranker scores each candidate Â⁽ᵐ⁾ using language and motion alone: action tokens query instruction tokens via cross-attention, a temporal Transformer summarizes the trajectory, and four heads estimate SR, nDTW, ATE, and RPE. These predictions are combined into a score S⁽ᵐ⁾ₜᵣ. The V-Ranker evaluates the candidate’s imagined visual consequences. Conditioning Eq. (2) on Â=Â⁽ᵐ⁾ yields video latents X̂⁽ᵐ⁾, which are pooled over horizon H and aligned with instruction embedding e_I to produce S⁽ᵐ⁾ᵥ. The two scores provide motion and visual evidence for selecting instruction-consistent trajectories. Due to space limits, kindly refer to Appendix for additional details.

    4.4 Inference with Selective Imagination

    At inference (Fig. 3c), the independently trained modules are composed into a two-stage selection pipeline without joint fine-tuning. The LDP first samples a diverse pool of stage-one candidates {Â⁽ᵐ⁾}ₘ₌₁^N using independent noise seeds. The Tr-Ranker then filters this pool into a stage-two shortlist S of size k prior to any simulation. Only these retained candidates are subsequently rolled out by the world model and evaluated by V-Ranker. Tiresias ultimately executes:

    Â^∗=Â^(m^∗), m^∗=\arg\max_m∈S λₜᵣ S⁽ᵐ⁾ₜᵣ+λᵥ S⁽ᵐ⁾ᵥ,

    		(4)

    where λₜᵣ and λᵥ weight the two scores, which are normalized within S prior to fusion.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Baselines. We first include two policy-only baselines, GNM [(Shah et al., 2022)] (lang) and NoMaD [(Sridhar et al., 2024)] (lang), which replace the image-goal encoder with a frozen CLIP text encoder projecting instructions into the goal-token space. The remaining baselines all leverage world models: Diamond [(Alonso et al., 2024)] (UNet-based diffusion), NWM [(Bar et al., 2025)] (CDiT-based diffusion), NWM (lang) which integrates CLIP-encoded instructions via the CDiT AdaLN block, and LCVN-WM [(Dong et al., 2026b)]. Each of these world models is paired with the latent actor-critic LCVN-AC to produce actions. We additionally include LCVN-Uni [(Dong et al., 2026b)], an autoregressive unified model that predicts observations and actions jointly. All baselines are trained on LCWM-Bench and evaluated under the shared protocol. Finally, Tiresias (MPC) replaces the LDP with sampling-based MPC for candidate generation while retaining two-stage ranking, thereby isolating contribution of learned language-conditioned proposal distribution.

    Evaluation Metrics. Planning is evaluated using the LCWM-Bench metrics detailed in Sec. 3: SR, nDTW, ATE, RPE, and the overall score. We also assess world-model imagination quality: @1 metrics compare the predicted next frame against the ground truth, while @n metrics evaluate n-step open-loop generation conditioned on ground-truth actions. Specifically, we adopt SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)], and DreamSim [(Fu et al., 2023)] for @1 and @10 evaluations, alongside FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)] at @32.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：世界模型能做内部推演，语言是最好用的任务描述；但两边的动作空间、数据集与评测协议全都不通。

要点：

  • 价值主张：世界模型通过内部模拟支持规划，而自然语言是最直观的任务指定方式——两者本该结合
  • 现实是碎的：语言条件化的世界建模分散在各领域，动作空间、数据集与评测协议彼此不通
  • Tiresias 提出一个共享任务 LCWM：输入初始视角观测 + 一句语言指令，输出能完成该指令的动作序列

为什么值得看：把「语言 → 动作序列」定为统一任务，等于给语言条件世界模型一个可比的共同底座。对做 AI 驱动 NPC 或自然语言操控的团队，这个任务定义本身就是可用的接口形态。

中文摘要：世界模型能通过内部模拟来支持规划，自然语言则是最直观的任务指定方式，两者结合显然是方向；但现实是语言条件化的世界建模被切碎在各领域，动作空间、数据集与评测协议互不兼容。Tiresias 提出一个共享任务 LCWM：给定智能体的初始视角观测与一句语言指令，输出一段能完成该指令的动作序列。把任务收紧成这个形式，一方面让不同来源的方法可以在同一口径下比较，另一方面也给出了「语言操控世界模型」在接口层应该长什么样。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

Tiresias: Towards Language-Conditioned
World Models

Abstract

World models enable planning through internal simulation, while natural language provides intuitive task specification. Yet, language-conditioned world modeling remains fragmented across domains with disparate action spaces, datasets, and evaluation protocols. We introduce LCWM, a shared task that maps an initial agent-view observation and a language instruction to an action sequence that fulfills the instruction. Its accompanying benchmark, LCWM-Bench, integrates 15 datasets across navigation, robotics, 3D gaming, and driving under a shared action interface and evaluation protocol, pairing 142,987 episodes with 428,961 instructions in three styles. We further propose Tiresias, an agent that plans via selective imagination: a language-conditioned diffusion policy generates candidate trajectories, a trajectory ranker shortlists them, and a video-pretrained world model imagines their visual consequences. A visual ranker evaluates these rollouts, complementing trajectory scores to select the final plan. Tiresias achieves competitive planning and imagination performance on LCWM-Bench. Ablations demonstrate the complementary benefits of trajectory ranking and visual verification, while experiments with alternative proposal methods show that the trained rankers remain effective beyond our diffusion policy. Together, LCWM-Bench and Tiresias provide a unified evaluation setting and an effective starting point for studying language-guided planning through world models.

Following [Dong et al. (2026b)], displacements are normalized by each source’s average step size to unify magnitudes. Agent-view frames are resized to 256×256. We then filter out backward, near-static, or overly short clips, segmenting the remainder into semantically coherent episodes following [Bar et al. (2025); Dong et al. (2026b)].

    Instruction Styles. We augment each episode with language instructions in three styles, probing grounding at varying depths: Concise (essential directional cues); Intricate (rich descriptions of objects, layouts, and motion); and Landmark-based (anchoring maneuvers to salient landmarks, e.g., “pass the parked van, then stop at the white door”). Instructions are generated via a coarse-to-fine pipeline. In the coarse stage, Qwen3.6-27B [(Qwen Team, 2026)] generates all three styles from sampled frames, supplemented by trajectory metadata and (for manipulation) native annotations. In the fine stage, these machine-generated instructions are manually verified against the videos for correctness and naturalness. Each episode yields one evaluation sample per style.

    Evaluation Protocol and Metrics. Each domain is partitioned at the source level into train, val seen (held-out episodes from training sources), val unseen (sources completely excluded from training), and test (a mixture of both for future leaderboards). For instance, in navigation, TartanDrive is reserved for val unseen to evaluate generalization against significant visual domain shifts. To assess goal completion and trajectory quality, we report four metrics: SR (Success Rate) requires the terminal position error to be within one average step [(Dong et al., 2026b)], plus a matching terminal gripper state for robotics; nDTW[(Ilharco et al., 2019)] measures path fidelity via order-preserving soft alignment; ATE and RPE[(Sturm et al., 2012)] compute the RMSE of absolute and relative position errors to capture global drift and local accuracy, respectively. The overall LCWM-Bench score is the macro-average of SR and nDTW across the four domains.

    3.3 Benchmark Statistics

    Fig. 2(b–d) summarizes LCWM-Bench. The benchmark comprises 142,987 episodes (≈4.4M frames) from 15 datasets (12 real, 3 simulated), which the three-style annotation expands into 428,961 evaluation samples, partitioned into training (300,276), val seen (38,607), val unseen (34,317), and test (55,761). Robotics contributes the largest share of samples (40%), followed by navigation (29%), gaming (21%), and driving (10%), and the split proportions are preserved within every domain. The domains complement one another in temporal structure (Fig. 2c): robotics episodes are the longest (43.1 steps on average) while navigation ones are the shortest (17.6), and the three instruction styles occupy separated verbosity bands in every domain (Fig. 2d), from 14–23 words for Concise to 57–73 for Intricate.

    4 Tiresias: Planning with a Language-Conditioned World Model

    We propose Tiresias to solve LCWM through selective imagination, combining language-guided trajectory proposals with scene-conditioned evaluation of their imagined consequences (Fig. 3). A language-conditioned diffusion policy (LDP) proposes trajectories, and a trajectory ranker (Tr-Ranker) shortlists them using language and motion alone. A language-conditioned world model imagines the retained candidates, whose rollouts are scored by a visual ranker (V-Ranker). The two ranker scores are fused to select the final plan.

    4.1 Language-Conditioned Diffusion Policy

    The LDP (Fig. 3a) is a DiT-based [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)] diffusion policy [(Chi et al., 2025)] that denoises action sequences under language guidance. Aside from diffusion timestep, conditioning is derived entirely from language, utilizing frozen umT5 [(Chung et al., 2023)] instruction embeddings processed via multi-head cross-attention within every DiT block. Trained to denoise expert trajectories, the LDP learns the distribution of motions corresponding to an instruction, allowing independent noise seeds at inference to yield diverse candidates for subsequent trajectory ranking and visual verification. By design, the LDP is scene-agnostic: its samples span language-permitted possibilities, leaving scene-dependent selection to the world model.

    4.2 Language-Conditioned World Model

    The language-conditioned world model of Tiresias (Fig. 3b) is a multimodal diffusion Transformer that adapts the pretrained Wan2.2 video backbone [(Wan et al., 2025)] to predict futures under trajectory, scene, and language conditions while preserving its native interfaces. Video frames follow the backbone’s original visual pathway, encoded by the frozen VAE [(Wan et al., 2025)], noised, and denoised as video tokens. Two conditioning routes steer this denoising process. First, the candidate trajectory, embedded via a lightweight MLP, directly conditions the denoiser to dictate embodiment motion. Second, cross-attention concatenates the initial frame’s DINOv3 [(Siméoni et al., 2025)] features with the umT5 instruction embedding and a per-domain prompt, supplying critical context: scene content, intended behavior, and embodiment specifics. Formally:

    X̂=(x̂₁,…,x̂_H)∼p_θ(·|xₛ, [fₛ; e_I], Â),

    		(2)

    where X̂ denotes imagined video latents over horizon H; xₛ and fₛ are the VAE latent and DINOv3 features of initial observation oₛ; e_I is the prompted umT5 instruction embedding; and Â is the conditioning trajectory.

    The initial frame thus enters twice: its VAE latent anchors visual appearance, while its DINOv3 features supply high-level semantics often lacking in generative latents, complementing the backbone’s motion and scene priors. Training optimizes the flow-matching objective:

    L(θ)=𝔼_X, c, ε, τ ∥u_θ(X_τ,τ,c)-(ε-X)∥₂²,

    		(3)

    where X denotes the VAE latents of the ground-truth future frames, X_τ=(1-τ)X+τε represents their interpolation toward Gaussian noise ε at flow time τ, u_θ is the denoiser predicting velocity ε-X, and c encapsulates the conditions in Eq. (2).

    4.3 Trajectory and Visual Rankers

    The Tr-Ranker scores each candidate Â⁽ᵐ⁾ using language and motion alone: action tokens query instruction tokens via cross-attention, a temporal Transformer summarizes the trajectory, and four heads estimate SR, nDTW, ATE, and RPE. These predictions are combined into a score S⁽ᵐ⁾ₜᵣ. The V-Ranker evaluates the candidate’s imagined visual consequences. Conditioning Eq. (2) on Â=Â⁽ᵐ⁾ yields video latents X̂⁽ᵐ⁾, which are pooled over horizon H and aligned with instruction embedding e_I to produce S⁽ᵐ⁾ᵥ. The two scores provide motion and visual evidence for selecting instruction-consistent trajectories. Due to space limits, kindly refer to Appendix for additional details.

    4.4 Inference with Selective Imagination

    At inference (Fig. 3c), the independently trained modules are composed into a two-stage selection pipeline without joint fine-tuning. The LDP first samples a diverse pool of stage-one candidates {Â⁽ᵐ⁾}ₘ₌₁^N using independent noise seeds. The Tr-Ranker then filters this pool into a stage-two shortlist S of size k prior to any simulation. Only these retained candidates are subsequently rolled out by the world model and evaluated by V-Ranker. Tiresias ultimately executes:

    Â^∗=Â^(m^∗), m^∗=\arg\max_m∈S λₜᵣ S⁽ᵐ⁾ₜᵣ+λᵥ S⁽ᵐ⁾ᵥ,

    		(4)

    where λₜᵣ and λᵥ weight the two scores, which are normalized within S prior to fusion.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Baselines. We first include two policy-only baselines, GNM [(Shah et al., 2022)] (lang) and NoMaD [(Sridhar et al., 2024)] (lang), which replace the image-goal encoder with a frozen CLIP text encoder projecting instructions into the goal-token space. The remaining baselines all leverage world models: Diamond [(Alonso et al., 2024)] (UNet-based diffusion), NWM [(Bar et al., 2025)] (CDiT-based diffusion), NWM (lang) which integrates CLIP-encoded instructions via the CDiT AdaLN block, and LCVN-WM [(Dong et al., 2026b)]. Each of these world models is paired with the latent actor-critic LCVN-AC to produce actions. We additionally include LCVN-Uni [(Dong et al., 2026b)], an autoregressive unified model that predicts observations and actions jointly. All baselines are trained on LCWM-Bench and evaluated under the shared protocol. Finally, Tiresias (MPC) replaces the LDP with sampling-based MPC for candidate generation while retaining two-stage ranking, thereby isolating contribution of learned language-conditioned proposal distribution.

    Evaluation Metrics. Planning is evaluated using the LCWM-Bench metrics detailed in Sec. 3: SR, nDTW, ATE, RPE, and the overall score. We also assess world-model imagination quality: @1 metrics compare the predicted next frame against the ground truth, while @n metrics evaluate n-step open-loop generation conditioned on ground-truth actions. Specifically, we adopt SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)], and DreamSim [(Fu et al., 2023)] for @1 and @10 evaluations, alongside FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)] at @32.

item.title: 视频条件的世界模型到底有没有「探索」能力：WanderBench 从真实录像出发查它会不会跑偏 ｜ WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?
item.description:
一句话：现有基准从单图或文本起步、只按单帧打分，测不出「滚动展开是否还忠实于录到的世界」。

要点：

  • 用途侧很具体：以输入视频为条件的视频世界模型，能让人探索真实录制的动态场景——重拍素材、自由视角回放、为具身智能体造 real-to-sim 环境
  • 这些用途的关键要求是：生成的 rollout 必须**忠实于被录制的世界**
  • 但现有基准要么从单张图像、要么从文本提示起步，而视频条件的生成主要按逐帧指标评——测不出「一路探索下去是否还忠于原世界」

为什么值得看：「能生成」与「能忠实探索」是两件事。评测口径不指向前者，工程上就只能靠肉眼看。WanderBench 把视频作为起点与判据，直接对准 real-to-sim 与重拍这两类实际用途。

中文摘要：以视频为条件的视频世界模型，让人可以探索真实录制过的动态场景：重拍素材、自由视角回放，或为具身智能体构建 real-to-sim 环境。这些用途的共同前提是，生成的 rollout 必须忠实于被录制的那个世界。但现有基准的起点是单张图像或文本提示，而视频条件生成又主要用逐帧指标衡量，因此「一路探索下去是否还忠于原世界」无法被检验。WanderBench 因此把视频同时当作起点与判据，评测世界模型在动态场景中被推着往外探索时的保真度。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?

Abstract

Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3–25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in video generation have steadily improved visual quality, motion realism, and temporal coherence, and the scope of the field has broadened beyond producing fixed-length clips to interactive world models, in which users continuously issue camera or action controls during generation to explore an unfolding visual world [20, 17, 40, 47, 49, 8, 14, 57]. Such models offer new tools for game creation [22, 48, 5, 36, 2, 68, 14, 57], virtual production [38, 50, 35, 34, 53], and robot policy learning [59, 62, 73]. However, most world models start from a single image or a text prompt, so the scene dynamics they produce are entirely imagined by the model and do not correspond to events that actually took place.

Video-conditioned world models open up a new possibility: given a real recorded video of a dynamic scene, users can re-observe the scenes and events it captures along new camera trajectories [52, 60, 44]. This capability directly supports re-framing real footage and free-viewpoint replay, and offers a way to build simulation environments for embodied agents from real videos. Unlike exploration from a single image, these applications impose stricter requirements on the generated results: the model must not only synthesize plausible novel views but also remain faithful to the world recorded in the source video [1, 65].

Despite these advances, it remains unclear whether current models can faithfully explore the dynamic world captured in a source video. Existing benchmarks evaluate visual quality [18, 69], interactive control [58, 64, 27], and world consistency [61, 63], including memory across revisits [12, 71]. However, success on these dimensions does not necessarily imply fidelity to the recorded event. A model may generate realistic views and follow the requested camera trajectory while altering the source action or its timing. It may also produce seemingly consistent revisits by retaining an outdated state of a dynamic subject. This leaves a central question: can models use the source video as evidence of an evolving world, preserving its events under viewpoint changes, integrating information across frames, and maintaining scene consistency during revisits while respecting the event’s temporal progression?

To address this gap, we introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for evaluating video-conditioned world exploration. Each test case pairs a single-shot source video of a dynamic scene with a camera route specified by discrete keyboard actions, which determines how the events in the source video should be observed from changing viewpoints. WanderBench contains 745 source videos spanning real-world footage such as dance, film, and natural scenes, together with AI-generated videos in realistic, anime, and artistic styles, organized into three difficulty tiers from 3 to 25 seconds. We provide random exploration and out-and-back camera routes to examine continuous viewpoint changes and revisits to previously observed regions, respectively. The evaluation comprises 24 sub-metrics across six complementary dimensions. By incorporating source-video references, event timing, and visibility, WanderBench assesses whether stable scene structure and subject identities are preserved and whether dynamic content evolves in accordance with the source event, providing a systematic evaluation of faithful reproduction and sustained exploration of dynamic worlds under camera control.

Benchmarking eight video-conditioned world models on WanderBench reveals two consistent failure modes. First, as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and their visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics: the output drifts from the commanded view and falls out of sync with the source events. Second, no model remembers what it has generated, so a revisited place is redrawn and changes appearance. Models limited to a few seconds of generation cannot even reach the longer tiers.

Beyond evaluation, we introduce WanderLand, a training-free inference-time framework for video-conditioned world exploration. WanderLand aims to preserve source-world identity and event progression while maintaining consistency throughout camera-controlled exploration and revisits. To this end, we develop an evidence-ordered conditioning scheme that rebuilds only the camera and source render a model already reads: every frame is anchored to the source camera of the same instant and rendered from the same-instant source frame, and on revisits, the regions the source cannot cover are filled with the static content the model itself generated earlier. It operates on pretrained video world models without updating their parameters, using only each model’s own geometry. We evaluate WanderLand on WanderBench across five video world models, demonstrating consistent gains across all six dimensions, with the largest improvements in source-dynamics fidelity (up to +8.3) and dynamic revisit consistency (up to +4.8), the two dimensions targeted by the failure modes above.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for world exploration from dynamic video inputs. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos organized into three difficulty tiers, with random camera exploration and long-horizon out-and-back revisit tasks across all tiers, providing a unified setting for evaluating exploration of source-video worlds from novel viewpoints.

  • •

    We establish an evaluation framework comprising six complementary dimensions and 24 sub-metrics. By incorporating source-video references, event timing, and visibility, it systematically assesses stable properties that should persist and dynamic content that should evolve with the source event. Benchmarking eight models with it, we identify loss of camera control and source dynamics over long horizons, and inconsistent revisits, as shared failure modes.

  • •

    We propose WanderLand, a training-free framework for enhancing existing video world models. Built upon these models, WanderLand uses evidence-ordered conditioning, which draws on the same-instant source and the model’s own earlier static content, to improve source-content preservation and dynamic-event reproduction. We evaluate it on WanderBench across five applicable models and observe gains on all six dimensions, most notably in source-dynamics fidelity and dynamic revisit consistency.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video World model

    Early world models explored robotic manipulation and autonomous driving, including UniSim [62], IRASim [73], GAIA-1 [15], and Vista [10]. With advances in video generation, world models can continuously generate subsequent frames from visual observations and user actions, enabling interactive exploration of generated environments. YUME [35, 34] introduces natural language into world event control, while HY-World [51] and LingBot-World [39] explore world generation that combines real-time interaction with long-term consistency. Hunyuan-GameCraft [22] and Matrix-Game [68, 14, 57] support keyboard-and-mouse-driven interactive generation. AlayaWorld [49] further supports sustained world exploration through compressed temporal history and geometrically aligned spatial memory.

    Further work uses source videos as references for scene appearance and dynamic content, allowing users to re-observe the events they contain along new camera trajectories. ReCamMaster [1] jointly conditions on a source video and a target camera trajectory to generate novel views while preserving the source video’s appearance consistency and dynamic synchronization. WorldForge [45, 46] improves trajectory-controlled video generation through reference-fusion correction and denoising guidance. InSpatio-World [52] supports spatiotemporal exploration through world states anchored to a reference video; Wonder [60] jointly designs visual camera control, sparse memory, and distillation strategies to support real-time world generation conditioned on images and videos; and World in World [44] converts source observations, target-view projections, and historical information into unified visual evidence, enabling training-free control through the pretrained model’s native self-attention. WanderBench addresses these requirements by systematically evaluating video world models’ ability to controllably explore dynamic worlds from source videos. Models must not only generate plausible novel views but also preserve the scene and subject identities in the source video, maintain the temporal progression of the original event, and remain consistent with the current event state when revisiting previously observed regions.

    2.2 World Models Evaluation

    Existing benchmarks broadly fall into two categories: non-interactive video evaluation and world model evaluation. VBench [18, 69, 19], EvalCrafter [29], and VideoPhy [3, 4] do not support action inputs or interaction, focusing primarily on video quality, text alignment, or physical commonsense. In contrast, WorldScore [7] evaluates camera-trajectory-conditioned generation, WorldModelBench [21] studies decision-oriented world-model quality, WorldArena [42] targets embodied agents in closed domains, MIND [63] probes closed-loop memory consistency, Omni-WorldBench [58] focuses on causal interaction, WorldLens [26] targets autonomous driving, and WorldMark [61] measures navigation consistency. WBench further introduces a multi-turn evaluation framework for open-domain interactive world models and R2M-Bench [12] evaluates consistency during long-horizon revisits in interactive video world models. Other efforts examine complementary aspects [13, 30, 11, 6, 55, 31, 37, 66, 67, 48, 72].

    These studies provide a foundation for evaluating generation quality, interactive control, and world consistency. However, in video-conditioned settings, evaluation must also determine whether the generated results remain faithful to the dynamic world recorded in the source video: models should preserve scene and subject identities while reproducing the actions and temporal progression of the original event. WanderBench addresses this problem by incorporating source-video references, event timing, and visibility into 24 sub-metrics across six complementary dimensions, systematically evaluating source-world fidelity, source-dynamics fidelity, and consistency during exploration and revisits under camera control.

    3 WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?

    Data Composition. WanderBench comprises 745 source videos, each a single continuous shot whose camera remains static or near-static, so that C(t)=I denotes the original view. 329 are real-world or rendered videos collected from the Internet (Bilibili and YouTube), covering dance, film, daily life, stage performances, and other scenes; 116 are drawn from existing video datasets [16, 24, 41]; and the remaining 300 are generated with MiniMax, spanning 13 realistic looks, 12 anime looks, and 48 artistic.

    Clip Screening. Candidate clips are screened in two stages. (1) Shot proposal. For Internet videos, static shots are automatically proposed by following Shi–Tomasi [43] corners with a pyramidal Lucas–Kanade [32] optical flow at 10 fps and fitting a RANSAC [9] similarity transform. (2) Camera and dynamics verification. For each candidate, we reconstruct the camera trajectory with VGGT [56], cross-checked with MegaSaM [25], and discard clips with noticeable camera rotation or translation. We further check scene dynamics with RAFT [54] optical flow.

    Difficulty Tiers. WanderBench is organized into three tiers of increasing difficulty: (1) Simple (451 clips) contains short clips with slow, mild subject motion; (2) Medium (157 clips) features longer clips with higher visual quality and richer lighting variation; and (3) Hard (137 clips) contains the longest clips, with the highest visual quality, large-amplitude subject motion, substantial background changes, and complex illumination. Across the benchmark, camera-compensated motion extends from a median of 0.029 to 0.12 image diagonals, and MUSIQ imaging quality spans from 22.9 to 74.8. To verify the single-shot filtering, four annotators independently labeled all 2,142 candidate clips as single-shot or not. The annotators agree with each other at Fleiss’ κ=0.93, yielding the final 745 clips.

    3.1 Evaluation Suite

    WanderBench decomposes evaluation into six complementary dimensions comprising 24 sub-metrics, detailed in the Appendix. Most of our metrics compare the output with a time-synchronized source reference: each output frame G(t) and the source frame S(τ(t)) depict the same instant from two viewpoints, so every frame has a reference without any temporal annotation. All sub-metric scores are rescaled to [0,100].

    • Visual Quality. We adopt [dQual]V.1 Aesthetic Quality, [dQual]V.2 Imaging Quality, [dQual]V.3 Temporal Flickering, and [dQual]V.4 Motion Smoothness from VBench [18], together with [dQual]V.5 HPSv3 Preference [33] and [dQual]V.6 Visual Plausibility scored by the PAVRM model of WBench [64]. Since the task is to re-render an input video, all scores are normalized by those of the source video.

    • Camera Control. [dCam]C.1 Synchronized Camera Following reconstructs the source and generated videos separately with VGGT [56] and compares the realized camera motion with the commanded one at one-second intervals.

    • Source-World Fidelity. [dWorld]W.1 Scene Adherence and [dWorld]W.2 Subject Adherence use a VLM and source subject tracks, respectively, to check whether the scene facts and subjects of the source are preserved. [dWorld]W.3 Synchronized View Fidelity reprojects the source frame of the same instant into the realized view and compares it with the output on co-visible regions.

    • Source-Dynamics Fidelity. [dDyn]D.1 Motion Timeline Agreement compares the camera-compensated motion curves of each subject between the source and the output. [dDyn]D.2 Event Adherence localizes the source events in the output. [dDyn]D.3 Temporal Synchronization finds the best-matching source time for each output frame and measures the proportion that falls within a tolerance of the correct time.

    • Spatiotemporal Consistency. [dCons]S.1 Subject Consistency and [dCons]S.2 Background Consistency penalize only the drift of subjects and static regions beyond the changes in the source. [dCons]S.3 Segment Continuity penalizes hard cuts absent from the source. [dCons]S.4 Static Geometric Consistency measures the reprojection consistency of static regions with Depth Anything 3 [28].

    • Dynamic Revisit Consistency. [dRev]R.1–[dRev]R.5 are based on DreamSim similarity (R.1), its pose-gated variant (R.2), place descriptors (R.3), geometric correspondence (R.4), and object appearance (R.5), respectively. [dRev]R.6 Object Semantic Persistence checks the objects that should appear in the source at the return time. [dRev]R.7 Revisit Event Currency measures whether the returning view shows the current state of a dynamic subject.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Evaluated Models and Protocol

    We evaluate eight video-conditioned world models that take a source video and a target camera trajectory, divided into two groups by generation length: (1) full-length models, which render the whole clip in one pass, including InSpatio-World 1.5 [52], World-in-World [44], and WorldForge v2 [46]; and (2) frame-limited models, which produce at most 81 frames (49 for TrajectoryCrafter), including ReCamMaster [1], CameraAnything [23], UniWorld-View [70], WorldForge v1 [45], and TrajectoryCrafter [65]. All models receive the same source video and the same action sequence. Each action sequence is converted into per-frame camera poses relative to the source camera and passed through the model’s native conditioning interface at its native resolution and frame rate; models with a different frame rate receive the same actions resampled to their own time grid. Frame-limited models process only the opening segment of each clip up to their maximum length (81 frames, or 49 for TrajectoryCrafter), conditioned on the corresponding prefix of the full trajectory, and are scored on that segment only. For scoring, (1) all metrics operate on a time grid in seconds; (2) scores are averaged over items, videos, and then models; and (3) a dimension score is the mean of its sub-metrics, and the overall score is the equal-weight mean of the six dimensions.

    4.2 Findings

    (1) Visual quality hides exploration failures. From Simple to Hard, the three full-length models lose little in Visual Quality and Spatiotemporal Consistency. Over the same range, they lose much more in Camera Control, Source-Dynamics Fidelity, and Dynamic Revisit Consistency. A rollout can therefore look clean and stable while following neither the command nor the source events, which per-frame quality metrics alone would not reveal.

    (2) Models keep the static world but lose the dynamic one. Source-World Fidelity is the highest-scoring dimension on every tier, so scenes and subjects are largely preserved. Source-Dynamics Fidelity, in contrast, falls to 37.2 on Hard, meaning the models keep what is in the scene but not when things happen in it.

    (3) Visual quality and camera control trade off. Across the eight models on Simple, Visual Quality and Camera Control are negatively correlated. WorldForge has the highest Visual Quality but only 44.8 in Camera Control, while UniWorld-View has the best Camera Control and the lowest Visual Quality. Faithfully executing a camera move appears to cost image quality in current models, and ranking them by quality alone favors models that move the camera less.
