    (4) Short horizons hide the differences that long horizons reveal. On Simple, the frame-limited UniWorld-View obtains the highest overall score, and the overall scores of the full-length models span only 4.3 points. On Hard, this span widens to 13.5 points, and WorldForge collapses to 10.4 in Camera Control. Their strong short-horizon scores do not show whether they can explore.

    (5) Model hardly remembers what it has generated. Dynamic Revisit Consistency is the weakest dimension overall: no model exceeds 68.6, the full-length models stay between 50.0 and 54.5 even on Simple, and WorldForge drops to 20.5 on Hard. Across models, Dynamic Revisit Consistency correlates with Camera Control, which suggests that a model must first reach the revisit pose before consistency there can be achieved.

    5 WanderLand: A Training-Free Enhancement of Exploration in Video World Models

    To explore how source-video evidence can help address the failure modes identified by WanderBench, we introduce WanderLand, a training-free enhancement for existing video world models. WanderLand constructs conditioning inputs by prioritizing time-aligned source observations and using previously generated static content to fill regions not covered by the source.

    5.1 Methods

    For each output frame, WanderLand takes evidence in a fixed order, in three steps.

    (1) Synchronized camera. The model’s own geometry front-end estimates the depth and camera of every source frame, and the commanded camera is then placed relative to the source camera of the same instant rather than to that of the first frame.

    (2) Same-instant source. The model’s own point-cloud renderer warps the source frame of the same instant into this camera. As a result, the render covers more of the view, and moving subjects appear at the correct time.

    (3) Static memory. When the camera returns to a place shown earlier, we lift the model’s nearest earlier outputs to 3D points using Depth Anything 3 [28] depth aligned to the render depth, and use them to fill the regions the source video cannot cover. Pixels whose source content changes over time, measured by a camera-compensated color difference, are discarded. Moving subjects are therefore never frozen, and all visible motion still comes from the source video.

    5.2 Properties

    WanderLand requires no training and introduces no additional weights. It relies only on the model’s own geometry module and renderer and never uses WanderBench’s evaluation tools. Wherever the evidence does not change, it reproduces the original output exactly, and its only extra cost is one additional generation when the camera revisits a place.

    5.3 WanderLand Results

    We apply WanderLand to five video world models and report the change on each dimension in Tab. 3. World-in-World and WorldForge are not included, since both are themselves training-free frameworks built on pretrained world models and do not expose the inputs that WanderLand rebuilds.

    (1) Consistent gains without trade-offs. WanderLand improves most backbone on every dimension and degrades none, so the better conditioning comes at no cost to visual quality or camera control.

    (2) Revisits benefit on every model. Dynamic Revisit Consistency rises by 2.4–4.8 points across all five backbones, as the holes at a revisit are filled with content the model has already shown instead of being redrawn.

    (3) Long horizons benefit the most. The largest single gain is on the full-length InSpatio-World 1.5, whose Source-Dynamics Fidelity rises by 8.3 points: over long rollouts, anchoring every frame to the source at the same instant keeps the generated events in sync with the recorded ones.

    6 Discussion

    WanderBench moves video world model evaluation from a single view to time-aligned multiple views: each explored trajectory is a new view of the same dynamic scene, synchronized with the source. We expect models that do well here to produce time-aligned multi-view videos from a single input, which could enable end-to-end generation of full-scene 4D Gaussian Splatting from one video. Current models still fall short on temporal synchronization and long-range revisits, and we hope WanderBench offers a concrete target for closing this gap.

    7 Conclusion

    We introduced WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video, with 745 single-shot source videos in three difficulty tiers and 24 sub-metrics over six dimensions. Current world models preserve static scenes and visual quality but lose camera control, source dynamics, and revisit consistency over longer horizons. Our training-free WanderLand improves five models by conditioning each frame on the same-instant source and the model’s own earlier content, though it requires camera and source-render inputs. We hope WanderBench drives world models that stay faithful to the recorded world as they explore it.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：现有基准从单图或文本起步、只按单帧打分，测不出「滚动展开是否还忠实于录到的世界」。

要点：

  • 用途侧很具体：以输入视频为条件的视频世界模型，能让人探索真实录制的动态场景——重拍素材、自由视角回放、为具身智能体造 real-to-sim 环境
  • 这些用途的关键要求是：生成的 rollout 必须**忠实于被录制的世界**
  • 但现有基准要么从单张图像、要么从文本提示起步，而视频条件的生成主要按逐帧指标评——测不出「一路探索下去是否还忠于原世界」

为什么值得看：「能生成」与「能忠实探索」是两件事。评测口径不指向前者，工程上就只能靠肉眼看。WanderBench 把视频作为起点与判据，直接对准 real-to-sim 与重拍这两类实际用途。

中文摘要：以视频为条件的视频世界模型，让人可以探索真实录制过的动态场景：重拍素材、自由视角回放，或为具身智能体构建 real-to-sim 环境。这些用途的共同前提是，生成的 rollout 必须忠实于被录制的那个世界。但现有基准的起点是单张图像或文本提示，而视频条件生成又主要用逐帧指标衡量，因此「一路探索下去是否还忠于原世界」无法被检验。WanderBench 因此把视频同时当作起点与判据，评测世界模型在动态场景中被推着往外探索时的保真度。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?

Abstract

Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3–25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

1 Introduction

Recent advances in video generation have steadily improved visual quality, motion realism, and temporal coherence, and the scope of the field has broadened beyond producing fixed-length clips to interactive world models, in which users continuously issue camera or action controls during generation to explore an unfolding visual world [20, 17, 40, 47, 49, 8, 14, 57]. Such models offer new tools for game creation [22, 48, 5, 36, 2, 68, 14, 57], virtual production [38, 50, 35, 34, 53], and robot policy learning [59, 62, 73]. However, most world models start from a single image or a text prompt, so the scene dynamics they produce are entirely imagined by the model and do not correspond to events that actually took place.

Video-conditioned world models open up a new possibility: given a real recorded video of a dynamic scene, users can re-observe the scenes and events it captures along new camera trajectories [52, 60, 44]. This capability directly supports re-framing real footage and free-viewpoint replay, and offers a way to build simulation environments for embodied agents from real videos. Unlike exploration from a single image, these applications impose stricter requirements on the generated results: the model must not only synthesize plausible novel views but also remain faithful to the world recorded in the source video [1, 65].

Despite these advances, it remains unclear whether current models can faithfully explore the dynamic world captured in a source video. Existing benchmarks evaluate visual quality [18, 69], interactive control [58, 64, 27], and world consistency [61, 63], including memory across revisits [12, 71]. However, success on these dimensions does not necessarily imply fidelity to the recorded event. A model may generate realistic views and follow the requested camera trajectory while altering the source action or its timing. It may also produce seemingly consistent revisits by retaining an outdated state of a dynamic subject. This leaves a central question: can models use the source video as evidence of an evolving world, preserving its events under viewpoint changes, integrating information across frames, and maintaining scene consistency during revisits while respecting the event’s temporal progression?

To address this gap, we introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for evaluating video-conditioned world exploration. Each test case pairs a single-shot source video of a dynamic scene with a camera route specified by discrete keyboard actions, which determines how the events in the source video should be observed from changing viewpoints. WanderBench contains 745 source videos spanning real-world footage such as dance, film, and natural scenes, together with AI-generated videos in realistic, anime, and artistic styles, organized into three difficulty tiers from 3 to 25 seconds. We provide random exploration and out-and-back camera routes to examine continuous viewpoint changes and revisits to previously observed regions, respectively. The evaluation comprises 24 sub-metrics across six complementary dimensions. By incorporating source-video references, event timing, and visibility, WanderBench assesses whether stable scene structure and subject identities are preserved and whether dynamic content evolves in accordance with the source event, providing a systematic evaluation of faithful reproduction and sustained exploration of dynamic worlds under camera control.

Benchmarking eight video-conditioned world models on WanderBench reveals two consistent failure modes. First, as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and their visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics: the output drifts from the commanded view and falls out of sync with the source events. Second, no model remembers what it has generated, so a revisited place is redrawn and changes appearance. Models limited to a few seconds of generation cannot even reach the longer tiers.

Beyond evaluation, we introduce WanderLand, a training-free inference-time framework for video-conditioned world exploration. WanderLand aims to preserve source-world identity and event progression while maintaining consistency throughout camera-controlled exploration and revisits. To this end, we develop an evidence-ordered conditioning scheme that rebuilds only the camera and source render a model already reads: every frame is anchored to the source camera of the same instant and rendered from the same-instant source frame, and on revisits, the regions the source cannot cover are filled with the static content the model itself generated earlier. It operates on pretrained video world models without updating their parameters, using only each model’s own geometry. We evaluate WanderLand on WanderBench across five video world models, demonstrating consistent gains across all six dimensions, with the largest improvements in source-dynamics fidelity (up to +8.3) and dynamic revisit consistency (up to +4.8), the two dimensions targeted by the failure modes above.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for world exploration from dynamic video inputs. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos organized into three difficulty tiers, with random camera exploration and long-horizon out-and-back revisit tasks across all tiers, providing a unified setting for evaluating exploration of source-video worlds from novel viewpoints.

  • •

    We establish an evaluation framework comprising six complementary dimensions and 24 sub-metrics. By incorporating source-video references, event timing, and visibility, it systematically assesses stable properties that should persist and dynamic content that should evolve with the source event. Benchmarking eight models with it, we identify loss of camera control and source dynamics over long horizons, and inconsistent revisits, as shared failure modes.

  • •

    We propose WanderLand, a training-free framework for enhancing existing video world models. Built upon these models, WanderLand uses evidence-ordered conditioning, which draws on the same-instant source and the model’s own earlier static content, to improve source-content preservation and dynamic-event reproduction. We evaluate it on WanderBench across five applicable models and observe gains on all six dimensions, most notably in source-dynamics fidelity and dynamic revisit consistency.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video World model

    Early world models explored robotic manipulation and autonomous driving, including UniSim [62], IRASim [73], GAIA-1 [15], and Vista [10]. With advances in video generation, world models can continuously generate subsequent frames from visual observations and user actions, enabling interactive exploration of generated environments. YUME [35, 34] introduces natural language into world event control, while HY-World [51] and LingBot-World [39] explore world generation that combines real-time interaction with long-term consistency. Hunyuan-GameCraft [22] and Matrix-Game [68, 14, 57] support keyboard-and-mouse-driven interactive generation. AlayaWorld [49] further supports sustained world exploration through compressed temporal history and geometrically aligned spatial memory.

    Further work uses source videos as references for scene appearance and dynamic content, allowing users to re-observe the events they contain along new camera trajectories. ReCamMaster [1] jointly conditions on a source video and a target camera trajectory to generate novel views while preserving the source video’s appearance consistency and dynamic synchronization. WorldForge [45, 46] improves trajectory-controlled video generation through reference-fusion correction and denoising guidance. InSpatio-World [52] supports spatiotemporal exploration through world states anchored to a reference video; Wonder [60] jointly designs visual camera control, sparse memory, and distillation strategies to support real-time world generation conditioned on images and videos; and World in World [44] converts source observations, target-view projections, and historical information into unified visual evidence, enabling training-free control through the pretrained model’s native self-attention. WanderBench addresses these requirements by systematically evaluating video world models’ ability to controllably explore dynamic worlds from source videos. Models must not only generate plausible novel views but also preserve the scene and subject identities in the source video, maintain the temporal progression of the original event, and remain consistent with the current event state when revisiting previously observed regions.

    2.2 World Models Evaluation

    Existing benchmarks broadly fall into two categories: non-interactive video evaluation and world model evaluation. VBench [18, 69, 19], EvalCrafter [29], and VideoPhy [3, 4] do not support action inputs or interaction, focusing primarily on video quality, text alignment, or physical commonsense. In contrast, WorldScore [7] evaluates camera-trajectory-conditioned generation, WorldModelBench [21] studies decision-oriented world-model quality, WorldArena [42] targets embodied agents in closed domains, MIND [63] probes closed-loop memory consistency, Omni-WorldBench [58] focuses on causal interaction, WorldLens [26] targets autonomous driving, and WorldMark [61] measures navigation consistency. WBench further introduces a multi-turn evaluation framework for open-domain interactive world models and R2M-Bench [12] evaluates consistency during long-horizon revisits in interactive video world models. Other efforts examine complementary aspects [13, 30, 11, 6, 55, 31, 37, 66, 67, 48, 72].

    These studies provide a foundation for evaluating generation quality, interactive control, and world consistency. However, in video-conditioned settings, evaluation must also determine whether the generated results remain faithful to the dynamic world recorded in the source video: models should preserve scene and subject identities while reproducing the actions and temporal progression of the original event. WanderBench addresses this problem by incorporating source-video references, event timing, and visibility into 24 sub-metrics across six complementary dimensions, systematically evaluating source-world fidelity, source-dynamics fidelity, and consistency during exploration and revisits under camera control.

    3 WanderBench: Can World Models Explore Dynamic Worlds from Video?

    Data Composition. WanderBench comprises 745 source videos, each a single continuous shot whose camera remains static or near-static, so that C(t)=I denotes the original view. 329 are real-world or rendered videos collected from the Internet (Bilibili and YouTube), covering dance, film, daily life, stage performances, and other scenes; 116 are drawn from existing video datasets [16, 24, 41]; and the remaining 300 are generated with MiniMax, spanning 13 realistic looks, 12 anime looks, and 48 artistic.

    Clip Screening. Candidate clips are screened in two stages. (1) Shot proposal. For Internet videos, static shots are automatically proposed by following Shi–Tomasi [43] corners with a pyramidal Lucas–Kanade [32] optical flow at 10 fps and fitting a RANSAC [9] similarity transform. (2) Camera and dynamics verification. For each candidate, we reconstruct the camera trajectory with VGGT [56], cross-checked with MegaSaM [25], and discard clips with noticeable camera rotation or translation. We further check scene dynamics with RAFT [54] optical flow.

    Difficulty Tiers. WanderBench is organized into three tiers of increasing difficulty: (1) Simple (451 clips) contains short clips with slow, mild subject motion; (2) Medium (157 clips) features longer clips with higher visual quality and richer lighting variation; and (3) Hard (137 clips) contains the longest clips, with the highest visual quality, large-amplitude subject motion, substantial background changes, and complex illumination. Across the benchmark, camera-compensated motion extends from a median of 0.029 to 0.12 image diagonals, and MUSIQ imaging quality spans from 22.9 to 74.8. To verify the single-shot filtering, four annotators independently labeled all 2,142 candidate clips as single-shot or not. The annotators agree with each other at Fleiss’ κ=0.93, yielding the final 745 clips.

    3.1 Evaluation Suite

    WanderBench decomposes evaluation into six complementary dimensions comprising 24 sub-metrics, detailed in the Appendix. Most of our metrics compare the output with a time-synchronized source reference: each output frame G(t) and the source frame S(τ(t)) depict the same instant from two viewpoints, so every frame has a reference without any temporal annotation. All sub-metric scores are rescaled to [0,100].

    • Visual Quality. We adopt [dQual]V.1 Aesthetic Quality, [dQual]V.2 Imaging Quality, [dQual]V.3 Temporal Flickering, and [dQual]V.4 Motion Smoothness from VBench [18], together with [dQual]V.5 HPSv3 Preference [33] and [dQual]V.6 Visual Plausibility scored by the PAVRM model of WBench [64]. Since the task is to re-render an input video, all scores are normalized by those of the source video.

    • Camera Control. [dCam]C.1 Synchronized Camera Following reconstructs the source and generated videos separately with VGGT [56] and compares the realized camera motion with the commanded one at one-second intervals.

    • Source-World Fidelity. [dWorld]W.1 Scene Adherence and [dWorld]W.2 Subject Adherence use a VLM and source subject tracks, respectively, to check whether the scene facts and subjects of the source are preserved. [dWorld]W.3 Synchronized View Fidelity reprojects the source frame of the same instant into the realized view and compares it with the output on co-visible regions.

    • Source-Dynamics Fidelity. [dDyn]D.1 Motion Timeline Agreement compares the camera-compensated motion curves of each subject between the source and the output. [dDyn]D.2 Event Adherence localizes the source events in the output. [dDyn]D.3 Temporal Synchronization finds the best-matching source time for each output frame and measures the proportion that falls within a tolerance of the correct time.

    • Spatiotemporal Consistency. [dCons]S.1 Subject Consistency and [dCons]S.2 Background Consistency penalize only the drift of subjects and static regions beyond the changes in the source. [dCons]S.3 Segment Continuity penalizes hard cuts absent from the source. [dCons]S.4 Static Geometric Consistency measures the reprojection consistency of static regions with Depth Anything 3 [28].

    • Dynamic Revisit Consistency. [dRev]R.1–[dRev]R.5 are based on DreamSim similarity (R.1), its pose-gated variant (R.2), place descriptors (R.3), geometric correspondence (R.4), and object appearance (R.5), respectively. [dRev]R.6 Object Semantic Persistence checks the objects that should appear in the source at the return time. [dRev]R.7 Revisit Event Currency measures whether the returning view shows the current state of a dynamic subject.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Evaluated Models and Protocol

    We evaluate eight video-conditioned world models that take a source video and a target camera trajectory, divided into two groups by generation length: (1) full-length models, which render the whole clip in one pass, including InSpatio-World 1.5 [52], World-in-World [44], and WorldForge v2 [46]; and (2) frame-limited models, which produce at most 81 frames (49 for TrajectoryCrafter), including ReCamMaster [1], CameraAnything [23], UniWorld-View [70], WorldForge v1 [45], and TrajectoryCrafter [65]. All models receive the same source video and the same action sequence. Each action sequence is converted into per-frame camera poses relative to the source camera and passed through the model’s native conditioning interface at its native resolution and frame rate; models with a different frame rate receive the same actions resampled to their own time grid. Frame-limited models process only the opening segment of each clip up to their maximum length (81 frames, or 49 for TrajectoryCrafter), conditioned on the corresponding prefix of the full trajectory, and are scored on that segment only. For scoring, (1) all metrics operate on a time grid in seconds; (2) scores are averaged over items, videos, and then models; and (3) a dimension score is the mean of its sub-metrics, and the overall score is the equal-weight mean of the six dimensions.

    4.2 Findings

    (1) Visual quality hides exploration failures. From Simple to Hard, the three full-length models lose little in Visual Quality and Spatiotemporal Consistency. Over the same range, they lose much more in Camera Control, Source-Dynamics Fidelity, and Dynamic Revisit Consistency. A rollout can therefore look clean and stable while following neither the command nor the source events, which per-frame quality metrics alone would not reveal.

    (2) Models keep the static world but lose the dynamic one. Source-World Fidelity is the highest-scoring dimension on every tier, so scenes and subjects are largely preserved. Source-Dynamics Fidelity, in contrast, falls to 37.2 on Hard, meaning the models keep what is in the scene but not when things happen in it.

    (3) Visual quality and camera control trade off. Across the eight models on Simple, Visual Quality and Camera Control are negatively correlated. WorldForge has the highest Visual Quality but only 44.8 in Camera Control, while UniWorld-View has the best Camera Control and the lowest Visual Quality. Faithfully executing a camera move appears to cost image quality in current models, and ranking them by quality alone favors models that move the camera less.

    (4) Short horizons hide the differences that long horizons reveal. On Simple, the frame-limited UniWorld-View obtains the highest overall score, and the overall scores of the full-length models span only 4.3 points. On Hard, this span widens to 13.5 points, and WorldForge collapses to 10.4 in Camera Control. Their strong short-horizon scores do not show whether they can explore.

    (5) Model hardly remembers what it has generated. Dynamic Revisit Consistency is the weakest dimension overall: no model exceeds 68.6, the full-length models stay between 50.0 and 54.5 even on Simple, and WorldForge drops to 20.5 on Hard. Across models, Dynamic Revisit Consistency correlates with Camera Control, which suggests that a model must first reach the revisit pose before consistency there can be achieved.

    5 WanderLand: A Training-Free Enhancement of Exploration in Video World Models

    To explore how source-video evidence can help address the failure modes identified by WanderBench, we introduce WanderLand, a training-free enhancement for existing video world models. WanderLand constructs conditioning inputs by prioritizing time-aligned source observations and using previously generated static content to fill regions not covered by the source.

    5.1 Methods

    For each output frame, WanderLand takes evidence in a fixed order, in three steps.

    (1) Synchronized camera. The model’s own geometry front-end estimates the depth and camera of every source frame, and the commanded camera is then placed relative to the source camera of the same instant rather than to that of the first frame.

    (2) Same-instant source. The model’s own point-cloud renderer warps the source frame of the same instant into this camera. As a result, the render covers more of the view, and moving subjects appear at the correct time.

    (3) Static memory. When the camera returns to a place shown earlier, we lift the model’s nearest earlier outputs to 3D points using Depth Anything 3 [28] depth aligned to the render depth, and use them to fill the regions the source video cannot cover. Pixels whose source content changes over time, measured by a camera-compensated color difference, are discarded. Moving subjects are therefore never frozen, and all visible motion still comes from the source video.

    5.2 Properties

    WanderLand requires no training and introduces no additional weights. It relies only on the model’s own geometry module and renderer and never uses WanderBench’s evaluation tools. Wherever the evidence does not change, it reproduces the original output exactly, and its only extra cost is one additional generation when the camera revisits a place.

    5.3 WanderLand Results

    We apply WanderLand to five video world models and report the change on each dimension in Tab. 3. World-in-World and WorldForge are not included, since both are themselves training-free frameworks built on pretrained world models and do not expose the inputs that WanderLand rebuilds.

    (1) Consistent gains without trade-offs. WanderLand improves most backbone on every dimension and degrades none, so the better conditioning comes at no cost to visual quality or camera control.

    (2) Revisits benefit on every model. Dynamic Revisit Consistency rises by 2.4–4.8 points across all five backbones, as the holes at a revisit are filled with content the model has already shown instead of being redrawn.

    (3) Long horizons benefit the most. The largest single gain is on the full-length InSpatio-World 1.5, whose Source-Dynamics Fidelity rises by 8.3 points: over long rollouts, anchoring every frame to the source at the same instant keeps the generated events in sync with the recorded ones.

    6 Discussion

    WanderBench moves video world model evaluation from a single view to time-aligned multiple views: each explored trajectory is a new view of the same dynamic scene, synchronized with the source. We expect models that do well here to produce time-aligned multi-view videos from a single input, which could enable end-to-end generation of full-scene 4D Gaussian Splatting from one video. Current models still fall short on temporal synchronization and long-range revisits, and we hope WanderBench offers a concrete target for closing this gap.

    7 Conclusion

    We introduced WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video, with 745 single-shot source videos in three difficulty tiers and 24 sub-metrics over six dimensions. Current world models preserve static scenes and visual quality but lose camera control, source dynamics, and revisit consistency over longer horizons. Our training-free WanderLand improves five models by conditioning each frame on the same-instant source and the model’s own earlier content, though it requires camera and source-render inputs. We hope WanderBench drives world models that stay faithful to the recorded world as they explore it.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 文本生成 3D 场景不只放刚体：SoftPAT3D 把布料、毛绒玩具、绳子也生成成「可仿真」的物体 ｜ SoftPAT3D: Physics-Augmented Text-to-3D Scene Generation with Deformables
item.description:
一句话：现有物理增强管线只会刚体，可变形物体一进场景就穿模、就不可仿真。

要点：

  • 缺口明确：既有的物理增强式生成管线只处理刚体，容纳不了可变形物体
  • SoftPAT3D 把布料、毛绒玩具、绳子这类**可变形物体生成为物理上有效、可直接仿真的物体**
  • 并且要求它们与支撑家具、彼此之间、以及自身都不发生穿插——也就是生成即处于无交叠的接触状态

为什么值得看：「生成的东西能不能直接拿去仿真」是文本生成 3D 进引擎的分水岭。把可变形体纳入，并保证初始状态无穿插，等于省掉了从生成到可交互资产之间最麻烦的一步。

中文摘要：文本生成 3D 场景已经在刚体上取得进展，但现有物理增强式管线只能处理刚体，无法容纳布料、毛绒玩具、绳子这类可变形物体。SoftPAT3D 因此把可变形体作为一等对象：生成结果必须是物理上有效、可直接进入仿真的物体，并且与支撑它们的家具、与彼此、以及与自身之间都不发生穿插——即生成出来就处在无交叠的接触状态。这种「生成即可仿真」的约束，正是把文本生成内容变成引擎可用资产的关键一步。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

SoftPAT3D: Physics-Augmented Text-to-3D Scene Generation with Deformables

Abstract

We present SoftPAT3D, a physics-augmented framework for text-to-3D scene generation in which deformable objects, such as cloth, stuffed toys and ropes, are generated as physically valid, simulation-ready bodies and placed in intersection-free contact with the furniture that supports them, with one another and with themselves. Existing physics-augmented pipelines simulate rigid bodies only and cannot accommodate a generated deformable object, which text-to-3D generation returns as a geometrically invalid mesh, sometimes self-intersecting, that has no rest shape, no material model and no admissible initial state. These are the inputs a deformable simulation requires, and we construct each from information already in the pipeline. The rest shape comes from how the object is manufactured rather than from the generated physically inconsistent deformed configuration, and a material library assigns each deformable object its initial elastic parameters, which can then be optimized. The occluded support is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, each object is released from an optimizable placement above the supporting part that the prompt specifies, and the complete scene is driven to static equilibrium under one unified contact model, with completion verified by geometric checks and a vision–language model. When a scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, and the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same contact energy reaches the targets the grid does not, places several bodies jointly and recovers and optimizes material parameters. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in a single simulation, and the pipeline also runs from the text prompt alone. On all sixty-five prompts, SoftPAT3D produces no undesired interpenetration of any kind, whereas every other system does, and its scenes directly support scene editing and robotic manipulation.

first contactlandingpilingrelaxing

1 Introduction

Generating 3D scenes from natural language has broad applications in robotics, embodied AI and content creation, and recent pipelines have progressed from retrieving and arranging assets [15, 16] to generating or reconstructing the objects and settling the layout with a physics engine [1, 21, 20]. This physics stage yields a scene in which objects rest on one another without interpenetration and which a simulator can edit.

However, every object in such a physics stage is rigid. The rooms that users describe contain deformable objects, a tablecloth, a throw over a sofa, pillows and a quilt on a bed, and on these the pipeline fails. Text-to-3D generation returns the deformable object already draped, as a closed, self-intersecting surface that is plausible from the generation viewpoint but has no rest shape, no material and no admissible initial state. Current systems either simulate this surface as a rigid body, which leaves it floating above or intersecting the furniture (Fig. 1), or demote it to a non-simulated covering [21].

Simulating a generated deformable object in this physics stage raises three challenges. First, the solver requires a rest shape, the geometry at which the elastic energy vanishes; the generated surface provides none, and thickening it would bake the generator’s folds into the rest shape. Second, the simulation requires an intersection-free initial state, yet the support beneath the object is occluded in the reference image and generated merged with its occluder, and the object must start above its support in the relation the prompt states. Third, a converged simulation is not necessarily a complete scene, since the object may slide to the floor or settle on a support generated as a solid block, so the pipeline needs a completion criterion.

To address these challenges, we propose SoftPAT3D, which constructs all three inputs while leaving the solver of the rigid pipeline unchanged. Our key observation is that the rest shape has a source that exists for every object class without any observation: the way the object is manufactured. Garments are sewn from parametric sewing patterns, linens are cut as single panels and pillows are stuffed from two seamed panels, under class-specific size priors, so the rest shape carries the construction of its class and none of the generator’s folds. SoftPAT3D then prepares the initial state from the prompt and the layout: the deformable object is inpainted out of its support, which is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, and a language model reads the supporting part off the prompt, above which placement rules position the object. All bodies are simulated to static equilibrium under one contact barrier, and two geometric checks and a vision–language model decide whether the scene is complete. Finally, when the scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, initialized by the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same energy, which also optimizes several bodies jointly and differentiates the material and the rest shape.

The result is a text-to-3D pipeline whose physics stage simulates deformable objects; the concurrent CoDimRecon [22] reconstructs such a scene from a multi-view capture instead (Sec. 2). We validate SoftPAT3D on sixty-five prompts, thirty-two of them written after the pipeline was frozen, against four baselines. Across every thin-shell and volumetric-solid scene in the paper, no equilibrated object intersects its support, whereas Holodeck [15] crosses at 71 edges per thousand, a cloth solver on the generated asset at 196, and the rigid pipeline leaves its cloth 15 mm inside the furniture; under one completion criterion applied to every system, SoftPAT3D completes 21 of 34 scenes against at most 8 for any baseline. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in one simulation, the pipeline also runs from the prompt alone, and the same solver edits and manipulates the result. We also compare the placement gradient with a grid search at equal compute and characterize the prompts outside the placement vocabulary (Sec. 5). In summary, our main contributions are:

  • •

    We construct rest shapes from manufacturing priors: garments sewn from parametric sewing patterns, linens cut as panels and pillows stuffed from seamed panels, under class-specific size priors, which give a generated deformable object the rest shape that its surface lacks.

  • •

    We propose a physics-aware initialization that regenerates the occluded support into a watertight collision mesh and maps the support relation in the prompt to a placement by one placement principle, so that thin shells, volumetric solids and rigid supports reach static equilibrium under a single contact barrier.

  • •

    We define a completion criterion of geometric checks and a VLM-based prompt check, and a placement optimization by grid search, compared at equal compute with the adjoint of a differentiable simulation, which reaches targets past an obstruction, extends to several bodies and recovers material parameters.

    • 2 Related Work

    Text-to-3D scene generation.

    Layout-based methods compose retrieved or generated assets [15, 16, 18, 19]. PAT3D [1] adds a rigid physics stage with differentiable layout optimization, concurrent systems equilibrate or verify rigid scenes [20, 21, 26, 27, 28], and procedural [33], program-authoring [23, 24] and single-image [29, 30] systems build scenes by other routes. None of these simulates a deformable object at the scene level (Table 1): SceneSmith [21] demotes tablecloths to non-simulated coverings, and systems that generate deformable assets place them by layout without scene-level simulation [25, 31, 32]. Amodal completion recovers an object occluded in the scene image [47, 45, 51, 46, 48, 49, 50] or its self-occluded parts [52]; here it is the support, which we regenerate and decompose into convex cells [12].

    Simulation-ready deformable assets and environments.

    Physics-grounded dynamics animate a given image or captured shape [2, 17, 60, 61], and simulation-ready asset generation [34, 35, 36, 31] produces one object at a time; neither brings a scene to equilibrium under contact. Elsewhere, soft objects enter a scene per asset or from a library [33, 67, 66, 64], or as dynamic episodes [62, 63, 65]. Sewing patterns provide garment rest shapes [53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59].

    Deformable simulation and differentiable physics.

    Discrete membrane and bending models [9] describe thin shells, incremental potential contact (IPC) keeps implicit time stepping intersection-free [3], its codimensional extension covers shells and rods [8], and vertex block descent minimizes the same potential by local block updates on the GPU [5]. Differentiable simulators propagate gradients through explicit [39] and implicit [38, 7] steps and estimate materials from captures [40, 41, 42, 44] or images [43], after gradient-free search [37]. CoDimRecon [22], concurrent with this work, reconstructs a simulation-ready scene of rods, shells and solids from multi-view RGB under IPC contact; the capture supplies resting geometry, layout and scale, so each object starts near equilibrium and is settled, whereas a generative pipeline has no observation to fit. We thus address this gap by constructing the inputs that a capture would otherwise supply.

    3 Method

    Given a text prompt, SoftPAT3D runs the generation stages of PAT3D [1] and then simulates the scene with its deformable objects to static equilibrium. Each stage constructs one input that the solver requires and generation does not supply (Fig. 2): support repair (Sec. 3.4), deformable-object initialization (Secs. 3.2 and 3.3), equilibration with a completion check (Sec. 3.5) and, when the prompt check fails, placement optimization (Sec. 3.6).

    3.1 Preliminaries

    PAT3D expands the prompt into a reference image, segments it [14], lifts each crop to a textured mesh [13], arranges the objects with a language model, converts them to simulation meshes [11] and simulates them as rigid bodies to static equilibrium. Following incremental potential contact [3], each time step advances the scene state x, the vector of all vertex positions, to the minimizer of

    E(x) = \tfrac12Δt² \lVertx-x̂\rVert²_M + ∑ₒΨₒ(xₒ) + B(x),

    		(1)

    where x̂=xₙ+Δt vₙ+Δt²M⁻¹fₑₓₜ is the predicted position, M the mass matrix, Ψₒ the elastic energy of object o and B the log-barrier contact potential,

    B(x)=κ∑ₖb(dₖ(x)), b(d)=-(d-d̂)²\ln\tfracdd̂,

    		(2)

    summed over every pair k of surface primitives whose distance dₖ is below the activation distance d̂, and zero beyond it, with lagged Coulomb friction. Each step is minimized by Newton’s method with a continuous-collision line search, so a trajectory that starts intersection-free remains so [4]. Rigid supports keep the affine-body energy Ψ_ABD(A)=κₐV\lVertA^⊤A-I\rVert_F² at κₐ=100 MPa and are fixed in place. SoftPAT3D changes only the energies Ψₒ of the deformable objects and the state x at the first step.

    3.2 Rest shapes

    The elastic energy requires a rest shape, and the generated asset does not provide one. A lifted towel arrives as a closed, already draped surface whose two layers lie closer than d̂, and thickening it would bake the generator’s folds into the rest shape (Table 4, first row).

    We therefore describe each deformable object by its manufacturing process, as flat panels cut to an outline, sewn along seams and optionally stuffed. Garments are sewn from parametric sewing patterns [53, 54], relaxed once to equilibrium and stored in a library of four patterns, T-shirt, trousers, skirt and dress, which every named garment in the paper draws on; plain linens are single panels discretized on a simulation grid, a 128×128 mesh on [0,w]×[0,ℓ], cut to an outline where the object has one, such as a round cloth or an apron; pillows are two seamed panels inflated into a superellipsoid |x/a|ᵖ+|y/b|ᵖ+|z/c|ᵖ=1 whose interior tetrahedralization serves as the stuffing. Since the scale of a monocular layout is ambiguous, every deformable object and support is clamped to the real-world size range of its class.

    3.3 Per-object energies

    Each object keeps or replaces its elastic energy according to its material class. A keyword classifier on the object’s name assigns it to rigid, thin-shell, volumetric-soft or rod, matching rigid compound names first. Cloth-class objects receive a Neo-Hookean membrane on the rest shape of the panel and discrete bending on its dihedral angles [9],

    Ψₛₕₑₗₗ(x)=∑ₜĀₜ h W(Fₜ)+k_b∑ₑ(\lVertē\rVert)/(h̄ₑ) (θₑ-θ̄ₑ)²,

    		(3)

    where Fₜ∈ℝ^3×2 is the deformation gradient of triangle t with rest area Āₜ, θₑ the dihedral angle at edge e with rest value θ̄ₑ, rest length \lVertē\rVert and height h̄ₑ, and the membrane energy density is

    W(F)=\tfracμ2(trF^⊤F-2)-μ\lnJ+\tfracλ2\ln²J,

    		(4)

    with J=√\detF^⊤F and Lamé parameters μ=E/2(1+ν) and λ=Eν/(1+ν)(1-2ν). Pillow-class objects are tetrahedralized and receive the rest-stabilized Neo-Hookean energy [10]

    Wᵥₒₗ(F)=\tfracμ2(trF^⊤F-3)+\tfracλ2(\detF-1-\tfracμλ)²

    		(5)

    with foam parameters. Cables, cords and ropes are an exploratory extension, a line mesh with the stretching and bending model of the codimensional solver’s rods [8] (supplementary material). A material library supplies the parameters of each class (Sec. 4.1). All energies share the barrier of Eq. (2), so mixed scenes of thin shells, volumetric solids, rods and rigid supports require no additional coupling.

    3.4 Physics-aware initialization

    The barrier requires an intersection-free initial state and collision meshes with a well-defined interior, neither of which generated assets provide.

    Support repair.

    The support is partly occluded by the deformable object in the reference image, and the generator fills the occluded region with the occluder, merging a seat with the pile on it. We inpaint the deformable object out of the crop of the support before lifting [47, 46, 50], regenerate the support from the completed image and align it to its slot in the layout. Without this step, the generator fills the mask with cloth merged into the support in 32 of 33 scenes. The regenerated mesh is then converted into a watertight collision mesh [11], since a single intersecting pair makes the solver reject the initial state. Contact is resolved against this closed surface, whose mean distance to the textured asset is 2.7 mm (development) and 3.0 mm (held-out).

    Placement.

    Objects visible in the reference image are placed at their layout positions. For objects the prompt introduces beyond the image, a language model, given a geometric summary of the candidate surfaces, returns a part such as the seat, backrest, arm or rim and a drop height. The cloth is sized from the top surface of its support with a 0.1 m overhang, or to the size the language model estimates, and placed at the drop height above the part. Every placement follows one principle: the object is placed above the part that the prompt names, at the lowest height at which its initial state is intersection-free, with its extent clamped to that part. The supplementary material lists the rules that apply this principle to the furniture classes of the scene set; a new support class needs no rule beyond the part vocabulary. Every placement is tested for intersection before the first step, and an intersecting placement is raised, y₀←y₀+δ, until \minₖdₖ(x₀)>d̂.

    3.5 Completion checks and rendering

    A converged simulation is not necessarily a complete scene. We therefore apply two geometric checks first. The containment check requires the centre of mass of the deformable object to project inside the ground projection F of its support. The support check rejects as a generation failure a support that is nearly as solid as its bounding box or far outside the size range of its class. Scenes that pass both geometric checks are then checked against the prompt by a vision–language model, the prompt check, queried twice on one render, J=[j₁=j₂=yes]; three further views and a second model agree with it on 49 and 44 of 60 scenes, and 5 human raters, who agree with one another on 92% of the renders, return its verdict on 94% of the scenes each on average (supplementary material). We call a scene complete when

    C = P∧S∧[X=0]∧G∧J,

    		(6)

    where P holds when every requested deformable object is present, S when the simulation converged without the solver rejecting an intersecting state, X is the number of deformable surface edges that intersect a collision mesh, and G holds when both geometric checks pass. In the main run the prompt check is recorded but not acted upon (Sec. 3.6).

    3.6 Placement optimization

    A scene that fails the prompt check has usually placed the object on a part of its support other than the one the prompt specifies. A language model maps the prompt to the intended part from a fixed vocabulary, or reports that no placement can satisfy it, and the part is resolved on the collision mesh to a target p, the area-weighted centroid of its faces, p=∑_f∈ℙA_fc_f/∑_fA_f. The placement θ=(cₓ,c_z) is then optimized so that the equilibrium state x^⋆(θ), rather than the initial one, meets the prompt,

    θ^⋆=\arg\min_θL(θ), L(θ)=\lVertΠ(x^⋆(θ))-p\rVert²,

    		(7)

    where Π projects the centre of mass of the equilibrated cloth onto the ground plane. We solve Eq. (7) with Adam using the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same energy. The simulation consists of N implicit steps, each solved by Newton’s method to stationarity of Eq. (1),

    Rₙ=\tfrac1Δt²M(xₙ₊₁-x̂ₙ)+∇(Ψ+B+D)|_xₙ₊₁=0,

    		(8)

    where x̂ₙ is the predicted position of Eq. (1), which carries the external force, D is the lagged friction potential, and θ enters through x₀. For a loss on x_N the gradient is dL/dθ=∑ₙwₙ^⊤∂Rₙ/∂θ, with adjoint variables wₙ obtained by a reverse sweep that solves one linear system per step with the Newton matrix ∂Rₙ/∂xₙ₊₁ of the converged step [6]; a solver-level alternative replays the block sweep in reverse [7]. The adjoint is exact as long as the active contact set does not change with θ, where it matches finite differences. For a single body the loss has two parameters, which a grid search covers: the pipeline re-simulates the placements

    θⱼ=θ₀+fⱼ (p_xz-θ₀), fⱼ∈{\tfrac12,\tfrac34,1},

    		(9)

    at the size the language model estimates and at the class size, subjects each candidate to the geometric checks and the prompt check, and keeps the first to pass. The adjoint serves where the search space grows: it optimizes the placements of several bodies jointly (Sec. 4.5) and, through the same sweep, the material parameters.

    4 Experimental Results

    4.1 Experimental setup

    Scenes.

    Since there is no standard benchmark for this task, we construct our own: thirty-two single-object scenes and three multi-body scenes generated end to end during development, and a second batch of thirty-two prompts written after the pipeline was frozen and run with one regeneration allowed and no other intervention. The main run is one run of the final code (scene set and prompts in the supplementary material).

    Baselines.

    The rigid pipeline runs the same prompt through the same stages and is measured after its own physics stage with the cloth asset kept rigid. Blender’s cloth solver runs on the generated asset as placed by the rigid pipeline (Blender) and on our inputs, the sewn cloth at our placement over our collision meshes (Blender∗), so that for cloth only the solver differs. Holodeck [15], a retrieval system, and GPT-6 Astra, a frontier model prompted to write a Blender program, build their own scenes from the same prompts (supplementary material). The baselines of PAT3D, GraphDreamer, Blender-MCP and MIDI, generate no deformable object and are not rerun.

    Metrics.

    All metrics are computed on the equilibrated geometry of the solver against its collision meshes: crossings, the number of deformable surface edges that intersect another body, per thousand edges; penetration, the mean depth of the vertices inside a closed body; contact, the fraction of vertices within 5 mm of another body; the number of bodies that touch nothing or are unsupported; and the completion criterion of Eq. (6). Crossings are the edge analogue of the penetrating-triangle ratio of PAT3D.

    Implementation details.

    Thin shells are simulated at Δt=0.02 s for up to 300 implicit steps, stopping once \maxᵢ\lVertxᵢⁿ-xᵢⁿ⁻⁴⁰\rVert<0.5 mm, with the cotton parameters of the material library for shells and its foam parameters for volumetric solids, effective rather than measured values (supplementary material). A sweep over time steps and mesh resolutions leaves every scene at static equilibrium with zero crossings (supplementary material).

    4.2 Comparison with other systems

    Table 2 scores six conditions under one protocol over the thirty-two single-object scenes, the clothes sofa and the hamper. The rigid pipeline starts from the same generated assets and layout as ours, but simulating the cloth as rigid bodies leaves them intersecting the furniture at 5.1 edges per thousand with 14.8 mm penetration, touching their supports over only 1.8% of their vertices and floating in 14 of 48 bodies, as in Fig. 4. Blender’s cloth solver diverges in 24 of 34 scenes and crosses at 196 per thousand edges on the generated asset, and still crosses at 66.2 per thousand given our inputs. Holodeck places a deformable object in only 8 of 32 scenes, and Astra models fabric without a cloth solver. By contrast, SoftPAT3D has zero crossings and zero penetration, the largest contact area, 39.9% of vertices, and no unsupported body; under Eq. (6) applied to every system, with the prompt check on the render of each system, 21 of our 34 scenes are complete, against 8 for Blender∗, 7 for Astra, 2 for Holodeck and 0 for the rigid pipeline. A render hides an intersection under the cloth, so these claims rest on the geometry; Fig. 5 shows a vertical section. Judged on renders under the protocol of PAT3D (Table 3), GPT-5.4 prefers our drape to that of the rigid pipeline in a side-swapped forced choice on 10 of 13 scenes, and its plausibility score rises from 43 to 90. In a blind study, 5 participants compare our render with a baseline’s on 10 prompts, systems unidentified and sides randomized, and prefer ours for physical validity and prompt satisfaction on every pair (supplementary material).

    4.3 End-to-end results

    Held-out prompts.

    The thirty-two prompts written after the pipeline was frozen are our primary measurement under Eq. (6). Every scene reaches static equilibrium with no crossing, five prompts lose an object upstream of the physics stage, and of the twenty-seven that reach it, 19 are complete with the placement optimization of Sec. 3.6 in the loop (19 of 32 overall). The physics stage alone completes 14, and the grid of Eq. (9) completes 5 of the 7 scenes whose prompt failure names a reachable part in six re-simulations per scene (supplementary material). On the same held-out inputs Blender’s cloth solver crosses at 24.4 per thousand edges and leaves 9 of 27 bodies unsupported, against zero and none for ours.

    Development set.

    Of the thirty-three development scenes, 21 are complete under the same criterion (Fig. 3), 25 with placement optimization, and none has a crossing; nine multi-body scenes with two to eight deformable objects (Fig. 3, bottom) reach equilibrium in one simulation and pass both checks.

    4.4 Applications

    Robotic manipulation.

    The same solver manipulates the equilibrated scene. A soft position constraint grips a patch G of the deformable object and adds

    Ψ_grip(x)=\tfrack_g2∑_i∈Gmᵢ \lVertxᵢ-gᵢ(t)\rVert²

    		(10)

    to Eq. (1), where gᵢ(t) is the gripper path along which the constraint moves the patch, holds it and releases it; the arm in Fig. 6 is posed for visualization only. Pull, lift and drag move a corner, the top centre or the patch, and press compresses a stuffed body by half its height. Over 28 episodes on 23 scenes, the patch reaches 90% of its commanded displacement in 23 of the 23 pull, lift and drag episodes, with a median grip error of 5.7 mm.

    Scene editing.

    The same mechanism removes a body by carrying it to the floor and adds one by holding and releasing it; on the messy bed (Fig. 6) the added pillow’s placement is optimized by the differentiable simulation (Sec. 4.5).

    4.5 Ablation studies

    Same-solver controls.

    In Table 4, the rest shape accounts for the largest share: with the closed surface of the generated asset in place of the sewn panel, the solver rejects the initial state on 11 scenes and the completed cloth scenes fall from 16 to 9. The watertight collision mesh brings every scene to equilibrium, placing each object on the part the language model names completes two more, and its size estimate one more, from 18 for a sewn panel placed centred over the support to 21 for the full physics stage (Fig. 7).

    Differentiable simulation.

    In the joint optimization of N bodies over an obstructed support, it lands about twice as many bodies as a coordinate grid search with twice its forward budget, and remains the best of the four methods over eight supports and 32 runs per N (supplementary material), because the gradient crosses the obstruction that a line search does not. The pillow added to the messy bed (Sec. 4) comes to rest 1.2 cm from its target under the adjoint’s placement, against 67 cm under the language model’s, and the same adjoint recovers a weight-to-stiffness ratio perturbed fourfold on 11 supports with a median error of 3% over 26 cases, against 16% for a random search at twice the budget (supplementary material). For a single body whose target lies on the grid’s line, the grid of Eq. (9) passes 9 of the 12 correctable scenes and the pipeline uses it; where an obstruction lies in between, the adjoint lands the body in 24 of 32 runs against 20 for the grid (supplementary material). From the prompt alone, without the reference image, all 65 scenes reach equilibrium and 57 pass both geometric checks, and 17 of the 32 held-out prompts pass the prompt check against 15 with the image.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented SoftPAT3D, which constructs the inputs a deformable simulation requires and brings deformable objects to equilibrium in text-to-3D scene generation. Limitations. A prompt that asks for a row of pillows or a folded towel is treated as a placement and fails the prompt check, and a support generated as a solid block has no part to place onto (Fig. 8). The sewn panel keeps the generated object’s kind in 48 of 60 scenes and its colour in 34; its size and folds follow the class prior. Materials are effective values [44]; plasticity is not modelled (cf. [22]).

    LLM Usage Statement

    Large language models are components of the method and are evaluated as such: a language model returns the supporting part and the size of each object the prompt introduces (Sec. 3.4), and a vision–language model performs the prompt check (Sec. 3.5). Beyond the method, LLM-based tools (Claude via Claude Code, and ChatGPT) were used at the assist level only, to edit and refine author-produced content: the text, the related work and citations, the code, the analysis of the experiments, the figures and the scene prompts. The authors take full responsibility for all submitted content.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Supplementary Material
    SoftPAT3D: Physics-Augmented Text-to-3D Scene Generation with Deformables

    Appendix A Scene Set

    In this section, we enumerate every scene that the pipeline is asked to equilibrate, including the rejected ones, so that each count in the main paper can be traced to its corresponding scenes. Table S1 is generated from the development runs rather than maintained by hand, and every rejected scene carries the check that rejects it. The final code’s outcome for each scene is given in the last block of Table S9, and Fig. S2 renders every scene that passes the geometric checks.

    Appendix B Held-out Prompts

    In this section, we provide the per-prompt record underlying the held-out count of the main paper. The thirty-two prompts of Table S1 are written while the pipeline is being built. After the pipeline is frozen, we write 32 more prompts over supports it has not been run on and run them end to end, with no asset redraw, placement override or parameter change, under the same solver settings as the main set. Table S4 lists every prompt with its outcome.

    We manually verify the routing against the prompts. Among the 63 objects that reach the solver, every towel, blanket, jacket, scarf, skirt, quilt, shirt, sweater, throw and tablecloth is routed to the shell energy, every cushion, pillow and plush toy is routed to the volumetric-body energy, and every support is routed to the rigid energy, with no error.

    The criterion is the one used throughout the paper. “Complete” means that the scene passes the containment and support checks, has zero cloth–support crossings on the colliders, and passes the prompt check of the main paper’s Sec. 3.5, run on one render per scene with the same script and the same two-answer rule as the main set and the controls. A second pass of the check over the same twenty-four renders, with two new answers each, returned the same verdict on every scene. “Upstream” means that the scene never reached the solver, because the generation stage’s own object list omitted one of the two requested objects. The outcome listed is that of the final code’s run over the held-out assets, the full-stage cell of Sec. C.1: 14 of 32 complete.

    Blender’s cloth solver.

    Given the same held-out inputs, the sewn sheet at our placement over our closed colliders exhibits crossings at 24.4 edges per thousand under Blender’s cloth solver and leaves 9 of its 27 bodies touching nothing, against zero and none for ours, and its cloth touches the support over 17% of its vertices against 53% for ours (Table S2). This is the shared-input condition that Blender∗ runs on the development set, here over the 25 held-out scenes that both solvers produced.

    Results with placement optimization.

    Seven of the scenes that fail the prompt check name a part that a placement can reach: the towel on the saddle, the counter towel, the skirt, the quilt on the footboard, the hamper towel, the marble-table cloth and the piano scarf. Sec. F re-solves them under the pipeline’s rule, and five pass, while the closed loop completes 19 of 32. The grid of Eq. 9 of the main paper passes these five at six re-simulations per scene (Table S3).

一句话：现有物理增强管线只会刚体，可变形物体一进场景就穿模、就不可仿真。

要点：

  • 缺口明确：既有的物理增强式生成管线只处理刚体，容纳不了可变形物体
  • SoftPAT3D 把布料、毛绒玩具、绳子这类**可变形物体生成为物理上有效、可直接仿真的物体**
  • 并且要求它们与支撑家具、彼此之间、以及自身都不发生穿插——也就是生成即处于无交叠的接触状态

为什么值得看：「生成的东西能不能直接拿去仿真」是文本生成 3D 进引擎的分水岭。把可变形体纳入，并保证初始状态无穿插，等于省掉了从生成到可交互资产之间最麻烦的一步。

中文摘要：文本生成 3D 场景已经在刚体上取得进展，但现有物理增强式管线只能处理刚体，无法容纳布料、毛绒玩具、绳子这类可变形物体。SoftPAT3D 因此把可变形体作为一等对象：生成结果必须是物理上有效、可直接进入仿真的物体，并且与支撑它们的家具、与彼此、以及与自身之间都不发生穿插——即生成出来就处在无交叠的接触状态。这种「生成即可仿真」的约束，正是把文本生成内容变成引擎可用资产的关键一步。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

SoftPAT3D: Physics-Augmented Text-to-3D Scene Generation with Deformables

Abstract

We present SoftPAT3D, a physics-augmented framework for text-to-3D scene generation in which deformable objects, such as cloth, stuffed toys and ropes, are generated as physically valid, simulation-ready bodies and placed in intersection-free contact with the furniture that supports them, with one another and with themselves. Existing physics-augmented pipelines simulate rigid bodies only and cannot accommodate a generated deformable object, which text-to-3D generation returns as a geometrically invalid mesh, sometimes self-intersecting, that has no rest shape, no material model and no admissible initial state. These are the inputs a deformable simulation requires, and we construct each from information already in the pipeline. The rest shape comes from how the object is manufactured rather than from the generated physically inconsistent deformed configuration, and a material library assigns each deformable object its initial elastic parameters, which can then be optimized. The occluded support is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, each object is released from an optimizable placement above the supporting part that the prompt specifies, and the complete scene is driven to static equilibrium under one unified contact model, with completion verified by geometric checks and a vision–language model. When a scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, and the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same contact energy reaches the targets the grid does not, places several bodies jointly and recovers and optimizes material parameters. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in a single simulation, and the pipeline also runs from the text prompt alone. On all sixty-five prompts, SoftPAT3D produces no undesired interpenetration of any kind, whereas every other system does, and its scenes directly support scene editing and robotic manipulation.

1 Introduction

Generating 3D scenes from natural language has broad applications in robotics, embodied AI and content creation, and recent pipelines have progressed from retrieving and arranging assets [15, 16] to generating or reconstructing the objects and settling the layout with a physics engine [1, 21, 20]. This physics stage yields a scene in which objects rest on one another without interpenetration and which a simulator can edit.

However, every object in such a physics stage is rigid. The rooms that users describe contain deformable objects, a tablecloth, a throw over a sofa, pillows and a quilt on a bed, and on these the pipeline fails. Text-to-3D generation returns the deformable object already draped, as a closed, self-intersecting surface that is plausible from the generation viewpoint but has no rest shape, no material and no admissible initial state. Current systems either simulate this surface as a rigid body, which leaves it floating above or intersecting the furniture (Fig. 1), or demote it to a non-simulated covering [21].

Simulating a generated deformable object in this physics stage raises three challenges. First, the solver requires a rest shape, the geometry at which the elastic energy vanishes; the generated surface provides none, and thickening it would bake the generator’s folds into the rest shape. Second, the simulation requires an intersection-free initial state, yet the support beneath the object is occluded in the reference image and generated merged with its occluder, and the object must start above its support in the relation the prompt states. Third, a converged simulation is not necessarily a complete scene, since the object may slide to the floor or settle on a support generated as a solid block, so the pipeline needs a completion criterion.

To address these challenges, we propose SoftPAT3D, which constructs all three inputs while leaving the solver of the rigid pipeline unchanged. Our key observation is that the rest shape has a source that exists for every object class without any observation: the way the object is manufactured. Garments are sewn from parametric sewing patterns, linens are cut as single panels and pillows are stuffed from two seamed panels, under class-specific size priors, so the rest shape carries the construction of its class and none of the generator’s folds. SoftPAT3D then prepares the initial state from the prompt and the layout: the deformable object is inpainted out of its support, which is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, and a language model reads the supporting part off the prompt, above which placement rules position the object. All bodies are simulated to static equilibrium under one contact barrier, and two geometric checks and a vision–language model decide whether the scene is complete. Finally, when the scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, initialized by the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same energy, which also optimizes several bodies jointly and differentiates the material and the rest shape.

The result is a text-to-3D pipeline whose physics stage simulates deformable objects; the concurrent CoDimRecon [22] reconstructs such a scene from a multi-view capture instead (Sec. 2). We validate SoftPAT3D on sixty-five prompts, thirty-two of them written after the pipeline was frozen, against four baselines. Across every thin-shell and volumetric-solid scene in the paper, no equilibrated object intersects its support, whereas Holodeck [15] crosses at 71 edges per thousand, a cloth solver on the generated asset at 196, and the rigid pipeline leaves its cloth 15 mm inside the furniture; under one completion criterion applied to every system, SoftPAT3D completes 21 of 34 scenes against at most 8 for any baseline. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in one simulation, the pipeline also runs from the prompt alone, and the same solver edits and manipulates the result. We also compare the placement gradient with a grid search at equal compute and characterize the prompts outside the placement vocabulary (Sec. 5). In summary, our main contributions are:

  • •

    We construct rest shapes from manufacturing priors: garments sewn from parametric sewing patterns, linens cut as panels and pillows stuffed from seamed panels, under class-specific size priors, which give a generated deformable object the rest shape that its surface lacks.

  • •

    We propose a physics-aware initialization that regenerates the occluded support into a watertight collision mesh and maps the support relation in the prompt to a placement by one placement principle, so that thin shells, volumetric solids and rigid supports reach static equilibrium under a single contact barrier.

  • •

    We define a completion criterion of geometric checks and a VLM-based prompt check, and a placement optimization by grid search, compared at equal compute with the adjoint of a differentiable simulation, which reaches targets past an obstruction, extends to several bodies and recovers material parameters.

    • 2 Related Work

    Text-to-3D scene generation.

    Layout-based methods compose retrieved or generated assets [15, 16, 18, 19]. PAT3D [1] adds a rigid physics stage with differentiable layout optimization, concurrent systems equilibrate or verify rigid scenes [20, 21, 26, 27, 28], and procedural [33], program-authoring [23, 24] and single-image [29, 30] systems build scenes by other routes. None of these simulates a deformable object at the scene level (Table 1): SceneSmith [21] demotes tablecloths to non-simulated coverings, and systems that generate deformable assets place them by layout without scene-level simulation [25, 31, 32]. Amodal completion recovers an object occluded in the scene image [47, 45, 51, 46, 48, 49, 50] or its self-occluded parts [52]; here it is the support, which we regenerate and decompose into convex cells [12].

    Simulation-ready deformable assets and environments.

    Physics-grounded dynamics animate a given image or captured shape [2, 17, 60, 61], and simulation-ready asset generation [34, 35, 36, 31] produces one object at a time; neither brings a scene to equilibrium under contact. Elsewhere, soft objects enter a scene per asset or from a library [33, 67, 66, 64], or as dynamic episodes [62, 63, 65]. Sewing patterns provide garment rest shapes [53, 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59].

    Deformable simulation and differentiable physics.

    Discrete membrane and bending models [9] describe thin shells, incremental potential contact (IPC) keeps implicit time stepping intersection-free [3], its codimensional extension covers shells and rods [8], and vertex block descent minimizes the same potential by local block updates on the GPU [5]. Differentiable simulators propagate gradients through explicit [39] and implicit [38, 7] steps and estimate materials from captures [40, 41, 42, 44] or images [43], after gradient-free search [37]. CoDimRecon [22], concurrent with this work, reconstructs a simulation-ready scene of rods, shells and solids from multi-view RGB under IPC contact; the capture supplies resting geometry, layout and scale, so each object starts near equilibrium and is settled, whereas a generative pipeline has no observation to fit. We thus address this gap by constructing the inputs that a capture would otherwise supply.

    3 Method

    Given a text prompt, SoftPAT3D runs the generation stages of PAT3D [1] and then simulates the scene with its deformable objects to static equilibrium. Each stage constructs one input that the solver requires and generation does not supply (Fig. 2): support repair (Sec. 3.4), deformable-object initialization (Secs. 3.2 and 3.3), equilibration with a completion check (Sec. 3.5) and, when the prompt check fails, placement optimization (Sec. 3.6).

    3.1 Preliminaries

    PAT3D expands the prompt into a reference image, segments it [14], lifts each crop to a textured mesh [13], arranges the objects with a language model, converts them to simulation meshes [11] and simulates them as rigid bodies to static equilibrium. Following incremental potential contact [3], each time step advances the scene state x, the vector of all vertex positions, to the minimizer of

    E(x) = \tfrac12Δt² \lVertx-x̂\rVert²_M + ∑ₒΨₒ(xₒ) + B(x),

    		(1)

    where x̂=xₙ+Δt vₙ+Δt²M⁻¹fₑₓₜ is the predicted position, M the mass matrix, Ψₒ the elastic energy of object o and B the log-barrier contact potential,

    B(x)=κ∑ₖb(dₖ(x)), b(d)=-(d-d̂)²\ln\tfracdd̂,

    		(2)

    summed over every pair k of surface primitives whose distance dₖ is below the activation distance d̂, and zero beyond it, with lagged Coulomb friction. Each step is minimized by Newton’s method with a continuous-collision line search, so a trajectory that starts intersection-free remains so [4]. Rigid supports keep the affine-body energy Ψ_ABD(A)=κₐV\lVertA^⊤A-I\rVert_F² at κₐ=100 MPa and are fixed in place. SoftPAT3D changes only the energies Ψₒ of the deformable objects and the state x at the first step.

    3.2 Rest shapes

    The elastic energy requires a rest shape, and the generated asset does not provide one. A lifted towel arrives as a closed, already draped surface whose two layers lie closer than d̂, and thickening it would bake the generator’s folds into the rest shape (Table 4, first row).

    We therefore describe each deformable object by its manufacturing process, as flat panels cut to an outline, sewn along seams and optionally stuffed. Garments are sewn from parametric sewing patterns [53, 54], relaxed once to equilibrium and stored in a library of four patterns, T-shirt, trousers, skirt and dress, which every named garment in the paper draws on; plain linens are single panels discretized on a simulation grid, a 128×128 mesh on [0,w]×[0,ℓ], cut to an outline where the object has one, such as a round cloth or an apron; pillows are two seamed panels inflated into a superellipsoid |x/a|ᵖ+|y/b|ᵖ+|z/c|ᵖ=1 whose interior tetrahedralization serves as the stuffing. Since the scale of a monocular layout is ambiguous, every deformable object and support is clamped to the real-world size range of its class.

    3.3 Per-object energies

    Each object keeps or replaces its elastic energy according to its material class. A keyword classifier on the object’s name assigns it to rigid, thin-shell, volumetric-soft or rod, matching rigid compound names first. Cloth-class objects receive a Neo-Hookean membrane on the rest shape of the panel and discrete bending on its dihedral angles [9],

    Ψₛₕₑₗₗ(x)=∑ₜĀₜ h W(Fₜ)+k_b∑ₑ(\lVertē\rVert)/(h̄ₑ) (θₑ-θ̄ₑ)²,

    		(3)

    where Fₜ∈ℝ^3×2 is the deformation gradient of triangle t with rest area Āₜ, θₑ the dihedral angle at edge e with rest value θ̄ₑ, rest length \lVertē\rVert and height h̄ₑ, and the membrane energy density is

    W(F)=\tfracμ2(trF^⊤F-2)-μ\lnJ+\tfracλ2\ln²J,

    		(4)

    with J=√\detF^⊤F and Lamé parameters μ=E/2(1+ν) and λ=Eν/(1+ν)(1-2ν). Pillow-class objects are tetrahedralized and receive the rest-stabilized Neo-Hookean energy [10]

    Wᵥₒₗ(F)=\tfracμ2(trF^⊤F-3)+\tfracλ2(\detF-1-\tfracμλ)²

    		(5)

    with foam parameters. Cables, cords and ropes are an exploratory extension, a line mesh with the stretching and bending model of the codimensional solver’s rods [8] (supplementary material). A material library supplies the parameters of each class (Sec. 4.1). All energies share the barrier of Eq. (2), so mixed scenes of thin shells, volumetric solids, rods and rigid supports require no additional coupling.

    3.4 Physics-aware initialization

    The barrier requires an intersection-free initial state and collision meshes with a well-defined interior, neither of which generated assets provide.

    Support repair.

    The support is partly occluded by the deformable object in the reference image, and the generator fills the occluded region with the occluder, merging a seat with the pile on it. We inpaint the deformable object out of the crop of the support before lifting [47, 46, 50], regenerate the support from the completed image and align it to its slot in the layout. Without this step, the generator fills the mask with cloth merged into the support in 32 of 33 scenes. The regenerated mesh is then converted into a watertight collision mesh [11], since a single intersecting pair makes the solver reject the initial state. Contact is resolved against this closed surface, whose mean distance to the textured asset is 2.7 mm (development) and 3.0 mm (held-out).

    Placement.

    Objects visible in the reference image are placed at their layout positions. For objects the prompt introduces beyond the image, a language model, given a geometric summary of the candidate surfaces, returns a part such as the seat, backrest, arm or rim and a drop height. The cloth is sized from the top surface of its support with a 0.1 m overhang, or to the size the language model estimates, and placed at the drop height above the part. Every placement follows one principle: the object is placed above the part that the prompt names, at the lowest height at which its initial state is intersection-free, with its extent clamped to that part. The supplementary material lists the rules that apply this principle to the furniture classes of the scene set; a new support class needs no rule beyond the part vocabulary. Every placement is tested for intersection before the first step, and an intersecting placement is raised, y₀←y₀+δ, until \minₖdₖ(x₀)>d̂.

    3.5 Completion checks and rendering

    A converged simulation is not necessarily a complete scene. We therefore apply two geometric checks first. The containment check requires the centre of mass of the deformable object to project inside the ground projection F of its support. The support check rejects as a generation failure a support that is nearly as solid as its bounding box or far outside the size range of its class. Scenes that pass both geometric checks are then checked against the prompt by a vision–language model, the prompt check, queried twice on one render, J=[j₁=j₂=yes]; three further views and a second model agree with it on 49 and 44 of 60 scenes, and 5 human raters, who agree with one another on 92% of the renders, return its verdict on 94% of the scenes each on average (supplementary material). We call a scene complete when

    C = P∧S∧[X=0]∧G∧J,

    		(6)

    where P holds when every requested deformable object is present, S when the simulation converged without the solver rejecting an intersecting state, X is the number of deformable surface edges that intersect a collision mesh, and G holds when both geometric checks pass. In the main run the prompt check is recorded but not acted upon (Sec. 3.6).

    3.6 Placement optimization

    A scene that fails the prompt check has usually placed the object on a part of its support other than the one the prompt specifies. A language model maps the prompt to the intended part from a fixed vocabulary, or reports that no placement can satisfy it, and the part is resolved on the collision mesh to a target p, the area-weighted centroid of its faces, p=∑_f∈ℙA_fc_f/∑_fA_f. The placement θ=(cₓ,c_z) is then optimized so that the equilibrium state x^⋆(θ), rather than the initial one, meets the prompt,

    θ^⋆=\arg\min_θL(θ), L(θ)=\lVertΠ(x^⋆(θ))-p\rVert²,

    		(7)

    where Π projects the centre of mass of the equilibrated cloth onto the ground plane. We solve Eq. (7) with Adam using the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same energy. The simulation consists of N implicit steps, each solved by Newton’s method to stationarity of Eq. (1),

    Rₙ=\tfrac1Δt²M(xₙ₊₁-x̂ₙ)+∇(Ψ+B+D)|_xₙ₊₁=0,

    		(8)

    where x̂ₙ is the predicted position of Eq. (1), which carries the external force, D is the lagged friction potential, and θ enters through x₀.
