For a loss on x_N the gradient is dL/dθ=∑ₙwₙ^⊤∂Rₙ/∂θ, with adjoint variables wₙ obtained by a reverse sweep that solves one linear system per step with the Newton matrix ∂Rₙ/∂xₙ₊₁ of the converged step [6]; a solver-level alternative replays the block sweep in reverse [7]. The adjoint is exact as long as the active contact set does not change with θ, where it matches finite differences. For a single body the loss has two parameters, which a grid search covers: the pipeline re-simulates the placements

    θⱼ=θ₀+fⱼ (p_xz-θ₀), fⱼ∈{\tfrac12,\tfrac34,1},

    		(9)

    at the size the language model estimates and at the class size, subjects each candidate to the geometric checks and the prompt check, and keeps the first to pass. The adjoint serves where the search space grows: it optimizes the placements of several bodies jointly (Sec. 4.5) and, through the same sweep, the material parameters.

    4 Experimental Results

    4.1 Experimental setup

    Scenes.

    Since there is no standard benchmark for this task, we construct our own: thirty-two single-object scenes and three multi-body scenes generated end to end during development, and a second batch of thirty-two prompts written after the pipeline was frozen and run with one regeneration allowed and no other intervention. The main run is one run of the final code (scene set and prompts in the supplementary material).

    Baselines.

    The rigid pipeline runs the same prompt through the same stages and is measured after its own physics stage with the cloth asset kept rigid. Blender’s cloth solver runs on the generated asset as placed by the rigid pipeline (Blender) and on our inputs, the sewn cloth at our placement over our collision meshes (Blender∗), so that for cloth only the solver differs. Holodeck [15], a retrieval system, and GPT-6 Astra, a frontier model prompted to write a Blender program, build their own scenes from the same prompts (supplementary material). The baselines of PAT3D, GraphDreamer, Blender-MCP and MIDI, generate no deformable object and are not rerun.

    Metrics.

    All metrics are computed on the equilibrated geometry of the solver against its collision meshes: crossings, the number of deformable surface edges that intersect another body, per thousand edges; penetration, the mean depth of the vertices inside a closed body; contact, the fraction of vertices within 5 mm of another body; the number of bodies that touch nothing or are unsupported; and the completion criterion of Eq. (6). Crossings are the edge analogue of the penetrating-triangle ratio of PAT3D.

    Implementation details.

    Thin shells are simulated at Δt=0.02 s for up to 300 implicit steps, stopping once \maxᵢ\lVertxᵢⁿ-xᵢⁿ⁻⁴⁰\rVert<0.5 mm, with the cotton parameters of the material library for shells and its foam parameters for volumetric solids, effective rather than measured values (supplementary material). A sweep over time steps and mesh resolutions leaves every scene at static equilibrium with zero crossings (supplementary material).

    4.2 Comparison with other systems

    Table 2 scores six conditions under one protocol over the thirty-two single-object scenes, the clothes sofa and the hamper. The rigid pipeline starts from the same generated assets and layout as ours, but simulating the cloth as rigid bodies leaves them intersecting the furniture at 5.1 edges per thousand with 14.8 mm penetration, touching their supports over only 1.8% of their vertices and floating in 14 of 48 bodies, as in Fig. 4. Blender’s cloth solver diverges in 24 of 34 scenes and crosses at 196 per thousand edges on the generated asset, and still crosses at 66.2 per thousand given our inputs. Holodeck places a deformable object in only 8 of 32 scenes, and Astra models fabric without a cloth solver. By contrast, SoftPAT3D has zero crossings and zero penetration, the largest contact area, 39.9% of vertices, and no unsupported body; under Eq. (6) applied to every system, with the prompt check on the render of each system, 21 of our 34 scenes are complete, against 8 for Blender∗, 7 for Astra, 2 for Holodeck and 0 for the rigid pipeline. A render hides an intersection under the cloth, so these claims rest on the geometry; Fig. 5 shows a vertical section. Judged on renders under the protocol of PAT3D (Table 3), GPT-5.4 prefers our drape to that of the rigid pipeline in a side-swapped forced choice on 10 of 13 scenes, and its plausibility score rises from 43 to 90. In a blind study, 5 participants compare our render with a baseline’s on 10 prompts, systems unidentified and sides randomized, and prefer ours for physical validity and prompt satisfaction on every pair (supplementary material).

    4.3 End-to-end results

    Held-out prompts.

    The thirty-two prompts written after the pipeline was frozen are our primary measurement under Eq. (6). Every scene reaches static equilibrium with no crossing, five prompts lose an object upstream of the physics stage, and of the twenty-seven that reach it, 19 are complete with the placement optimization of Sec. 3.6 in the loop (19 of 32 overall). The physics stage alone completes 14, and the grid of Eq. (9) completes 5 of the 7 scenes whose prompt failure names a reachable part in six re-simulations per scene (supplementary material). On the same held-out inputs Blender’s cloth solver crosses at 24.4 per thousand edges and leaves 9 of 27 bodies unsupported, against zero and none for ours.

    Development set.

    Of the thirty-three development scenes, 21 are complete under the same criterion (Fig. 3), 25 with placement optimization, and none has a crossing; nine multi-body scenes with two to eight deformable objects (Fig. 3, bottom) reach equilibrium in one simulation and pass both checks.

    4.4 Applications

    Robotic manipulation.

    The same solver manipulates the equilibrated scene. A soft position constraint grips a patch G of the deformable object and adds

    Ψ_grip(x)=\tfrack_g2∑_i∈Gmᵢ \lVertxᵢ-gᵢ(t)\rVert²

    		(10)

    to Eq. (1), where gᵢ(t) is the gripper path along which the constraint moves the patch, holds it and releases it; the arm in Fig. 6 is posed for visualization only. Pull, lift and drag move a corner, the top centre or the patch, and press compresses a stuffed body by half its height. Over 28 episodes on 23 scenes, the patch reaches 90% of its commanded displacement in 23 of the 23 pull, lift and drag episodes, with a median grip error of 5.7 mm.

    Scene editing.

    The same mechanism removes a body by carrying it to the floor and adds one by holding and releasing it; on the messy bed (Fig. 6) the added pillow’s placement is optimized by the differentiable simulation (Sec. 4.5).

    4.5 Ablation studies

    Same-solver controls.

    In Table 4, the rest shape accounts for the largest share: with the closed surface of the generated asset in place of the sewn panel, the solver rejects the initial state on 11 scenes and the completed cloth scenes fall from 16 to 9. The watertight collision mesh brings every scene to equilibrium, placing each object on the part the language model names completes two more, and its size estimate one more, from 18 for a sewn panel placed centred over the support to 21 for the full physics stage (Fig. 7).

    Differentiable simulation.

    In the joint optimization of N bodies over an obstructed support, it lands about twice as many bodies as a coordinate grid search with twice its forward budget, and remains the best of the four methods over eight supports and 32 runs per N (supplementary material), because the gradient crosses the obstruction that a line search does not. The pillow added to the messy bed (Sec. 4) comes to rest 1.2 cm from its target under the adjoint’s placement, against 67 cm under the language model’s, and the same adjoint recovers a weight-to-stiffness ratio perturbed fourfold on 11 supports with a median error of 3% over 26 cases, against 16% for a random search at twice the budget (supplementary material). For a single body whose target lies on the grid’s line, the grid of Eq. (9) passes 9 of the 12 correctable scenes and the pipeline uses it; where an obstruction lies in between, the adjoint lands the body in 24 of 32 runs against 20 for the grid (supplementary material). From the prompt alone, without the reference image, all 65 scenes reach equilibrium and 57 pass both geometric checks, and 17 of the 32 held-out prompts pass the prompt check against 15 with the image.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented SoftPAT3D, which constructs the inputs a deformable simulation requires and brings deformable objects to equilibrium in text-to-3D scene generation. Limitations. A prompt that asks for a row of pillows or a folded towel is treated as a placement and fails the prompt check, and a support generated as a solid block has no part to place onto (Fig. 8). The sewn panel keeps the generated object’s kind in 48 of 60 scenes and its colour in 34; its size and folds follow the class prior. Materials are effective values [44]; plasticity is not modelled (cf. [22]).

    LLM Usage Statement

    Large language models are components of the method and are evaluated as such: a language model returns the supporting part and the size of each object the prompt introduces (Sec. 3.4), and a vision–language model performs the prompt check (Sec. 3.5). Beyond the method, LLM-based tools (Claude via Claude Code, and ChatGPT) were used at the assist level only, to edit and refine author-produced content: the text, the related work and citations, the code, the analysis of the experiments, the figures and the scene prompts. The authors take full responsibility for all submitted content.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Supplementary Material
    SoftPAT3D: Physics-Augmented Text-to-3D Scene Generation with Deformables

    Appendix A Scene Set

    In this section, we enumerate every scene that the pipeline is asked to equilibrate, including the rejected ones, so that each count in the main paper can be traced to its corresponding scenes. Table S1 is generated from the development runs rather than maintained by hand, and every rejected scene carries the check that rejects it. The final code’s outcome for each scene is given in the last block of Table S9, and Fig. S2 renders every scene that passes the geometric checks.

    Appendix B Held-out Prompts

    In this section, we provide the per-prompt record underlying the held-out count of the main paper. The thirty-two prompts of Table S1 are written while the pipeline is being built. After the pipeline is frozen, we write 32 more prompts over supports it has not been run on and run them end to end, with no asset redraw, placement override or parameter change, under the same solver settings as the main set. Table S4 lists every prompt with its outcome.

    We manually verify the routing against the prompts. Among the 63 objects that reach the solver, every towel, blanket, jacket, scarf, skirt, quilt, shirt, sweater, throw and tablecloth is routed to the shell energy, every cushion, pillow and plush toy is routed to the volumetric-body energy, and every support is routed to the rigid energy, with no error.

    The criterion is the one used throughout the paper. “Complete” means that the scene passes the containment and support checks, has zero cloth–support crossings on the colliders, and passes the prompt check of the main paper’s Sec. 3.5, run on one render per scene with the same script and the same two-answer rule as the main set and the controls. A second pass of the check over the same twenty-four renders, with two new answers each, returned the same verdict on every scene. “Upstream” means that the scene never reached the solver, because the generation stage’s own object list omitted one of the two requested objects. The outcome listed is that of the final code’s run over the held-out assets, the full-stage cell of Sec. C.1: 14 of 32 complete.

    Blender’s cloth solver.

    Given the same held-out inputs, the sewn sheet at our placement over our closed colliders exhibits crossings at 24.4 edges per thousand under Blender’s cloth solver and leaves 9 of its 27 bodies touching nothing, against zero and none for ours, and its cloth touches the support over 17% of its vertices against 53% for ours (Table S2). This is the shared-input condition that Blender∗ runs on the development set, here over the 25 held-out scenes that both solvers produced.

    Results with placement optimization.

    Seven of the scenes that fail the prompt check name a part that a placement can reach: the towel on the saddle, the counter towel, the skirt, the quilt on the footboard, the hamper towel, the marble-table cloth and the piano scarf. Sec. F re-solves them under the pipeline’s rule, and five pass, while the closed loop completes 19 of 32. The grid of Eq. 9 of the main paper passes these five at six re-simulations per scene (Table S3).

item.title: 教 VLA 玩游戏缺的是数据：这个框架让 LLM 自己造关卡、自己录专家演示，省掉人工采集 ｜ From Game Generation to Game Playing: Fully Automated Ability Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description:
一句话：跨游戏训练 VLA 卡在演示采集成本上；解法是把「造环境」也交给 agent。

要点：

  • 瓶颈是数据：要让 VLA 模型在多种游戏里遵循玩法指令，采集演示的成本极高
  • 框架分两段：先用 LLM 驱动的 agent 调用**游戏构建工具**，造出可执行的环境与针对特定技能的任务
  • 再用程序化的「专家」借助模拟器的特权信息（privileged information）产出专家演示，从而自动化整条数据链路

为什么值得看：「让 agent 自己造关卡、自己打出示范」是一条很有引擎意味的闭环：环境生成与行为数据同时被自动化。对做 AI 训练环境、或者想用自家引擎批量造训练数据的团队，这个结构可以直接照搬。

中文摘要：要让视觉-语言-动作（VLA）模型在多种游戏中遵循玩法指令，最大的限制是演示数据的采集成本。这篇提出一条把「造游戏」和「玩游戏」连起来的自动化链路：先用 LLM 驱动的 agent 调用游戏构建工具，生成可执行的环境与针对特定技能的任务；再由程序化专家利用模拟器提供的特权信息，在这些环境里产出专家演示。这样环境生成与行为数据被同一条流水线自动产出，绕开了人工采集这一最贵的环节。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

From Game Generation to Game Playing:
Fully Automated Ability Training for Vision-Language-Action Models

Abstract

Training vision-language-action (VLA) models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. We introduce a framework that automatically generates game environments and expert demonstrations. An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and tasks targeting specified skills. Programmatic experts then use privileged simulator state to generate aligned instructions, rendered observations, and keyboard and mouse actions. We train our game policy, Script2Play, by post-training a 4B vision-language model with behavior cloning on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning. Evaluation on multiple public game benchmarks demonstrates that Script2Play follows gameplay instructions effectively and generalizes across game engines, highlighting the effectiveness of targeted synthetic supervision.

1 Introduction

Developing generalist agents that ground free-form language instructions in visual observations and execute low-level actions in interactive environments is a central step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence [25, 26, 36, 27]. Video games offer a rich testbed for studying these capabilities: a single agent must map an instruction and rendered frames into human-compatible actions, such as key presses and mouse movements, across worlds with varying visuals, physics, and interaction logic [25, 12, 41]. However, training vision-language-action (VLA) models that generalize across games faces a persistent supervision bottleneck. Existing approaches largely rely on human gameplay demonstrations [3, 25, 16, 36, 37, 38] or online reinforcement learning (RL) [15, 23]. Collecting human demonstrations with aligned instructions and actions is costly across diverse tasks and titles. Public gameplay recordings and internet video corpora [13, 3, 11, 37, 9, 20, 38, 21] may lack explicit task boundaries and verifiable completion signals, or require retrospective captioning. RL requires interactive access, reward shaping, and extensive rollouts for each game. Hand-built training suites [10, 23] also require substantial engineering effort whenever a new gameplay skill or mechanic is introduced.

Our core insight is that both skill-targeted game creation and expert demonstration generation can be framed as coding-agent tasks [1, 2]. Because game engines represent scenes, mechanics, and task logic as code, an LLM-powered agent can invoke game-building tools from a natural-language skill specification (such as navigation, dynamic obstacle avoidance, moving-target aiming, combat, or object interaction) to construct playable environments paired with programmatic task verifiers. Crucially, unlike commercial games that expose only rendered pixels, a generated environment exposes its full privileged ground-truth state, including character poses, target locations, enemy trajectories, and collision geometry. The coding agent can therefore also write programmatic expert controllers (using pathfinding, analytic target tracking, or finite-state machines) that read this privileged state to solve each task while issuing actions strictly through standard keyboard and mouse inputs. Automated playability and verification checks retain only successful rollouts, turning privileged simulator state into a purely synthetic, data-efficient stream of aligned instructions, frames, and actions. Every trajectory targets a specified skill, with exact instruction boundaries and verified completion, avoiding the idle traversal and label noise of raw human gameplay.

We obtain Script2Play by post-training Qwen3.5-4B on 150.3 hours of synthetic gameplay: 26.9 hours from Minecraft and 123.4 hours from Roblox, with zero human gameplay demonstrations. The same unified checkpoint is evaluated on all three benchmarks [35, 18, 15]. Script2Play outperforms policies trained on thousands of hours of human play on OpenHA and OmniGameArena [36, 20, 38, 41]. A separate comparison holds the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone fixed and uses only our Minecraft subset to compare programmatic supervision with human-play and RL-based training pipelines. These results show that our framework can train game agents with strong instruction-following abilities and cross-engine generalization using a modest amount of scripted demonstration data.

Our contributions are three-fold:

  • 1.

    We design an automated, skill-conditioned game generation framework in which a tool-using coding agent constructs executable game environments, diverse instruction-following tasks, and state-based verifiers directly from natural-language specifications.

  • 2.

    We introduce a purely synthetic, data-efficient programmatic expert supervision pipeline that leverages privileged simulator state to synthesize verified, human-compatible keyboard-and-mouse demonstrations for post-training pixel-to-action VLA models without human gameplay data.

  • 3.

    Using only 150.3 h of scripted teacher data, Script2Play outperforms policies trained on thousands of hours of human gameplay on public game benchmarks.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Visual Game-Playing Agents

    Visual game agents learn low-level control directly from rendered frames and human-native input interfaces. In Minecraft, early policies learn behavioral priors from video [3, 17, 6], while recent approaches post-train VLMs for keyboard-and-mouse actions [34, 16] or combine high-level planners with frame-level controllers [35, 29, 30]. Across broader virtual worlds, generalist agents scale screen-to-action learning through unified keyboard, mouse, or gamepad interfaces [25, 26, 28, 24, 36, 27], large-scale behavior cloning [37, 20, 38], joint world-action modeling [12], and multi-world continued pretraining [41]. Our work differs in the source of post-training supervision: we use programmatic experts in automatically generated game environments rather than newly collected human gameplay or target-game RL.

    2.2 RL in Generated Environments

    Procedural generation [10, 7] and generative world models [4] diversify training experience, whereas LLM-driven pipelines can further synthesize executable tasks and environments in code for embodied agents [39, 31, 32], tool use [33], and game engines [8, 19, 43]. Gym-Anything-RT [2] uses coding agents to construct real-time minigames for evaluation, while Gym-Anything for Robotics [1] builds audited robotics simulations and uses privileged code policies to train VLAs. Our pipeline targets transferable game-playing skills: it generates games from skill specifications, audits them to reject trivial and instruction-agnostic tasks, and records scripted teachers acting in real time at the student’s control rate. These demonstrations train visual policies by behavior cloning without VLM annotation.

    2.3 Game Datasets and Benchmarks

    Large-scale datasets for training game and computer-use agents include Minecraft recordings and knowledge corpora [13, 3, 11], multi-game and desktop action trajectories such as Pixels2Play (Open-P2P) [37, 38], D2E [9], Gaming-500-Hours [21], and NitroGen [20], as well as synthetic capture platforms such as Isekai3D SDG [14]. For evaluation, public benchmarks span first-person combat in ViZDoom [15], open-world Minecraft tasks in MineStudio [5], MCU [42], and OpenHA [35], classic console and DOS titles in VideoGameBench [40], verifiable browser games in GameWorld [22], and real-time UE5 games in OmniGameArena [18]. Rather than relying on human recordings or retrospective video labeling, our pipeline synthesizes aligned instruction, frame, and action trajectories with programmatic verifiers, and evaluates transfer across these public benchmarks.

    3 Method

    Figure1 gives an overview. A coding agent turns a natural-language specification of a gameplay skill into a playable game. For each episode, the game samples a scene—its layout, assets, and dynamics—and assigns an instruction with a task verifier. A scripted teacher attempts the task, and successful episodes become training demonstrations. We first define the student, teacher, and behavior-cloning objective (Sec.3.1), then describe game generation and verification (Sec.3.2).

    3.1 Instruction-Following Training

    Student and teacher.

    Let t index control decisions, spaced 200 ms apart; sₜ is the engine state, oₜ=R(sₜ) the rendered observation, g the instruction, and aₜ=(kₜ,mₜ) a keyboard-and-mouse action chunk. The student policy, Script2Play, is denoted by π_θ(aₜ|xₜ) and observes xₜ=(g,o_t-h:t,a_t-h:t-1): the instruction, current frame, and h previous frame–action pairs. It never observes engine state. All reported benchmark policies use h=0, so each decision depends on the instruction and current frame alone. The teacher π^*(aₜ|sₜ,g) is a program written by the coding agent for each game. It reads character poses and velocities, target coordinates, enemy and projectile states, and collision geometry. Depending on the task, it uses pathfinding, motion prediction for aiming, finite-state control, or timing rules to select actions. The teacher executes these actions through the same keyboard-and-mouse interface and at the same control rate as the student. It never teleports objects or bypasses game physics.

    Teacher rollouts.

    A task τ=(s₀,g,V) consists of an initial scene s₀, an instruction g, and a verifier V. The verifier uses engine state to check task completion within a time budget T_τ and to detect prohibited events, such as reaching the wrong target or falling. A teacher rollout with L_τ control decisions is

    ξ_τ=((g,oₜ,a^*ₜ))ₜ₌₁^L_τ,

    		(1)

    and the training corpus retains only successful rollouts: D={ξ_τ:V(ξ_τ)=1}. Videos are recorded at 20 fps and aligned with 200 ms action windows. Instructions come from the task specification, action labels from the teacher, and success labels from the verifier; no human gameplay demonstration or retrospective VLM annotation is needed.

    Behavior cloning.

    Starting from a pretrained open-weight VLM, we train on the teacher’s action labels. The unweighted gameplay loss is

    L_BC(θ)=-𝔼_τ, t[\logπ_θ(a^*ₜ|g,o_t-h:t,a^*_t-h:t-1)],

    		(2)

    where τ indexes a retained rollout and t a control decision within it. For h>0, training uses the teacher’s action history; this history is empty in the reported h=0 setting. All of our benchmark policies in Sec.4 use behavior cloning on synthetic gameplay. To emphasize changes in control, we increase the token-loss weight for action windows whose held-key set differs from the preceding window: by a factor of 5 for Roblox and 3 for Minecraft. We also include generic visual question answering, optical character recognition, and text examples in 15% of each batch to help retain general capabilities. These auxiliary examples contain no gameplay. At inference, the model runs in closed loop on each benchmark’s native engine, mapping frames and instructions directly to keyboard and mouse actions. Following Lumine [27], the model generates each action chunk autoregressively as plain text: ΔX ΔY ; K₁ ; K₂ ; K₃ ; K₄. The mouse displacement (ΔX,ΔY) is distributed across the 200 ms window, while K₁ through K₄ specify the keys and mouse buttons held in its four successive 50 ms intervals. Unlisted keys are released. At each new control decision, the model receives the latest frame and instruction; if h>0, the context also includes its previous predicted actions and observations.

    3.2 Data Generation

    From specification to game.

    A specification has five fields: the gameplay skill, camera, dynamics ranges, controls, and task contract (Tab.5). The contract defines which target the instruction refers to and which events invalidate an episode. The coding agent implements the scene, interactive mechanics, task verifier, and teacher using a shared runtime library (AppendixB). It also writes a scene generator to vary layouts, spawn points, targets, dynamics, and assets, and an offline mirror: a separate implementation of the game rules for fast teacher and verifier checks. When a scene supports multiple targets, we construct paired tasks that share the scene but request different targets. These counterfactual pairs test whether the verifier distinguishes the requested target from a distractor; pursuing the other target must fail. Visual and physical randomization varies the world theme, player and NPC appearances, camera, layout, dynamics, and instruction wording while preserving the underlying mechanic, as illustrated by Melee arena (Fig.2). This variation is intended to reduce dependence on a particular visual setting; Sec.4 evaluates transfer to other engines.

    Audit and validation.

    A game’s rollouts enter D only after it passes five automated gates, in the spirit of the creation-audit loop of [1] (checks detailed in Tab.6):

  • •

    G1 Static: the code compiles, and paired tasks share the same scene.

  • •

    G2 Solvable: the teacher solves at least 95% of tested episodes in the offline mirror, both under nominal timing and with added latency.

  • •

    G3 Non-trivial: idle, hold-forward, and random-key policies rarely succeed, and a teacher pursuing the other task’s target also rarely succeeds on the instructed task.

  • •

    G4 Engine parity: the teacher’s success rate in the engine is within five percentage points of its rate in the mirror.

  • •

    G5 Visual: recorded frames are non-blank and change over the episode.

    • G3 screens for two failure modes: tasks that can be solved without observing the scene, and verifiers that accept the wrong instructed target. For recoverable failures, the agent adjusts task tolerances to improve teacher success or eliminate trivial solutions, then reruns the audit, with at most three repair rounds. Games that fail G1 or the wrong-target check are discarded (Algorithm1).

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments test the central premise of this work: generating games around general skills can provide sufficient supervision for capable and transferable game-playing policies. We examine whether synthetic demonstrations support competitive instruction following, whether the learned control skills transfer to engines excluded from post-training, and whether the advantage persists when methods use the same VLM backbone. All of our benchmark policies are trained by behavior cloning, without human gameplay demonstrations, RL, or DAgger.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Training data and model.

    Script2Play uses a Qwen3.5-4B backbone jointly trained on Minecraft and Roblox demonstrations, totaling 150.3 h of verified scripted-teacher gameplay: 26.9 h from Minecraft and 123.4 h from Roblox. The OpenHA, OmniGameArena, and ViZDoom results in Tabs.1, 2 and 4 all use this same unified checkpoint. The student receives rendered frames and an instruction; privileged engine state is used only by the teacher and verifier during data generation. Frames are recorded at 20 fps. Each training example pairs an instruction and a single 480p frame with a 200 ms action window containing four 50 ms key groups and a mouse displacement; the context length is h=0. We freeze the vision encoder and projector and train on 8 H200 GPUs using bfloat16 and a global batch size of 384 windows. The learning rate is 2×10⁻⁵, with 5% warmup followed by cosine decay to 10% of its peak value.

    Skill coverage.

    We determine the game mixture by surveying games on mainstream gaming platforms and tasks in public game benchmarks, and estimating the relative frequency of the gameplay skills they require. This empirical skill distribution guides both the proportions of generated game categories and the allocation of demonstration collection across them (Fig.3). The 123.4 h of Roblox demonstrations come from 41 generated games across six categories: combat and shooting (56.4 h), traversal and parkour (21.5 h), object interaction (20.8 h), dodging and survival (19.7 h), GUI operation (3.7 h), and ball games (1.3 h). The 26.9 h of Minecraft demonstrations comprise 31,494 verified episodes and cover three categories: Embodied mining and workstation interaction (5.0 h), GUI crafting and smelting (19.0 h), and Combat (2.9 h). Scripted teachers collect these demonstrations in MineStudio [5] using 48 custom world seeds disjoint from the evaluation worlds, with randomized spawn locations, tool and inventory loadouts, and surrounding distractors.

    Benchmarks and metrics.

    OpenHA [35] evaluates Minecraft instruction following across Embodied, GUI, and Combat tasks; we report success rates for each group and their average.Because Minecraft demonstrations are included in training, OpenHA tests downstream performance within a training engine. OmniGameArena [18] and ViZDoom [15] test cross-engine transfer: neither UE5 nor Doom gameplay is included in our policy post-training. For OmniGameArena, we evaluate the five solo games in Tab.2 using their native normalized scores and the mean across games. Following the official benchmark protocols, we evaluate each OpenHA task over three trials and each OmniGameArena task over 5 trials. For ViZDoom, we follow the four-map protocol of [36, 12] and report the mean episode reward over 50 episodes per map, with the simulator running at 35,Hz.

    Comparisons.

    We include commercial VLMs, open-weight VLMs, and trained game policies based on human gameplay, RL, or both. The benchmark tables compare complete systems; the shared-backbone comparison in Sec.4.4 narrows the architectural differences. Data scale refers to gameplay used for policy training; hour equivalents inferred from tokens or frames are approximate (AppendixC).

    4.2 Learning from Synthetic Demonstrations

    The first question is whether skill-targeted synthetic supervision is sufficient to train a strong instruction-following policy from a pretrained VLM. On OpenHA (Tab.1), Script2Play reaches 69.6% average success, exceeding the strongest prior trained policy, Game-TARS MoE-mini (64.5%), by 5.1 percentage points. These results establish state-of-the-art performance among the trained game policies compared here using only 150.3 h of synthetic post-training data and a behavior-cloning objective. They demonstrate that human gameplay and online RL are not prerequisites for this level of downstream performance.

    4.3 Transfer to Unseen Game Engines

    Strong Minecraft performance alone does not establish that generated skills transfer beyond a training engine. We therefore evaluate the same unified checkpoint on UE5 and Doom, whose environments and trajectories are excluded from the training mixture. The generated mechanics target relevant gameplay skills, making these benchmarks a test of whether those skills can be reused under changes in visual appearance, dynamics, and task composition.

    OmniGameArena: transfer beyond the training worlds.

    Script2Play achieves a mean score of 0.640 (Tab.2), the highest score among all compared agents. It exceeds the best commercial VLM in this comparison, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (0.473), by 0.167, and the strongest human-gameplay policy, GameScaling-9B-S3 (0.361), by 0.279. The latter uses 1,600 h of human gameplay, compared with our 150.3 h of synthetic demonstrations. This result supports the value of targeted skill coverage: a comparatively small generated corpus can produce effective control in an engine absent from policy post-training. Because the systems differ in backbone, training procedure, and data composition, the comparison establishes an efficient operating point rather than a sample-complexity ratio.

    ViZDoom: transfer of combat skills.

    On ViZDoom (Tab.4), Script2Play achieves a mean reward of 12.92 without ViZDoom trajectories or target-game RL, approaching the zero-shot Game-TARS MoE-mini (14.54) with a much smaller model and substantially less gameplay data. The comparisons differ in training domain and model capacity. GameWAM is trained directly on expert APPO trajectories from the four evaluation maps, whereas Script2Play transfers zero-shot. Game-TARS is built on the substantially larger Seed1.5-VL mixture-of-experts backbone and uses explicit sparse thinking [36]; Script2Play is a 4B model that omits explicit reasoning traces to reduce inference latency. The Battle maps also require more than shooting: the agent must infer when to search for and collect health and ammunition even though the instruction only asks it to kill enemies. These implicit subgoals, together with finding enemies outside the current field of view, are difficult for a history-free policy (h=0), which cannot use previous observations to track searched areas or supply locations. On DefendLine, Script2Play reaches 22.94, nearly matching the in-domain GameWAM result of 23.52 and exceeding Game-TARS at 15.24.

    Action sequences reveal how control transfers.

    Figure4 connects the aggregate results to the actions of the learned policy. In the OpenHA combat example, the policy turns and advances toward the target before issuing attack inputs; the GUI example combines mouse positioning with item-manipulation clicks. On the held-out UE5 engine, ObstacleRun3D requires the policy to interleave forward motion with timed jump inputs, while CueChase combines camera adjustment, approach, and interaction. The same action-chunk representation therefore supports distinct control behaviors across Minecraft and UE5. These selected successful episodes illustrate how the policy uses the interface; the benchmark scores quantify how reliably it succeeds.

    4.4 Effect of the Supervision Source

    The main comparisons combine changes in supervision with changes in model and training procedure. To examine whether the benefit persists with a shared backbone, we compare three Minecraft policies initialized from Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Tab.4): OpenHA trained on human play, HiSTEVE trained with human-derived supervision and RL, and our policy trained by behavior cloning on 26.9 h of verified Minecraft teacher demonstrations. This experiment uses a separate 7B, Minecraft-only variant of Script2Play, excluding both the Roblox data and the Qwen3.5-4B backbone used for the main results.

    The advantage persists with a shared backbone.

    On in-domain Minecraft tasks (Tab.4a), scripted supervision reaches 45.9% average success, exceeding OpenHA (31.5%) by 14.4 points and HiSTEVE (37.4%) by 8.5 points, and leads both baselines across all three task groups: Embodied (49.7% versus 30.1% and 46.0%), GUI (39.0% versus 32.5% and 27.2%), and Combat (49.0% versus 31.9% and 39.0%). The shared initialization rules out a newer backbone as the sole explanation for the in-domain gain. We also evaluate OpenHA and our 7B variant zero-shot on OmniGameArena (Tab.4b); HiSTEVE weights are unavailable for this comparison. Our variant achieves a similar mean score to OpenHA (0.028 versus 0.023), so its in-domain gains are accompanied by comparable zero-shot performance in this evaluation.

    5 Conclusion

    We introduced a fully automated framework that generates games, task verifiers, and programmatic experts from gameplay skill specifications. Behavior cloning on 150.3 h of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay produces Script2Play, a unified 4B VLA policy trained without human gameplay demonstrations or online RL. The same checkpoint is used across three benchmarks, leading the compared trained policies on OpenHA and achieving the highest mean score on the evaluated OmniGameArena games. These results demonstrate how pretrained visual knowledge and programmatic action supervision can support transferable game control. Extending skill coverage to more complex interactions and longer-horizon objectives is a promising next step.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Fully Generated Games

    This section details the workflow in Sec.3.2, from a gameplay skill specification to verified demonstrations for policy training. Each specification describes the target skills, camera, dynamics, controls, and a task contract defining the instructed target and failure conditions. The coding agent implements the game, its scene generator, a scripted teacher, a task verifier, and an offline mirror of the game rules. The scene generator varies layouts, appearances, and dynamics, while instruction paraphrases preserve the task’s meaning. Counterfactual task pairs share a scene but request different targets; we refer to each member of a pair as an arm. These pairs allow the audit to check whether success depends on following the instruction.

    The full loop.

    Algorithm1 summarizes game generation, verification, demonstration collection, and behavior cloning.

    Specification fields.

    Table5 describes the specification fields and their role in game generation.

    Creation-audit gates.

    Table6 summarizes the audit checks. The offline mirror provides a fast way to test teachers and verifiers before recording in the game engine. Engine rollouts then check whether the same behavior remains valid under actual rendering and input timing.

    Teacher success alone does not establish that a task provides useful supervision. The audit must also detect goals already satisfied at spawn, tasks solvable by waiting, and verifiers that accept the wrong target. For sustained actions, the verifier must distinguish an uninterrupted hold from time accumulated across separate attempts. These checks prevent successful but uninformative episodes from entering the training corpus.

    Repair and acceptance.

    For recoverable failures, the agent adjusts task tolerances and reruns the audit. Wider tolerances can make a task solvable, while narrower tolerances can eliminate trivial solutions. A candidate is discarded if it fails static validity or wrong-target checks, or if it cannot pass the audit within the repair budget. Accepted games proceed to demonstration collection.

    Teacher decision loop.

    Algorithm2 describes the teacher’s latency-compensated decision loop (Sec.3.2). At each control step, the teacher reads privileged state and accounts for inputs that have been issued but have not yet taken effect. It then selects a task-specific action and converts it into the same keyboard-and-mouse representation used by the student.

    Demonstration collection.

    The teacher executes each task through the game’s normal input interface, while the recorder aligns rendered observations with instructions and action chunks. The verifier checks completion and prohibited events throughout the episode. Only successful, verified rollouts enter the training corpus. Behavior cloning then trains the student on the recorded instructions, images, and actions; privileged state remains available only to the teacher and verifier.

    Using feedback to guide generation.

    Evaluation episodes can be grouped by primary skill, secondary skill, camera, and control family to identify recurring failures. Groups with high failure rates guide the next game specifications. When failures mainly involve timeouts, falls, or hazard collisions, the generator can create an easier version to introduce the skill gradually. The resulting games pass through the same audit and demonstration-collection workflow before contributing training data.

    Appendix B Coding Agent, Tools, and an Example Game

    Coding agent.

    Each Roblox game in Fig.3 was written by a Cursor agent in Agent mode with Claude Opus 5.5, one game at a time, with access to the game repository and run directories. For each game, the agent writes four components and registers the task templates. The scenario module, written in server-side Luau, declares the templates and constructs an episode from its seed. The game module, written in client-side Luau, implements the mechanics in a custom fixed-step simulation at 60 Hz, without Roblox’s physics engine. The teacher is a Python controller that reads published engine state and returns a 200 ms action chunk containing four 50 ms key groups and mouse motion. The offline mirror reimplements the game in Python and runs it in closed loop with the teacher. The agent then runs the checks, recording, and export commands described in Sec.3.2, and inspects frames from the recordings. A person provides the specifications and shared asset packs as input; during development, a person also spot-checked each new game’s code and a short video, but the pipeline does not require this, and all fixes were made by the agent.

    Tools.

    The agent’s own tools are reading and editing files, a shell, and viewing images. Each server session constructs its Roblox environment from source files through Rojo; environments are not edited manually in Roblox Studio. The environment-editing, terrain, asset-placement, and scripting tools of Sec.3.2 are a runtime library that the generated code calls, and the checks are command-line tools (Tab.7).

    Prompt.

    A prompt provides the game specification, required steps, and files to read first: the runtime library and the most relevant existing game, teacher, and mirror. A repository guide defines coding conventions and runtime limits: at most eight engine workers, one recording at a time, and no changes to game files during recording. Prompts took this form:

    Add a template game to the gym following GAME_CREATION.md: . Read GameKit.lua, GymGameSpec.lua, GymContext.lua and (game, scenario, teacher, mirror) first. Write the scenario, the game module, the teacher and the offline mirror, register them, get the mirror to 95% on both arms, then run a 16-episode engine check and show me frames from a passed and a failed episode.

    Example: Laser Maintenance Bridge.

    Table8 gives the specification of a traversal-and-parkour game using the fields in Tab.5; Fig.5 shows the two counterfactual arms for one scene in the generated game. The agent wrote a 159-line scenario module, a 144-line game module, a 176-line teacher, and a 176-line mirror. The teacher keeps the camera facing down the bridge and predicts the player’s position when the next action takes effect, accounting for previously issued inputs. It waits for a safe interval in the sweeping laser’s motion, approaches a gap and jumps while holding W, crouches under the low laser with C, and stops at the center of the instructed marker. It estimates input latency online from the distance traveled after issuing W. In the mirror, the teacher passed all 120 episodes (40 seeds per template) under nominal timing and 119 of 120 with three extra frames of latency and 12–24-frame decision gaps; the single failure was a laser contact. The engine check passed all 48 episodes (16 per template, covering both arms). Of the 990 recorded episodes (165 counterfactual pairs per template), 988 passed, yielding 1.6 h of demonstrations recorded at 20 fps.

    Appendix C Experimental Data Accounting

    Our training mixture.

    The Script2Play benchmark policy is initialized from Qwen3.5-4B and jointly trained on 150.3 h of synthetic demonstrations, comprising 26.9 h from Minecraft and 123.4 h from Roblox. The same unified checkpoint is evaluated on OpenHA, OmniGameArena, and ViZDoom in Tabs.1, 2 and 4. The separate Qwen2.5-VL-7B variant in the supervision comparison uses only the Minecraft component. All of our benchmark policies use behavior cloning; neither RL nor DAgger contributes to our results.

    Baseline scales.

    Tables 1 and 4 report approximate hour equivalents, marked with †. The original conversion assumes 20 fps and approximately 350 tokens per frame, or 25M tokens per hour. Its inputs are: ROCKET-1, 1.6B frames; OpenHA, 3.62B tokens; JARVIS-VLA and HiSTEVE, 7.4M world frames and 6.4M GUI entries (also described as approximately 10B tokens); UI-TARS-1.5, approximately 50B general GUI tokens and 14–16B Minecraft tokens; GameWAM, 200k 96-frame VPT clips plus additional VPT and scripted GUI trajectories (2.79B tokens); and Game-TARS, approximately 14B Minecraft tokens out of 233B/566B total tokens [36]. For STEVE-1, the approximately 70,750 h estimate combines 70,000 h of inherited VPT pretraining with 54M human and VPT-generated fine-tuning frames (approximately 750 h at 20 fps) [3, 17]. The ViZDoom estimate was derived from 7.71M training windows (21,900 updates with batch size 352) [12]. These quantities mix source frames, GUI entries, tokens, and samples processed during optimization, so they do not define a uniform measure of unique gameplay duration or training compute. We use them only to describe the reported training scale, not to infer a controlled data-efficiency ratio.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：跨游戏训练 VLA 卡在演示采集成本上；解法是把「造环境」也交给 agent。

要点：

  • 瓶颈是数据：要让 VLA 模型在多种游戏里遵循玩法指令，采集演示的成本极高
  • 框架分两段：先用 LLM 驱动的 agent 调用**游戏构建工具**，造出可执行的环境与针对特定技能的任务
  • 再用程序化的「专家」借助模拟器的特权信息（privileged information）产出专家演示，从而自动化整条数据链路

为什么值得看：「让 agent 自己造关卡、自己打出示范」是一条很有引擎意味的闭环：环境生成与行为数据同时被自动化。对做 AI 训练环境、或者想用自家引擎批量造训练数据的团队，这个结构可以直接照搬。

中文摘要：要让视觉-语言-动作（VLA）模型在多种游戏中遵循玩法指令，最大的限制是演示数据的采集成本。这篇提出一条把「造游戏」和「玩游戏」连起来的自动化链路：先用 LLM 驱动的 agent 调用游戏构建工具，生成可执行的环境与针对特定技能的任务；再由程序化专家利用模拟器提供的特权信息，在这些环境里产出专家演示。这样环境生成与行为数据被同一条流水线自动产出，绕开了人工采集这一最贵的环节。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

From Game Generation to Game Playing:
Fully Automated Ability Training for Vision-Language-Action Models

Abstract

Training vision-language-action (VLA) models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. We introduce a framework that automatically generates game environments and expert demonstrations. An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and tasks targeting specified skills. Programmatic experts then use privileged simulator state to generate aligned instructions, rendered observations, and keyboard and mouse actions. We train our game policy, Script2Play, by post-training a 4B vision-language model with behavior cloning on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning. Evaluation on multiple public game benchmarks demonstrates that Script2Play follows gameplay instructions effectively and generalizes across game engines, highlighting the effectiveness of targeted synthetic supervision.

1 Introduction

Developing generalist agents that ground free-form language instructions in visual observations and execute low-level actions in interactive environments is a central step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence [25, 26, 36, 27]. Video games offer a rich testbed for studying these capabilities: a single agent must map an instruction and rendered frames into human-compatible actions, such as key presses and mouse movements, across worlds with varying visuals, physics, and interaction logic [25, 12, 41]. However, training vision-language-action (VLA) models that generalize across games faces a persistent supervision bottleneck. Existing approaches largely rely on human gameplay demonstrations [3, 25, 16, 36, 37, 38] or online reinforcement learning (RL) [15, 23]. Collecting human demonstrations with aligned instructions and actions is costly across diverse tasks and titles. Public gameplay recordings and internet video corpora [13, 3, 11, 37, 9, 20, 38, 21] may lack explicit task boundaries and verifiable completion signals, or require retrospective captioning. RL requires interactive access, reward shaping, and extensive rollouts for each game. Hand-built training suites [10, 23] also require substantial engineering effort whenever a new gameplay skill or mechanic is introduced.

Our core insight is that both skill-targeted game creation and expert demonstration generation can be framed as coding-agent tasks [1, 2]. Because game engines represent scenes, mechanics, and task logic as code, an LLM-powered agent can invoke game-building tools from a natural-language skill specification (such as navigation, dynamic obstacle avoidance, moving-target aiming, combat, or object interaction) to construct playable environments paired with programmatic task verifiers. Crucially, unlike commercial games that expose only rendered pixels, a generated environment exposes its full privileged ground-truth state, including character poses, target locations, enemy trajectories, and collision geometry. The coding agent can therefore also write programmatic expert controllers (using pathfinding, analytic target tracking, or finite-state machines) that read this privileged state to solve each task while issuing actions strictly through standard keyboard and mouse inputs. Automated playability and verification checks retain only successful rollouts, turning privileged simulator state into a purely synthetic, data-efficient stream of aligned instructions, frames, and actions. Every trajectory targets a specified skill, with exact instruction boundaries and verified completion, avoiding the idle traversal and label noise of raw human gameplay.

We obtain Script2Play by post-training Qwen3.5-4B on 150.3 hours of synthetic gameplay: 26.9 hours from Minecraft and 123.4 hours from Roblox, with zero human gameplay demonstrations. The same unified checkpoint is evaluated on all three benchmarks [35, 18, 15]. Script2Play outperforms policies trained on thousands of hours of human play on OpenHA and OmniGameArena [36, 20, 38, 41]. A separate comparison holds the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone fixed and uses only our Minecraft subset to compare programmatic supervision with human-play and RL-based training pipelines. These results show that our framework can train game agents with strong instruction-following abilities and cross-engine generalization using a modest amount of scripted demonstration data.

Our contributions are three-fold:

  • 1.

    We design an automated, skill-conditioned game generation framework in which a tool-using coding agent constructs executable game environments, diverse instruction-following tasks, and state-based verifiers directly from natural-language specifications.

  • 2.

    We introduce a purely synthetic, data-efficient programmatic expert supervision pipeline that leverages privileged simulator state to synthesize verified, human-compatible keyboard-and-mouse demonstrations for post-training pixel-to-action VLA models without human gameplay data.

  • 3.

    Using only 150.3 h of scripted teacher data, Script2Play outperforms policies trained on thousands of hours of human gameplay on public game benchmarks.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Visual Game-Playing Agents

    Visual game agents learn low-level control directly from rendered frames and human-native input interfaces. In Minecraft, early policies learn behavioral priors from video [3, 17, 6], while recent approaches post-train VLMs for keyboard-and-mouse actions [34, 16] or combine high-level planners with frame-level controllers [35, 29, 30]. Across broader virtual worlds, generalist agents scale screen-to-action learning through unified keyboard, mouse, or gamepad interfaces [25, 26, 28, 24, 36, 27], large-scale behavior cloning [37, 20, 38], joint world-action modeling [12], and multi-world continued pretraining [41]. Our work differs in the source of post-training supervision: we use programmatic experts in automatically generated game environments rather than newly collected human gameplay or target-game RL.

    2.2 RL in Generated Environments

    Procedural generation [10, 7] and generative world models [4] diversify training experience, whereas LLM-driven pipelines can further synthesize executable tasks and environments in code for embodied agents [39, 31, 32], tool use [33], and game engines [8, 19, 43]. Gym-Anything-RT [2] uses coding agents to construct real-time minigames for evaluation, while Gym-Anything for Robotics [1] builds audited robotics simulations and uses privileged code policies to train VLAs. Our pipeline targets transferable game-playing skills: it generates games from skill specifications, audits them to reject trivial and instruction-agnostic tasks, and records scripted teachers acting in real time at the student’s control rate. These demonstrations train visual policies by behavior cloning without VLM annotation.

    2.3 Game Datasets and Benchmarks

    Large-scale datasets for training game and computer-use agents include Minecraft recordings and knowledge corpora [13, 3, 11], multi-game and desktop action trajectories such as Pixels2Play (Open-P2P) [37, 38], D2E [9], Gaming-500-Hours [21], and NitroGen [20], as well as synthetic capture platforms such as Isekai3D SDG [14]. For evaluation, public benchmarks span first-person combat in ViZDoom [15], open-world Minecraft tasks in MineStudio [5], MCU [42], and OpenHA [35], classic console and DOS titles in VideoGameBench [40], verifiable browser games in GameWorld [22], and real-time UE5 games in OmniGameArena [18]. Rather than relying on human recordings or retrospective video labeling, our pipeline synthesizes aligned instruction, frame, and action trajectories with programmatic verifiers, and evaluates transfer across these public benchmarks.

    3 Method

    Figure1 gives an overview. A coding agent turns a natural-language specification of a gameplay skill into a playable game. For each episode, the game samples a scene—its layout, assets, and dynamics—and assigns an instruction with a task verifier. A scripted teacher attempts the task, and successful episodes become training demonstrations. We first define the student, teacher, and behavior-cloning objective (Sec.3.1), then describe game generation and verification (Sec.3.2).

    3.1 Instruction-Following Training

    Student and teacher.

    Let t index control decisions, spaced 200 ms apart; sₜ is the engine state, oₜ=R(sₜ) the rendered observation, g the instruction, and aₜ=(kₜ,mₜ) a keyboard-and-mouse action chunk. The student policy, Script2Play, is denoted by π_θ(aₜ|xₜ) and observes xₜ=(g,o_t-h:t,a_t-h:t-1): the instruction, current frame, and h previous frame–action pairs. It never observes engine state. All reported benchmark policies use h=0, so each decision depends on the instruction and current frame alone. The teacher π^*(aₜ|sₜ,g) is a program written by the coding agent for each game. It reads character poses and velocities, target coordinates, enemy and projectile states, and collision geometry. Depending on the task, it uses pathfinding, motion prediction for aiming, finite-state control, or timing rules to select actions. The teacher executes these actions through the same keyboard-and-mouse interface and at the same control rate as the student. It never teleports objects or bypasses game physics.

    Teacher rollouts.

    A task τ=(s₀,g,V) consists of an initial scene s₀, an instruction g, and a verifier V. The verifier uses engine state to check task completion within a time budget T_τ and to detect prohibited events, such as reaching the wrong target or falling. A teacher rollout with L_τ control decisions is

    ξ_τ=((g,oₜ,a^*ₜ))ₜ₌₁^L_τ,

    		(1)

    and the training corpus retains only successful rollouts: D={ξ_τ:V(ξ_τ)=1}. Videos are recorded at 20 fps and aligned with 200 ms action windows. Instructions come from the task specification, action labels from the teacher, and success labels from the verifier; no human gameplay demonstration or retrospective VLM annotation is needed.

    Behavior cloning.

    Starting from a pretrained open-weight VLM, we train on the teacher’s action labels. The unweighted gameplay loss is

    L_BC(θ)=-𝔼_τ, t[\logπ_θ(a^*ₜ|g,o_t-h:t,a^*_t-h:t-1)],

    		(2)

    where τ indexes a retained rollout and t a control decision within it. For h>0, training uses the teacher’s action history; this history is empty in the reported h=0 setting. All of our benchmark policies in Sec.4 use behavior cloning on synthetic gameplay. To emphasize changes in control, we increase the token-loss weight for action windows whose held-key set differs from the preceding window: by a factor of 5 for Roblox and 3 for Minecraft. We also include generic visual question answering, optical character recognition, and text examples in 15% of each batch to help retain general capabilities. These auxiliary examples contain no gameplay. At inference, the model runs in closed loop on each benchmark’s native engine, mapping frames and instructions directly to keyboard and mouse actions. Following Lumine [27], the model generates each action chunk autoregressively as plain text: ΔX ΔY ; K₁ ; K₂ ; K₃ ; K₄. The mouse displacement (ΔX,ΔY) is distributed across the 200 ms window, while K₁ through K₄ specify the keys and mouse buttons held in its four successive 50 ms intervals. Unlisted keys are released. At each new control decision, the model receives the latest frame and instruction; if h>0, the context also includes its previous predicted actions and observations.

    3.2 Data Generation

    From specification to game.

    A specification has five fields: the gameplay skill, camera, dynamics ranges, controls, and task contract (Tab.5). The contract defines which target the instruction refers to and which events invalidate an episode. The coding agent implements the scene, interactive mechanics, task verifier, and teacher using a shared runtime library (AppendixB). It also writes a scene generator to vary layouts, spawn points, targets, dynamics, and assets, and an offline mirror: a separate implementation of the game rules for fast teacher and verifier checks. When a scene supports multiple targets, we construct paired tasks that share the scene but request different targets. These counterfactual pairs test whether the verifier distinguishes the requested target from a distractor; pursuing the other target must fail. Visual and physical randomization varies the world theme, player and NPC appearances, camera, layout, dynamics, and instruction wording while preserving the underlying mechanic, as illustrated by Melee arena (Fig.2). This variation is intended to reduce dependence on a particular visual setting; Sec.4 evaluates transfer to other engines.

    Audit and validation.

    A game’s rollouts enter D only after it passes five automated gates, in the spirit of the creation-audit loop of [1] (checks detailed in Tab.6):

  • •

    G1 Static: the code compiles, and paired tasks share the same scene.

  • •

    G2 Solvable: the teacher solves at least 95% of tested episodes in the offline mirror, both under nominal timing and with added latency.

  • •

    G3 Non-trivial: idle, hold-forward, and random-key policies rarely succeed, and a teacher pursuing the other task’s target also rarely succeeds on the instructed task.

  • •

    G4 Engine parity: the teacher’s success rate in the engine is within five percentage points of its rate in the mirror.

  • •

    G5 Visual: recorded frames are non-blank and change over the episode.

    • G3 screens for two failure modes: tasks that can be solved without observing the scene, and verifiers that accept the wrong instructed target. For recoverable failures, the agent adjusts task tolerances to improve teacher success or eliminate trivial solutions, then reruns the audit, with at most three repair rounds. Games that fail G1 or the wrong-target check are discarded (Algorithm1).

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments test the central premise of this work: generating games around general skills can provide sufficient supervision for capable and transferable game-playing policies. We examine whether synthetic demonstrations support competitive instruction following, whether the learned control skills transfer to engines excluded from post-training, and whether the advantage persists when methods use the same VLM backbone. All of our benchmark policies are trained by behavior cloning, without human gameplay demonstrations, RL, or DAgger.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Training data and model.

    Script2Play uses a Qwen3.5-4B backbone jointly trained on Minecraft and Roblox demonstrations, totaling 150.3 h of verified scripted-teacher gameplay: 26.9 h from Minecraft and 123.4 h from Roblox. The OpenHA, OmniGameArena, and ViZDoom results in Tabs.1, 2 and 4 all use this same unified checkpoint. The student receives rendered frames and an instruction; privileged engine state is used only by the teacher and verifier during data generation. Frames are recorded at 20 fps. Each training example pairs an instruction and a single 480p frame with a 200 ms action window containing four 50 ms key groups and a mouse displacement; the context length is h=0. We freeze the vision encoder and projector and train on 8 H200 GPUs using bfloat16 and a global batch size of 384 windows. The learning rate is 2×10⁻⁵, with 5% warmup followed by cosine decay to 10% of its peak value.

    Skill coverage.

    We determine the game mixture by surveying games on mainstream gaming platforms and tasks in public game benchmarks, and estimating the relative frequency of the gameplay skills they require. This empirical skill distribution guides both the proportions of generated game categories and the allocation of demonstration collection across them (Fig.3). The 123.4 h of Roblox demonstrations come from 41 generated games across six categories: combat and shooting (56.4 h), traversal and parkour (21.5 h), object interaction (20.8 h), dodging and survival (19.7 h), GUI operation (3.7 h), and ball games (1.3 h). The 26.9 h of Minecraft demonstrations comprise 31,494 verified episodes and cover three categories: Embodied mining and workstation interaction (5.0 h), GUI crafting and smelting (19.0 h), and Combat (2.9 h). Scripted teachers collect these demonstrations in MineStudio [5] using 48 custom world seeds disjoint from the evaluation worlds, with randomized spawn locations, tool and inventory loadouts, and surrounding distractors.

    Benchmarks and metrics.

    OpenHA [35] evaluates Minecraft instruction following across Embodied, GUI, and Combat tasks; we report success rates for each group and their average.Because Minecraft demonstrations are included in training, OpenHA tests downstream performance within a training engine. OmniGameArena [18] and ViZDoom [15] test cross-engine transfer: neither UE5 nor Doom gameplay is included in our policy post-training. For OmniGameArena, we evaluate the five solo games in Tab.2 using their native normalized scores and the mean across games. Following the official benchmark protocols, we evaluate each OpenHA task over three trials and each OmniGameArena task over 5 trials. For ViZDoom, we follow the four-map protocol of [36, 12] and report the mean episode reward over 50 episodes per map, with the simulator running at 35,Hz.

    Comparisons.

    We include commercial VLMs, open-weight VLMs, and trained game policies based on human gameplay, RL, or both. The benchmark tables compare complete systems; the shared-backbone comparison in Sec.4.4 narrows the architectural differences. Data scale refers to gameplay used for policy training; hour equivalents inferred from tokens or frames are approximate (AppendixC).

    4.2 Learning from Synthetic Demonstrations

    The first question is whether skill-targeted synthetic supervision is sufficient to train a strong instruction-following policy from a pretrained VLM. On OpenHA (Tab.1), Script2Play reaches 69.6% average success, exceeding the strongest prior trained policy, Game-TARS MoE-mini (64.5%), by 5.1 percentage points. These results establish state-of-the-art performance among the trained game policies compared here using only 150.3 h of synthetic post-training data and a behavior-cloning objective. They demonstrate that human gameplay and online RL are not prerequisites for this level of downstream performance.

    4.3 Transfer to Unseen Game Engines

    Strong Minecraft performance alone does not establish that generated skills transfer beyond a training engine. We therefore evaluate the same unified checkpoint on UE5 and Doom, whose environments and trajectories are excluded from the training mixture. The generated mechanics target relevant gameplay skills, making these benchmarks a test of whether those skills can be reused under changes in visual appearance, dynamics, and task composition.

    OmniGameArena: transfer beyond the training worlds.

    Script2Play achieves a mean score of 0.640 (Tab.2), the highest score among all compared agents. It exceeds the best commercial VLM in this comparison, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (0.473), by 0.167, and the strongest human-gameplay policy, GameScaling-9B-S3 (0.361), by 0.279. The latter uses 1,600 h of human gameplay, compared with our 150.3 h of synthetic demonstrations. This result supports the value of targeted skill coverage: a comparatively small generated corpus can produce effective control in an engine absent from policy post-training. Because the systems differ in backbone, training procedure, and data composition, the comparison establishes an efficient operating point rather than a sample-complexity ratio.

    ViZDoom: transfer of combat skills.

    On ViZDoom (Tab.4), Script2Play achieves a mean reward of 12.92 without ViZDoom trajectories or target-game RL, approaching the zero-shot Game-TARS MoE-mini (14.54) with a much smaller model and substantially less gameplay data. The comparisons differ in training domain and model capacity. GameWAM is trained directly on expert APPO trajectories from the four evaluation maps, whereas Script2Play transfers zero-shot. Game-TARS is built on the substantially larger Seed1.5-VL mixture-of-experts backbone and uses explicit sparse thinking [36]; Script2Play is a 4B model that omits explicit reasoning traces to reduce inference latency. The Battle maps also require more than shooting: the agent must infer when to search for and collect health and ammunition even though the instruction only asks it to kill enemies. These implicit subgoals, together with finding enemies outside the current field of view, are difficult for a history-free policy (h=0), which cannot use previous observations to track searched areas or supply locations. On DefendLine, Script2Play reaches 22.94, nearly matching the in-domain GameWAM result of 23.52 and exceeding Game-TARS at 15.24.

    Action sequences reveal how control transfers.

    Figure4 connects the aggregate results to the actions of the learned policy. In the OpenHA combat example, the policy turns and advances toward the target before issuing attack inputs; the GUI example combines mouse positioning with item-manipulation clicks. On the held-out UE5 engine, ObstacleRun3D requires the policy to interleave forward motion with timed jump inputs, while CueChase combines camera adjustment, approach, and interaction. The same action-chunk representation therefore supports distinct control behaviors across Minecraft and UE5. These selected successful episodes illustrate how the policy uses the interface; the benchmark scores quantify how reliably it succeeds.

    4.4 Effect of the Supervision Source

    The main comparisons combine changes in supervision with changes in model and training procedure. To examine whether the benefit persists with a shared backbone, we compare three Minecraft policies initialized from Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Tab.4): OpenHA trained on human play, HiSTEVE trained with human-derived supervision and RL, and our policy trained by behavior cloning on 26.9 h of verified Minecraft teacher demonstrations. This experiment uses a separate 7B, Minecraft-only variant of Script2Play, excluding both the Roblox data and the Qwen3.5-4B backbone used for the main results.

    The advantage persists with a shared backbone.

    On in-domain Minecraft tasks (Tab.4a), scripted supervision reaches 45.9% average success, exceeding OpenHA (31.5%) by 14.4 points and HiSTEVE (37.4%) by 8.5 points, and leads both baselines across all three task groups: Embodied (49.7% versus 30.1% and 46.0%), GUI (39.0% versus 32.5% and 27.2%), and Combat (49.0% versus 31.9% and 39.0%). The shared initialization rules out a newer backbone as the sole explanation for the in-domain gain. We also evaluate OpenHA and our 7B variant zero-shot on OmniGameArena (Tab.4b); HiSTEVE weights are unavailable for this comparison. Our variant achieves a similar mean score to OpenHA (0.028 versus 0.023), so its in-domain gains are accompanied by comparable zero-shot performance in this evaluation.

    5 Conclusion

    We introduced a fully automated framework that generates games, task verifiers, and programmatic experts from gameplay skill specifications. Behavior cloning on 150.3 h of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay produces Script2Play, a unified 4B VLA policy trained without human gameplay demonstrations or online RL. The same checkpoint is used across three benchmarks, leading the compared trained policies on OpenHA and achieving the highest mean score on the evaluated OmniGameArena games. These results demonstrate how pretrained visual knowledge and programmatic action supervision can support transferable game control. Extending skill coverage to more complex interactions and longer-horizon objectives is a promising next step.
