    Appendix A Fully Generated Games

    This section details the workflow in Sec.3.2, from a gameplay skill specification to verified demonstrations for policy training. Each specification describes the target skills, camera, dynamics, controls, and a task contract defining the instructed target and failure conditions. The coding agent implements the game, its scene generator, a scripted teacher, a task verifier, and an offline mirror of the game rules. The scene generator varies layouts, appearances, and dynamics, while instruction paraphrases preserve the task’s meaning. Counterfactual task pairs share a scene but request different targets; we refer to each member of a pair as an arm. These pairs allow the audit to check whether success depends on following the instruction.

    The full loop.

    Algorithm1 summarizes game generation, verification, demonstration collection, and behavior cloning.

    Specification fields.

    Table5 describes the specification fields and their role in game generation.

    Creation-audit gates.

    Table6 summarizes the audit checks. The offline mirror provides a fast way to test teachers and verifiers before recording in the game engine. Engine rollouts then check whether the same behavior remains valid under actual rendering and input timing.

    Teacher success alone does not establish that a task provides useful supervision. The audit must also detect goals already satisfied at spawn, tasks solvable by waiting, and verifiers that accept the wrong target. For sustained actions, the verifier must distinguish an uninterrupted hold from time accumulated across separate attempts. These checks prevent successful but uninformative episodes from entering the training corpus.

    Repair and acceptance.

    For recoverable failures, the agent adjusts task tolerances and reruns the audit. Wider tolerances can make a task solvable, while narrower tolerances can eliminate trivial solutions. A candidate is discarded if it fails static validity or wrong-target checks, or if it cannot pass the audit within the repair budget. Accepted games proceed to demonstration collection.

    Teacher decision loop.

    Algorithm2 describes the teacher’s latency-compensated decision loop (Sec.3.2). At each control step, the teacher reads privileged state and accounts for inputs that have been issued but have not yet taken effect. It then selects a task-specific action and converts it into the same keyboard-and-mouse representation used by the student.

    Demonstration collection.

    The teacher executes each task through the game’s normal input interface, while the recorder aligns rendered observations with instructions and action chunks. The verifier checks completion and prohibited events throughout the episode. Only successful, verified rollouts enter the training corpus. Behavior cloning then trains the student on the recorded instructions, images, and actions; privileged state remains available only to the teacher and verifier.

    Using feedback to guide generation.

    Evaluation episodes can be grouped by primary skill, secondary skill, camera, and control family to identify recurring failures. Groups with high failure rates guide the next game specifications. When failures mainly involve timeouts, falls, or hazard collisions, the generator can create an easier version to introduce the skill gradually. The resulting games pass through the same audit and demonstration-collection workflow before contributing training data.

    Appendix B Coding Agent, Tools, and an Example Game

    Coding agent.

    Each Roblox game in Fig.3 was written by a Cursor agent in Agent mode with Claude Opus 5.5, one game at a time, with access to the game repository and run directories. For each game, the agent writes four components and registers the task templates. The scenario module, written in server-side Luau, declares the templates and constructs an episode from its seed. The game module, written in client-side Luau, implements the mechanics in a custom fixed-step simulation at 60 Hz, without Roblox’s physics engine. The teacher is a Python controller that reads published engine state and returns a 200 ms action chunk containing four 50 ms key groups and mouse motion. The offline mirror reimplements the game in Python and runs it in closed loop with the teacher. The agent then runs the checks, recording, and export commands described in Sec.3.2, and inspects frames from the recordings. A person provides the specifications and shared asset packs as input; during development, a person also spot-checked each new game’s code and a short video, but the pipeline does not require this, and all fixes were made by the agent.

    Tools.

    The agent’s own tools are reading and editing files, a shell, and viewing images. Each server session constructs its Roblox environment from source files through Rojo; environments are not edited manually in Roblox Studio. The environment-editing, terrain, asset-placement, and scripting tools of Sec.3.2 are a runtime library that the generated code calls, and the checks are command-line tools (Tab.7).

    Prompt.

    A prompt provides the game specification, required steps, and files to read first: the runtime library and the most relevant existing game, teacher, and mirror. A repository guide defines coding conventions and runtime limits: at most eight engine workers, one recording at a time, and no changes to game files during recording. Prompts took this form:

    Add a template game to the gym following GAME_CREATION.md: . Read GameKit.lua, GymGameSpec.lua, GymContext.lua and (game, scenario, teacher, mirror) first. Write the scenario, the game module, the teacher and the offline mirror, register them, get the mirror to 95% on both arms, then run a 16-episode engine check and show me frames from a passed and a failed episode.

    Example: Laser Maintenance Bridge.

    Table8 gives the specification of a traversal-and-parkour game using the fields in Tab.5; Fig.5 shows the two counterfactual arms for one scene in the generated game. The agent wrote a 159-line scenario module, a 144-line game module, a 176-line teacher, and a 176-line mirror. The teacher keeps the camera facing down the bridge and predicts the player’s position when the next action takes effect, accounting for previously issued inputs. It waits for a safe interval in the sweeping laser’s motion, approaches a gap and jumps while holding W, crouches under the low laser with C, and stops at the center of the instructed marker. It estimates input latency online from the distance traveled after issuing W. In the mirror, the teacher passed all 120 episodes (40 seeds per template) under nominal timing and 119 of 120 with three extra frames of latency and 12–24-frame decision gaps; the single failure was a laser contact. The engine check passed all 48 episodes (16 per template, covering both arms). Of the 990 recorded episodes (165 counterfactual pairs per template), 988 passed, yielding 1.6 h of demonstrations recorded at 20 fps.

    Appendix C Experimental Data Accounting

    Our training mixture.

    The Script2Play benchmark policy is initialized from Qwen3.5-4B and jointly trained on 150.3 h of synthetic demonstrations, comprising 26.9 h from Minecraft and 123.4 h from Roblox. The same unified checkpoint is evaluated on OpenHA, OmniGameArena, and ViZDoom in Tabs.1, 2 and 4. The separate Qwen2.5-VL-7B variant in the supervision comparison uses only the Minecraft component. All of our benchmark policies use behavior cloning; neither RL nor DAgger contributes to our results.

    Baseline scales.

    Tables 1 and 4 report approximate hour equivalents, marked with †. The original conversion assumes 20 fps and approximately 350 tokens per frame, or 25M tokens per hour. Its inputs are: ROCKET-1, 1.6B frames; OpenHA, 3.62B tokens; JARVIS-VLA and HiSTEVE, 7.4M world frames and 6.4M GUI entries (also described as approximately 10B tokens); UI-TARS-1.5, approximately 50B general GUI tokens and 14–16B Minecraft tokens; GameWAM, 200k 96-frame VPT clips plus additional VPT and scripted GUI trajectories (2.79B tokens); and Game-TARS, approximately 14B Minecraft tokens out of 233B/566B total tokens [36]. For STEVE-1, the approximately 70,750 h estimate combines 70,000 h of inherited VPT pretraining with 54M human and VPT-generated fine-tuning frames (approximately 750 h at 20 fps) [3, 17]. The ViZDoom estimate was derived from 7.71M training windows (21,900 updates with batch size 352) [12]. These quantities mix source frames, GUI entries, tokens, and samples processed during optimization, so they do not define a uniform measure of unique gameplay duration or training compute. We use them only to describe the reported training scale, not to infer a controlled data-efficiency ratio.

item.title: 神经纹理压缩一直拿不到 GPU 的各向异性过滤：这篇让金字塔按 LOD 显式建模，滤核不再靠猜 ｜ Explicit LOD-Conditioned Anisotropic Filtering for Neural Texture Compression

要点：

  • 症结：神经纹理压缩（NTC）能紧凑存材质，但主流特征金字塔设计**得不到 GPU 纹理单元的过滤能力**——它在固定 UV 与固定 LOD 上学习每个材质，没有显式的各向异性过滤机制
  • 作者进一步指出：仅靠足迹长宽比设置滤波是不够的，单一输入无法同时携带足迹的**形状与尺寸**
  • 解法是按 LOD 显式条件化（explicit LOD-conditioned），让网络在正确的层级上给出过滤后的结果

为什么值得看：纹理压缩省的是显存，但省下来的如果拿不到硬件各向异性过滤，画面在斜面上就会糊或者闪烁——这正是 NTC 落地的最大障碍。把 LOD 显式建模进去，等于把「能不能上生产」这件事往前推了一大步。

中文摘要：神经纹理压缩（NTC）能紧凑地存储材质纹理，但主流的特征金字塔设计享受不到 GPU 纹理单元的过滤能力：它在一个固定的 UV 与固定的 level-of-detail 上学习每个材质，没有显式的各向异性过滤机制。作者指出，仅按足迹的长宽比来设定滤波并不足够——单一输入无法同时承载足迹的形状与尺寸两件事。这篇因此提出按 LOD 显式条件化的做法，让网络在正确的层级上产出过滤结果。对考虑把 NTC 上生产的团队，这解决的是「省了显存但斜面上糊/闪」这个最现实的障碍。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

Explicit LOD-Conditioned Anisotropic Filtering for Neural Texture Compression

© none

Abstract.

Neural texture compression (NTC) stores material textures compactly, but the dominant feature-pyramid design receives no filtering from the GPU texture unit: it learns each material at a fixed UV and level of detail and has no explicit anisotropic-filtering (AF) mechanism. Setting the filter from the footprint aspect ratio alone is not enough: a single input cannot carry both the shape of the footprint and its size, so the image is too blurry near the camera by the same amount at every distance. Our method, AF-NTC, instead conditions the decoder on the same three bounded values a hardware sampler uses: minor-axis scale (LOD), aspect ratio, and major-axis orientation. These drive a tap line along the major axis and a level blend across the minor axis, and we train against anisotropically filtered ground truth. At 25% of a full BC7 mip chain, AF-NTC beats the no-AF trilinear-BC7 baseline on all ten material–scene pairs we compare (+1.3 to +7.6 dB), and it is 0.0 to 3.4 dB below the 4×-larger anisotropic-BC7, depending on the material.

Keywords:

Texture Compression, Neural Networks, Anisotropic Filtering

1. Introduction

Neural texture compression (NTC) aims to store material textures below the on-disk size of fixed-rate block compression (BC1–BC7 depending on texture types), at equal or better quality [(Vaidyanathan et al., 2023; Microsoft, 2020)]. A texture is sampled many times during rendering under minification and at grazing angles, so anisotropic filtering (AF) is necessary: it keeps detail near the camera and correctly removes it with distance. NTC must therefore be evaluated not only on compressed size but also on filtering quality.

Two families of NTC handle AF in opposite ways. Latent-in-BC methods store learned features inside BC textures and let the GPU texture unit filter the latents in hardware, so AF is provided by the hardware sampler at no additional cost [(Belcour and Benyoub, 2025; Weinreich et al., 2024)]. Feature-pyramid NTC instead learns multi-resolution feature grids with a small multilayer perceptron (MLP) decoder [(Vaidyanathan et al., 2023)]. It has no hardware filtering and no explicit anisotropic filtering mechanism, so it aliases at one sample per pixel and relies on stochastic texture filtering (STF) [(Pharr et al., 2024)]. This work makes AF an explicit operation in a feature-pyramid decoder, conditioned on the pixel footprint and trained against anisotropically filtered ground truth, so that the result is sharp near the camera and blurry far away, which a naive tap blend cannot do. We call this decoder AF-NTC.

Because the aspect ratio alone cannot carry the footprint’s size, we instead condition the decoder on the same bounded (\textttrot, stretch, LOD) triple that hardware AF uses (i.e., minor-axis scale (level of detail (LOD)), aspect ratio (stretch), and major-axis orientation (rot)), and drive it along two paths: a major-axis tap line and a minor-axis level blend. On the pavement scene in Fig. 1, AF-NTC is sharp near the camera and blurry far away, and stays closer to a supersampled reference than the no-AF baseline.

Our contributions are:

Diagnosis and a minimal fix.:

The aspect ratio alone cannot set the filter; the bounded (\textttrot,\textttstretch,LOD) triple restores the quality.

Two-axis learned filter.:

For a decoder without hardware filtering, we combine a major-axis tap-line length with a minor-axis level blend.

Compression vs. filtering.:

An ablation on model size shows which part of the error is compression and which is filtering.

2. Related Work

Feature-pyramid NTC

The dominant NTC design stores a material as a stack of learnable multi-resolution feature grids plus a small MLP decoder, and reports state-of-the-art quality at a matched on-disk size [(Vaidyanathan et al., 2023)]. NTBC [(Fujieda and Harada, 2024)] follows the same idea but packs the neural features into BC blocks so that a standard asset pipeline can carry them. These decoders receive no filtering from the GPU texture unit. They learn the material at fixed UV and LOD, so one sample per pixel aliases, and practical systems rely on STF, which samples a random subset of taps, reducing temporal aliasing at the cost of added noise [(Pharr et al., 2024)]. [Vaidyanathan et al. (2023)] report that software AF requires too many taps for real time. We target this family.

Latent-in-BC NTC

A second family stores latent feature vectors inside BC textures, lets the GPU sampler filter the latents in hardware, and then decodes with a tiny MLP [(Weinreich et al., 2024; Belcour and Benyoub, 2025)]. Anisotropic filtering is then effectively free: no filtering logic is added to the decoder, a property we call free AF. A network trained only on isotropic samples generalizes to well-filtered output, because the sampler gives the actual, bounded footprint, and AF is just a weighted blend of taps over that footprint. This is the property a feature-pyramid decoder lacks: it sees only UV, so the footprint must be an explicit, learned input.

Hardware AF, EWA, and the footprint

Classic high-quality filtering, such as the elliptical weighted average (EWA) [(Heckbert, 1989)], integrates the texture over the elliptical footprint of a pixel. Approximated hardware AF samples several trilinear taps along the footprint’s major axis over a mip pyramid [(Williams, 1983; McCormack et al., 1999)]. Hardware AF derives the footprint ellipse from the screen-to-UV Jacobian; we give the derivation and the bounded inputs the sampler uses in Sec. 3.2.

3. Method

AF-NTC makes AF explicit inside the feature-pyramid decoder. Fig. 2 shows the pipeline of our proposed method.

3.1. Failure of Ratio-only Conditioning

The naive anisotropy-aware design derives its filter length from stretch alone, e.g., a length of the form

(1)

\textttlength=\textttstretch·k,

with stretch the ratio of the long to short footprint axis and k a single fixed constant.

This fails because the correct filter is set by two things that vary independently: the footprint’s absolute size (how much to blur (i.e., mip level)) and its aspect ratio (how elongated it is). stretch encodes only the ratio, so a ratio-only decoder must apply a fixed size k that is correct at only one distance; it can never represent a near and grazing footprint, which is small yet strongly elongated. The Naive column of Fig. 1 shows the result: the image is too blurry near the camera, by the same amount at every distance. The missing quantity, absolute size, must therefore be an input of its own, which motivates the bounded (\textttrot,\textttstretch,LOD) triple.

3.2. Bounded Hardware-AF Footprint Triple

From the screen-to-UV Jacobian J, we form the metric A=J J^⊤, whose eigenvalues are σ_\max²≥σ_\min²; their square roots σ_\max≥σ_\min are the major- and minor-axis lengths, and the major eigenvector gives the orientation. From these, we form the triple as follows:

(2)LOD=\log₂ (σ_\min·\texttttex_res),∈[0,12] at 4K,
(3)stretch=σ_\max/σ_\min,∈[1,16],
(4)rot=∠(major axis),∈[0,π).

σ_\min sets the LOD level, stretch sets the tap count and, together with σ_\min, the tap-line length, and rot gives the major-axis orientation. The renderer supplies LOD per pixel; from it, we recover the minor-axis length by inverting Eq. 2:

(5)

σ_\min=2^LOD/ \texttttex_res.

LOD and σ_\min should be consistent, and we use this single recovered σ_\min everywhere it is needed: both to place the taps (Eq. 6) and to build the anisotropically filtered ground truth (Sec. 3.4). An elliptical footprint is fully described by its size, elongation, and orientation, and the triple (\textttrot,\textttstretch,LOD) gives exactly these three.

3.3. Two-Axis Learned Filter

The decoder reads input features from a four-level feature pyramid of 2D grids, each storing a 12d feature, bilinearly sampled on each tap and concatenated across levels into a 48d grid-feature vector. The footprint triple conditions the decoder both geometrically and as explicit inputs. Geometrically, as shown in Fig. 2, it sets how the grids are filtered along the two footprint axes: rot orients the major axis, σ_\min, which is recovered from LOD with Eq. 5, and stretch together set the major-axis tap-line length (Eq. 6), and LOD selects the mip level and weights that the minor-axis level blend. As explicit inputs, the 48d grid-feature vector is concatenated with the single normalized scalar LOD/\textttlod_max, forming the 49d vector that feeds the MLP; rot and stretch are used only through the tap geometry, as tap orientation and tap-line length, not as MLP inputs. An ablation in Appendix B shows that also feeding (\textttrot,\textttstretch) to the MLP as an 18d positional encoding changes quality only slightly, because the tap geometry already uses rot and stretch.

Major axis: absolute tap-line length

The major-axis tap-line length is set from the absolute minor-axis length, not the ratio:

(6)

\textttlength_major=σ_\min·\textttstretch (=σ_\max),

with σ_\min from Eq. 5. Unlike the naive form of Eq. 1, where stretch is multiplied by the fixed constant k, here it is multiplied by the absolute length σ_\min, so the tap line spans the true major-axis length σ_\max rather than a distance-independent length. Taps are placed along the major axis, one budget per grid level, with fixed counts [16,8,4,2] (30 taps in total) from the finest to the coarsest level. We choose this 30-tap budget to match hardware-AF tap counts and lower decode cost rather than for peak quality.

Minor axis: level blend

Taps along the major axis alone leave the minor axis unfiltered. We band-limit the minor axis with an LOD-weighted blend across the four grid levels. Each level l has an LOD center,

(7)

cₗ=\log₂(\texttttex_res/\textttresₗ),

and its 12d feature is weighted by a Gaussian in LOD about its center with σ=0.7. Then, the weighted features are concatenated, keeping the grid-feature width fixed at 48.

3.4. Training, Architecture, and Model Size

Ground truth

The training target simulates hardware AF instead of computing an exact EWA integral: we place ⌈\textttstretch⌉ taps along the major axis over a length of (2^LOD/\texttttex_res)·\textttstretch, and fetch each tap trilinearly at mip=LOD, which filters the minor axis. It is therefore an approximation: it agrees with a supersampled EWA reference to 37–41 dB PSNR on our scenes. We use it only for training and measure quality on the rendered image (Sec. 4). Note that the decoder’s tap budget [16,8,4,2] is fixed, while this target uses ⌈\textttstretch⌉ taps.

Filter-parameter sampling

Instead of generating training footprints from rendered views, we sample the (\textttrot,\textttstretch,LOD) triple directly from parameter space, independently of one another. rot and stretch are sampled uniformly over their ranges, and LOD is sampled area-proportionally, p(LOD)∝4^-LOD, so that coverage matches the screen area each LOD occupies. Independent sampling gives the decoder footprint size and ratio as uncorrelated inputs, so it sees combinations that no single view provides.

Training

As in other NTC work, our model is fitted to one 4K material and shipped with it, so training and evaluation share that texture set. The model is implemented, trained, and evaluated in PyTorch. We train our model with an L₂ loss, with optional LOD-weighting and the normal-map channels up-weighted. We then quantize to int8 by quantization-aware training (QAT) with the Brevitas quantization library [(Franco et al., 2026)].

Architecture and model size

The encoder holds a four-level 2D feature grid at resolutions 1024/512/256/128, so the per-level LOD centers cₗ in Eq. 7 are 2,3,4,5. The decoder is an MLP that maps the 49d conditioned feature vector through hidden widths [192,192], leaky-ReLU activations, and a final sigmoid, outputting 9 channels: albedo (3), an ARM channel packing ambient occlusion, roughness, and metallic into one texture (3), and a normal (3). AF-NTC has an on-disk size of 16.75 MB (int8-packed grids and MLP), about 25% of the 67 MB that these same three 4K maps (albedo, ARM, and normal) occupy as a full BC7 mip chain.

4. Results

Setup

All our numbers are PSNR measured in rendering space rather than texture space: we render with the maps that each method produces and compare against a supersampled EWA ground truth rendered under the same lighting, so the two images differ only in the maps. We evaluate five 4K materials, ordered from low to high spatial frequency in Table 1, each rendered in two scenes: a flat plane (sharp near, blurred far) and a curved sphere. We compare AF-NTC against two BC7 baselines that use the same software AF implementation as AF-NTC and store the full mip chain, about 4× the AF-NTC size: aniso-BC7 (full anisotropic filtering, a strong upper reference) and trilinear-BC7 (the same BC7 maps filtered only isotropically, with trilinear mip sampling and no AF, a weaker baseline). Unless noted, we default to the int8 model (Sec. 3.4).

Conditioning

Table 1 builds up AF-NTC one part at a time on top of an isotropic baseline: first training on anisotropic ground truth (+aniso), then feeding LOD to the decoder (AF-NTC). The isotropic baseline follows the free-AF approach [(Weinreich et al., 2024; Belcour and Benyoub, 2025)]: the same decoder trained on isotropic samples only, with no footprint input. Learning the AF footprint explicitly improves it throughout: each part raises PSNR on all materials and both scenes. The gain is smallest on low-frequency blue_metal (+1.02 dB plane) and largest on the high-frequency materials, up to +4.66 dB (plane, stone_floor) and +5.85 dB (sphere, pavement).

Comparison

The same table places AF-NTC, at 25% of the BC7 mip-chain budget, between the two BC7 baselines. AF-NTC beats trilinear-BC7 on all ten material–scene rows, by +1.31 to +7.63 dB, including the highest-frequency stone_wall. It stays below aniso-BC7 on every row, by 0.03 to 3.37 dB (mean 1.57): closest on stone_floor and furthest on pavement plane. Renders and error maps for all ten rows are in Appendix D (Fig. 6).

Meshes

To test AF-NTC on real 3D models, not just the flat and curved test surfaces, we train it per asset on two PolyHaven meshes whose 4K maps are non-stationary, with a unique UV layout rather than a tiling pattern: a concrete cat statue and a wine barrel. Table 2 shows PSNR in rendering space on each asset, and Fig. 3 shows the cat images. At 25% of the BC7 size, AF-NTC stays just below the full-4K aniso-BC7 reference by at most 0.07 dB on the two assets and beats the no-AF trilinear-BC7 by +2.0 (cat) to +3.5 dB (barrel). Against the equal-byte, half-resolution (2K) aniso-BC7, AF-NTC is +0.28 dB on cat and -0.07 dB on barrel. On both assets, the footprints are large (LOD ≈1.4–2.4), so AF already removes most fine detail and a 2K map loses little; we do not claim this equal-byte result for the finer footprints of Table 1, where the 2K chain is 0.4 to 3.3 dB better than AF-NTC. The barrel images are in Appendix C (Fig. 5).

Ablations

Two ablations on pavement and stone_floor show where the error comes from; the table and discussion are in Appendix A (Table 3). Removing the minor-axis level blend costs 5.3 to 9.3 dB, most of it near the camera where footprints are smallest, so the blend is the most important part of the filter. A ∼4× larger model gains at most 0.4 dB: at this budget, the error left is set by compression, not by model size.

5. Conclusion and Discussion

We showed that a feature-pyramid NTC decoder can filter anisotropically when given explicit control: a bounded (\textttrot,\textttstretch,LOD) triple plus a two-axis filter—a tap line along the major axis and a level blend across the minor axis.

Unlike stochastic filtering [(Pharr et al., 2024)], which keeps one decode per pixel but trades aliasing for noise that a temporal post-process must resolve, our filter is deterministic. A single decode returns a noise-free filtered value that needs no post-processing and is therefore easy to integrate into an existing pipeline, at the cost of more taps per decode.

Scope and limitations

We claim correct filtering at a fixed compression budget, not a general size–quality win, and we do not claim to match BC7. AF-NTC comes within 0.5 dB of the 4×-larger aniso-BC7 on stone_floor, but stays below it on every row, by up to 3.4 dB (Table 1). We report no runtime evaluation: our AF is a PyTorch software emulation, not an optimised GPU implementation on a texture sampler. How that tap budget trades quality against decoding performance, measured on real hardware, is future work.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Combined Ablations

All numbers in this appendix are PSNR in rendering space, as in Sec. 4; higher is better. Every AF-NTC number is an average over several training runs that differ only in their random seed.

Table 3 gives the filtering and model-size ablations. Its AF-NTC column is our default model, so it repeats the AF-NTC numbers of Table 1.

Filtering

Our filter has two parts: a tap line along the major axis and a level blend across the minor axis. The no-blend column keeps the tap line and removes the blend, so it still filters along the major axis but no longer across it. The blend is the more important of the two: without it, PSNR drops by 5.3 to 9.3 dB. Fig. 4 shows where that error is. Near the camera, the footprints are small, and the decoder has to read the grids at a fine level; without the blend, it cannot, and the pattern is washed out. Far from the camera, where a coarse level is the right one anyway, the two look the same.

Model size

We made the model larger in two ways: doubling the feature dimension and using higher-resolution grids. Both change PSNR by at most 0.4 dB (Table 3). The error left at this budget is thus set by compression, not by model size: a larger model cannot bring back detail that the footprint filter has already averaged away.

Appendix B Feeding (\textttrot,\textttstretch) to the MLP

Our decoder gives the multilayer perceptron (MLP) only the level of detail (LOD). rot and stretch reach it another way: they place the taps, as their orientation and the length of the tap line. Table 4 asks whether the MLP should be given them as an additional 18d positional encoding. It should not: the two differ by at most 0.05 dB, so we keep the smaller input.

Appendix C Mesh Assets

Fig. 5 shows the barrel asset in Table 2. The inset covers the side of the barrel, where the surface turns away from the camera, and the footprints are the most stretched. There, trilinear-BC7 leaves clearly more error on the wooden planks and the metal rings, while AF-NTC and aniso-BC7 look the same.

Appendix D All Ten Material–Scene Pairs

Sec. 4 shows only one of the ten material–scene rows of Table 1 as a picture, the pavement plane in the teaser (Fig. 1); Fig. 6 shows all ten. Trilinear-BC7 blurs the surface pattern away wherever the footprint is stretched, most visibly on the clay_roof plane, the row where AF-NTC gains the most over it (+7.6 dB). AF-NTC keeps the pattern, and on most rows its error is close to that of the 4×-larger aniso-BC7; it is worse only on the pavement plane (-3.4 dB) and the stone_wall sphere (-2.8 dB), and even there the two stay visually close.

A network trained only on isotropic samples generalizes to well-filtered output, because the sampler gives the actual, bounded footprint, and AF is just a weighted blend of taps over that footprint. This is the property a feature-pyramid decoder lacks: it sees only UV, so the footprint must be an explicit, learned input.

Hardware AF, EWA, and the footprint

Classic high-quality filtering, such as the elliptical weighted average (EWA) [(Heckbert, 1989)], integrates the texture over the elliptical footprint of a pixel. Approximated hardware AF samples several trilinear taps along the footprint’s major axis over a mip pyramid [(Williams, 1983; McCormack et al., 1999)]. Hardware AF derives the footprint ellipse from the screen-to-UV Jacobian; we give the derivation and the bounded inputs the sampler uses in Sec. 3.2.

3. Method

AF-NTC makes AF explicit inside the feature-pyramid decoder. Fig. 2 shows the pipeline of our proposed method.

3.1. Failure of Ratio-only Conditioning

The naive anisotropy-aware design derives its filter length from stretch alone, e.g., a length of the form

(1)

\textttlength=\textttstretch·k,

with stretch the ratio of the long to short footprint axis and k a single fixed constant.

This fails because the correct filter is set by two things that vary independently: the footprint’s absolute size (how much to blur (i.e., mip level)) and its aspect ratio (how elongated it is). stretch encodes only the ratio, so a ratio-only decoder must apply a fixed size k that is correct at only one distance; it can never represent a near and grazing footprint, which is small yet strongly elongated. The Naive column of Fig. 1 shows the result: the image is too blurry near the camera, by the same amount at every distance. The missing quantity, absolute size, must therefore be an input of its own, which motivates the bounded (\textttrot,\textttstretch,LOD) triple.

3.2. Bounded Hardware-AF Footprint Triple

From the screen-to-UV Jacobian J, we form the metric A=J J^⊤, whose eigenvalues are σ_\max²≥σ_\min²; their square roots σ_\max≥σ_\min are the major- and minor-axis lengths, and the major eigenvector gives the orientation. From these, we form the triple as follows:

(2)LOD=\log₂ (σ_\min·\texttttex_res),∈[0,12] at 4K,
(3)stretch=σ_\max/σ_\min,∈[1,16],
(4)rot=∠(major axis),∈[0,π).

σ_\min sets the LOD level, stretch sets the tap count and, together with σ_\min, the tap-line length, and rot gives the major-axis orientation. The renderer supplies LOD per pixel; from it, we recover the minor-axis length by inverting Eq. 2:

(5)

σ_\min=2^LOD/ \texttttex_res.

LOD and σ_\min should be consistent, and we use this single recovered σ_\min everywhere it is needed: both to place the taps (Eq. 6) and to build the anisotropically filtered ground truth (Sec. 3.4). An elliptical footprint is fully described by its size, elongation, and orientation, and the triple (\textttrot,\textttstretch,LOD) gives exactly these three.

3.3. Two-Axis Learned Filter

The decoder reads input features from a four-level feature pyramid of 2D grids, each storing a 12d feature, bilinearly sampled on each tap and concatenated across levels into a 48d grid-feature vector. The footprint triple conditions the decoder both geometrically and as explicit inputs. Geometrically, as shown in Fig. 2, it sets how the grids are filtered along the two footprint axes: rot orients the major axis, σ_\min, which is recovered from LOD with Eq. 5, and stretch together set the major-axis tap-line length (Eq. 6), and LOD selects the mip level and weights that the minor-axis level blend. As explicit inputs, the 48d grid-feature vector is concatenated with the single normalized scalar LOD/\textttlod_max, forming the 49d vector that feeds the MLP; rot and stretch are used only through the tap geometry, as tap orientation and tap-line length, not as MLP inputs. An ablation in Appendix B shows that also feeding (\textttrot,\textttstretch) to the MLP as an 18d positional encoding changes quality only slightly, because the tap geometry already uses rot and stretch.

Major axis: absolute tap-line length

The major-axis tap-line length is set from the absolute minor-axis length, not the ratio:

(6)

\textttlength_major=σ_\min·\textttstretch (=σ_\max),

with σ_\min from Eq. 5. Unlike the naive form of Eq. 1, where stretch is multiplied by the fixed constant k, here it is multiplied by the absolute length σ_\min, so the tap line spans the true major-axis length σ_\max rather than a distance-independent length. Taps are placed along the major axis, one budget per grid level, with fixed counts [16,8,4,2] (30 taps in total) from the finest to the coarsest level. We choose this 30-tap budget to match hardware-AF tap counts and lower decode cost rather than for peak quality.

Minor axis: level blend

Taps along the major axis alone leave the minor axis unfiltered. We band-limit the minor axis with an LOD-weighted blend across the four grid levels. Each level l has an LOD center,

(7)

cₗ=\log₂(\texttttex_res/\textttresₗ),

and its 12d feature is weighted by a Gaussian in LOD about its center with σ=0.7. Then, the weighted features are concatenated, keeping the grid-feature width fixed at 48.

3.4. Training, Architecture, and Model Size

Ground truth

The training target simulates hardware AF instead of computing an exact EWA integral: we place ⌈\textttstretch⌉ taps along the major axis over a length of (2^LOD/\texttttex_res)·\textttstretch, and fetch each tap trilinearly at mip=LOD, which filters the minor axis. It is therefore an approximation: it agrees with a supersampled EWA reference to 37–41 dB PSNR on our scenes. We use it only for training and measure quality on the rendered image (Sec. 4). Note that the decoder’s tap budget [16,8,4,2] is fixed, while this target uses ⌈\textttstretch⌉ taps.

Filter-parameter sampling

Instead of generating training footprints from rendered views, we sample the (\textttrot,\textttstretch,LOD) triple directly from parameter space, independently of one another. rot and stretch are sampled uniformly over their ranges, and LOD is sampled area-proportionally, p(LOD)∝4^-LOD, so that coverage matches the screen area each LOD occupies. Independent sampling gives the decoder footprint size and ratio as uncorrelated inputs, so it sees combinations that no single view provides.

Training

As in other NTC work, our model is fitted to one 4K material and shipped with it, so training and evaluation share that texture set. The model is implemented, trained, and evaluated in PyTorch. We train our model with an L₂ loss, with optional LOD-weighting and the normal-map channels up-weighted. We then quantize to int8 by quantization-aware training (QAT) with the Brevitas quantization library [(Franco et al., 2026)].

Architecture and model size

The encoder holds a four-level 2D feature grid at resolutions 1024/512/256/128, so the per-level LOD centers cₗ in Eq. 7 are 2,3,4,5. The decoder is an MLP that maps the 49d conditioned feature vector through hidden widths [192,192], leaky-ReLU activations, and a final sigmoid, outputting 9 channels: albedo (3), an ARM channel packing ambient occlusion, roughness, and metallic into one texture (3), and a normal (3). AF-NTC has an on-disk size of 16.75 MB (int8-packed grids and MLP), about 25% of the 67 MB that these same three 4K maps (albedo, ARM, and normal) occupy as a full BC7 mip chain.

4. Results

Setup

All our numbers are PSNR measured in rendering space rather than texture space: we render with the maps that each method produces and compare against a supersampled EWA ground truth rendered under the same lighting, so the two images differ only in the maps. We evaluate five 4K materials, ordered from low to high spatial frequency in Table 1, each rendered in two scenes: a flat plane (sharp near, blurred far) and a curved sphere. We compare AF-NTC against two BC7 baselines that use the same software AF implementation as AF-NTC and store the full mip chain, about 4× the AF-NTC size: aniso-BC7 (full anisotropic filtering, a strong upper reference) and trilinear-BC7 (the same BC7 maps filtered only isotropically, with trilinear mip sampling and no AF, a weaker baseline). Unless noted, we default to the int8 model (Sec. 3.4).

Conditioning

Table 1 builds up AF-NTC one part at a time on top of an isotropic baseline: first training on anisotropic ground truth (+aniso), then feeding LOD to the decoder (AF-NTC). The isotropic baseline follows the free-AF approach [(Weinreich et al., 2024; Belcour and Benyoub, 2025)]: the same decoder trained on isotropic samples only, with no footprint input. Learning the AF footprint explicitly improves it throughout: each part raises PSNR on all materials and both scenes. The gain is smallest on low-frequency blue_metal (+1.02 dB plane) and largest on the high-frequency materials, up to +4.66 dB (plane, stone_floor) and +5.85 dB (sphere, pavement).

Comparison

The same table places AF-NTC, at 25% of the BC7 mip-chain budget, between the two BC7 baselines. AF-NTC beats trilinear-BC7 on all ten material–scene rows, by +1.31 to +7.63 dB, including the highest-frequency stone_wall. It stays below aniso-BC7 on every row, by 0.03 to 3.37 dB (mean 1.57): closest on stone_floor and furthest on pavement plane. Renders and error maps for all ten rows are in Appendix D (Fig. 6).

Meshes

To test AF-NTC on real 3D models, not just the flat and curved test surfaces, we train it per asset on two PolyHaven meshes whose 4K maps are non-stationary, with a unique UV layout rather than a tiling pattern: a concrete cat statue and a wine barrel. Table 2 shows PSNR in rendering space on each asset, and Fig. 3 shows the cat images. At 25% of the BC7 size, AF-NTC stays just below the full-4K aniso-BC7 reference by at most 0.07 dB on the two assets and beats the no-AF trilinear-BC7 by +2.0 (cat) to +3.5 dB (barrel). Against the equal-byte, half-resolution (2K) aniso-BC7, AF-NTC is +0.28 dB on cat and -0.07 dB on barrel. On both assets, the footprints are large (LOD ≈1.4–2.4), so AF already removes most fine detail and a 2K map loses little; we do not claim this equal-byte result for the finer footprints of Table 1, where the 2K chain is 0.4 to 3.3 dB better than AF-NTC. The barrel images are in Appendix C (Fig. 5).

Ablations

Two ablations on pavement and stone_floor show where the error comes from; the table and discussion are in Appendix A (Table 3). Removing the minor-axis level blend costs 5.3 to 9.3 dB, most of it near the camera where footprints are smallest, so the blend is the most important part of the filter. A ∼4× larger model gains at most 0.4 dB: at this budget, the error left is set by compression, not by model size.

5. Conclusion and Discussion

We showed that a feature-pyramid NTC decoder can filter anisotropically when given explicit control: a bounded (\textttrot,\textttstretch,LOD) triple plus a two-axis filter—a tap line along the major axis and a level blend across the minor axis.

Unlike stochastic filtering [(Pharr et al., 2024)], which keeps one decode per pixel but trades aliasing for noise that a temporal post-process must resolve, our filter is deterministic. A single decode returns a noise-free filtered value that needs no post-processing and is therefore easy to integrate into an existing pipeline, at the cost of more taps per decode.

Scope and limitations

We claim correct filtering at a fixed compression budget, not a general size–quality win, and we do not claim to match BC7. AF-NTC comes within 0.5 dB of the 4×-larger aniso-BC7 on stone_floor, but stays below it on every row, by up to 3.4 dB (Table 1). We report no runtime evaluation: our AF is a PyTorch software emulation, not an optimised GPU implementation on a texture sampler. How that tap budget trades quality against decoding performance, measured on real hardware, is future work.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Combined Ablations

All numbers in this appendix are PSNR in rendering space, as in Sec. 4; higher is better. Every AF-NTC number is an average over several training runs that differ only in their random seed.

Table 3 gives the filtering and model-size ablations. Its AF-NTC column is our default model, so it repeats the AF-NTC numbers of Table 1.

Filtering

Our filter has two parts: a tap line along the major axis and a level blend across the minor axis. The no-blend column keeps the tap line and removes the blend, so it still filters along the major axis but no longer across it. The blend is the more important of the two: without it, PSNR drops by 5.3 to 9.3 dB. Fig. 4 shows where that error is. Near the camera, the footprints are small, and the decoder has to read the grids at a fine level; without the blend, it cannot, and the pattern is washed out. Far from the camera, where a coarse level is the right one anyway, the two look the same.

Model size

We made the model larger in two ways: doubling the feature dimension and using higher-resolution grids. Both change PSNR by at most 0.4 dB (Table 3). The error left at this budget is thus set by compression, not by model size: a larger model cannot bring back detail that the footprint filter has already averaged away.

Appendix B Feeding (\textttrot,\textttstretch) to the MLP

Our decoder gives the multilayer perceptron (MLP) only the level of detail (LOD). rot and stretch reach it another way: they place the taps, as their orientation and the length of the tap line. Table 4 asks whether the MLP should be given them as an additional 18d positional encoding. It should not: the two differ by at most 0.05 dB, so we keep the smaller input.

Appendix C Mesh Assets

Fig. 5 shows the barrel asset in Table 2. The inset covers the side of the barrel, where the surface turns away from the camera, and the footprints are the most stretched. There, trilinear-BC7 leaves clearly more error on the wooden planks and the metal rings, while AF-NTC and aniso-BC7 look the same.

Appendix D All Ten Material–Scene Pairs

Sec. 4 shows only one of the ten material–scene rows of Table 1 as a picture, the pavement plane in the teaser (Fig. 1); Fig. 6 shows all ten. Trilinear-BC7 blurs the surface pattern away wherever the footprint is stretched, most visibly on the clay_roof plane, the row where AF-NTC gains the most over it (+7.6 dB). AF-NTC keeps the pattern, and on most rows its error is close to that of the 4×-larger aniso-BC7; it is worse only on the pavement plane (-3.4 dB) and the stone_wall sphere (-2.8 dB), and even there the two stay visually close.

item.title: 体积渲染别再靠路径追踪估亮度：这篇用场景特征直接推「最终光传输解」，省掉每像素的路径采样 ｜ Real-Time Volumetric Light Transport Inference without a Path
item.description:
一句话：蒙特卡洛降噪依赖昂贵的光追辐射度估计；这条路直接推断最终解。

要点：

  • 对比对象很明确：体积渲染常用的蒙特卡洛降噪管线，依赖计算量很大的路径追踪辐射度估计
  • 这篇改为用紧凑、低成本的场景特征与统计量，**直接推断出最终的像素辐射解**（含直接光与环境光）
  • 也就是跳过「先路径追踪再降噪」这条路，直接给出完整的集成光传输结果

为什么值得看：体积效果（雾、烟、云）在实时渲染里长期是「要么糊、要么贵」。如果最终光传输解可以直接推断，省掉的是每像素的路径采样预算——对想在游戏里开体积光的团队是最直接的一笔账。

中文摘要：在直接光与环境光照下，这篇给出一种实时的体积介质像素辐射重建方法：它只用紧凑、成本很低的场景特征与统计量，就直接推断出最终的集成光传输解。与体积渲染常用的蒙特卡洛降噪管线相比，差别在于后者必须先算出昂贵的路径追踪辐射度估计、再靠降噪器清理噪声，而这里把「路径」这一步整个绕过。对实时渲染来说，这意味着体积雾、烟、云这类效果不必再在「糊」与「贵」之间二选一。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

Real-Time Volumetric Light Transport Inference
without a Path

Abstract

We present a real-time method for reconstructing fully integrated pixel radiance in rendered volumetric media under direct and ambient environmental illumination, using compact, low-cost scene features and statistics. Unlike Monte Carlo denoising pipelines for volumetric rendering, which depend on computationally expensive path-traced radiance estimates, our approach directly infers the final light-transport solution from inexpensive primary-ray and environment sample evaluations. We show that these features form a near-sufficient representation of the scene, enabling accurate reconstruction at substantially lower computational cost. Using an attention-augmented image-to-image network, we demonstrate that complete pixel radiance can be inferred directly from these auxiliary features, without requiring the original radiance signal. Operating in image space also provides a more stable computational cost as the camera zooms into or out of the volume, with substantially less dependence on volume density than approaches based on explicit multiple-scattering simulation. We demonstrate real-time performance and high reconstruction accuracy in challenging volumetric cloud scenarios.

1 Introduction

Monte Carlo (MC) path tracing achieves photorealistic rendering by simulating the full light transport pipeline, including emission, scattering, and absorption along importance-sampled light paths [Kaj86, Coo86, AK90, NGHJ18, PJH23]. For surface rendering, light paths terminate after a few bounces, yet each pixel still requires hundreds to thousands of samples to converge to a noise-free result. For volumetric media, the problem is substantially more severe: light scatters at every point along a ray, turning each sample into a recursive integration problem. Rendering a single frame of participating media such as clouds, smoke, or fog often requires seconds to minutes even on high-end GPUs, making real-time applications prohibitive.

To mitigate the cost of path tracing, many modern rendering systems rely on MC denoising. For surface rendering, denoisers leverage auxiliary features—often called G-buffers in surface graphics—like albedo, normals, depth, and variance buffers to filter sparse path samples (given as samples per pixel, or spp) into smooth outputs [BVM∗17, VRM∗18, SKW∗17], or to use them as input for neural networks that predict noise-free images directly [CKS∗17, IMF∗21, VVF24].

These MC denoisers must evaluate at least a few full light transport paths to accurately transform the noisy rendering into a high-quality image. This becomes especially costly for volumetric media, where simulating light transport is computationally expensive. Moreover, paths in volumetric media exhibit complex, view-dependent correlations across samples that surface-based auxiliary features cannot exploit, rendering such features less predictive (Fig. 1 OIDN). Due to the nature of participating media, the noise distribution itself varies spatially and spectrally, further complicating inference.

One approach to addressing these challenges is MC denoising guided by auxiliary features specifically designed to represent volumetric light transport characteristics, such as transmittance and first-scatter event estimates [HMES20, HHCM21]. While effective in principle, such methods still require path-traced radiance samples as input: their cost grows with medium density, and the noise of these samples propagates into the reconstruction, leading to blurring and instability across realizations (Fig. 1 Denoiser).

In another research line, radiance-predicting neural networks replace path tracing for atmospheric clouds, albeit at considerably higher computational cost than MC denoisers [KMM∗17] or requiring progressive inference updates to simulate full environment lighting [HYL∗23] (Fig. 1).

Both lines of work still depend on simulating light transport through the volume at inference time, either through path samples or through per-sample network queries. This raises a simple question: are path samples needed at all? Prior work on surfaces shows that localized illumination effects can be inferred from auxiliary buffers alone [NAM∗17], and Deep Scattering shows that networks can learn volumetric transport [KMM∗17]. We build upon both insights: we keep the feature-based design of volumetric denoisers, but drop the radiance input entirely and regress the final radiance from features computed along primary rays.

We show that optical depth, multi-scale interaction depths, transmittance towards the light, environment illumination at the expected first interaction, and local medium properties form a near-sufficient representation of the transport solution. We formalize this as two testable assumptions, sufficiency and noise invariance, and learn the mapping from features to radiance with an attention-augmented image-to-image network. Since the features are deterministic except for low-variance light-visibility estimates, the output is stable across realizations without requiring accumulation over frames.

We demonstrate real-time performance and high reconstruction accuracy in challenging volumetric cloud scenes (Fig.  and Fig. 1 Ours), where state-of-the-art MC denoisers struggle to maintain both stability and fine detail. By moving from sample denoising to primary-ray feature regression, our method offers a new pathway toward practical real-time volumetric light transport.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    The formulation of volumetric rendering as a deterministic decoding from inexpensive transport features, replacing path sampling at inference time.

  • •

    A compact set of primary-ray features for participating media, which we show to be near-sufficient for inferring full multiple scattering in clouds.

  • •

    A real-time image-to-image network with local self-attention, which infers directional and environmental scattering separately and scales to high resolutions.

  • •

    A real-time cloud renderer simulating full radiance transport in unseen clouds and environments, showing high accuracy, low variance across realizations, and stable cost even for high densities.

    • 2 Related Work

    MC denoising for surfaces. Early denoisers handle the spatially varying noise of MC renderings with nonlinear image filters, such as bilateral and edge-avoiding filters [Lee83, RW94, DSHL10] or non-local means [RKZ12], often guided by G-buffers to preserve edges. Spatiotemporal variance-guided filtering [SKW∗17] additionally reuses samples from past frames to improve temporal continuity. With the advent of deep learning, denoising has shifted from handcrafted filters to data-driven prediction [HY21, YGH∗25]. Learning the mapping from noisy features to filter parameters [KBS15] gave rise to two paradigms: radiance-prediction networks regress clean pixel values directly [CKS∗17, XZW∗19, LXS20], whereas kernel-prediction networks estimate spatially varying filter kernels that keep the output consistent with the input colors [BVM∗17, VRM∗18, IMF∗21]. Sampling and temporal denoising networks can further be trained jointly [HMS∗20]. These methods achieve near-reference quality by treating rendering as conditional image synthesis, but they are designed for surfaces and all require path-traced radiance as input.

    Volumetric denoising and sample reuse. Volumetric path tracing converges far more slowly than its surface counterpart, since each radiance sample involves many scattering events along the ray. At low sample counts this yields severely noisy images, while auxiliary buffers that are effective for surfaces, such as depth or normals, become noisy or ill-defined in media [YGH∗25, DFNB25]. Hofmann et al. [HMES20] were the first to extend neural MC denoising to volumetric path tracing of medical data, introducing a set of auxiliary features designed specifically for volumes and increasing the effective sample count through spatial and temporal filtering; this was later extended to sparse volumes [HHCM21]. Our features build on this idea. Subsequent work decomposes the image into a surface and a volume layer with dedicated denoisers and a network that learns to blend both [HHM23]. Xu et al. [XXZ∗25] decouple radiance samples according to their noise level and fuse them with auxiliary features in a lightweight network, reducing the bias of earlier decoupling strategies. In contrast, Iglesias-Guitian et al. [IGMM22] explicitly avoid auxiliary features and exploit temporal coherence instead, reprojecting linear models across frames and combining past and current estimates by weighted recursive least squares. Orthogonally, the quality of the input samples can be improved. Zhou et al. [ZZL∗17] fit Gaussian mixtures to single-scattered radiance to guide visibility-aware sampling in participating media, and spatiotemporal reservoir resampling [BWP∗20] has been extended to volumetric path space by ReSTIR-Volume [LWY21]. All these approaches still trace paths through the medium; our method requires none at inference time.

    Radiance-free neural rendering. Concurrently with learned denoisers, Deep Shading [NAM∗17] showed that CNNs can synthesize the final appearance directly from screen-space G-buffers, circumventing hand-crafted shaders and requiring no radiance input at all. Subsequent work explicitly frames G-buffers as the input representation for learning light transport, positioning G-buffer-based neural rendering as a modern alternative to precomputed radiance transfer [RBRD22]. G-buffers have since been combined with reflective shadow maps to reconstruct complex indirect lighting [UKK∗26], used to synthesize global illumination including transparent objects [ZSS26], and shown to remain valuable even when the primary transport data comes from other sources [HSG∗22]. Beyond screen space, transformer-based models infer global illumination directly from a 3D scene description: RenderFormer [ZDP∗25] maps triangle tokens with their reflectance properties to images with full global illumination, and Xu et al. [XTW∗26] learn a generalizable light transport embedding from scene point clouds, queried through cross-attention to predict diffuse global illumination in unseen scenes. These approaches recover local and global illumination effects on surfaces, but none addresses the direct inference of global illumination in volumetric media. We transfer their central idea, radiance-free inference from auxiliary buffers, to participating media.

    Learned volumetric light transport. Instead of denoising rendered images, neural networks can approximate components of volumetric light transport itself. Deep Scattering [KMM∗17] predicts the radiance caused by multiple scattering in clouds from a hierarchical 3D descriptor of the density around each shading point, oriented towards the light source. Learned statistical path models replace long stochastic scattering chains with a surrogate based on a more structured probabilistic model of the local geometry [LHW21]. MRPNN [HYL∗23] brings Deep Scattering to real time with a lightweight multi-feature fusion network that combines precomputed transmittance fields with a frequency-sensitive density stencil. For environment illumination, however, it requires progressive sampling over light directions, repeating the full ray accumulation for each direction. Rather than evaluating a network per sample, Liang et al. [LYG∗26] bake a compact low-rank latent approximation of the scattering operator, gaining performance and avoiding over-illumination artifacts, but at the cost of a baking step per volume. Similarly, Relightable Neural Assets [MLSH24] encode all shading and scattering of an asset in a feature grid decoded by a small MLP, an approach adapted to relight volumetric clouds under environment illumination within a rasterization pipeline [ODG26]; such representations are tied to the specific volume they were trained on. In contrast, our network operates in image space on features computed on the fly, requires neither per-point 3D descriptors nor precomputed volumetric fields or per-volume training, and generalizes to unseen volumes.

    3 Method

    Fig. 2 gives an overview of our method. We first formulate rendering as a deterministic decoding of image features (Secs. 3.1–3.2), then define a set of inexpensive primary-ray and environment features for optically thick media (Sec. 3.3), and finally describe how the decoder is learned and structured to separate directional and environmental light (Secs. 3.4–3.5).

    3.1 Physically-Based Volume Rendering

    Let θ denote a scene parameterization including geometry, materials, illumination, and participating media. We define a physically-based rendering operator R such that I=R(θ) corresponds to the solution of the light transport equation. Evaluating R is computationally expensive due to high-dimensional path integrals required for global illumination with multiple scattering.

    Light transport in participating media is governed by the volume rendering equation, which accounts for attenuation, absorption, emission, and multiple scattering along a ray. Let xₜ=x₀-tω denote a point along direction -ω from an origin x₀. The outgoing radiance is given by

    L(x₀,ω)=∫₀ᵈT(x₀↔xₜ) σₜ(xₜ) [⋯] dt+T(x₀↔x_d) L(x_d,ω),

    where σₜ is the extinction coefficient and

    T(xₐ↔x_b)=\exp (-∫_xₐ^x_bσₜ(x) dx)

    denotes transmittance between two points in the medium.

    The term [⋯] represents the local source contribution,

    φ(xₜ) Lₛ(xₜ,ω)+(1-φ(xₜ)) Lₑ(xₜ,ω),

    where φ is the single-scattering albedo, Lₑ denotes emitted radiance, and Lₛ is the in-scattered radiance. The latter integrates incident illumination over the sphere of directions:

    Lₛ(xₜ,ω)=∫_S²ρ(xₜ,ω,ωᵢ) L(xₜ,ωᵢ) dωᵢ,

    where ρ is the phase function describing angular scattering. In this paper, media with emissive particles are not considered, i.e., Lₑ(x,ω)=0. We employ the Henyey–Greenstein phase function, parameterized by an anisotropy coefficient g, which provides an efficient approximation of highly forward-scattering volumetric transport.

    3.2 Problem Formulation

    We introduce a set of auxiliary forward operators {Fₖ}ₖ₌₁ⁿ producing intermediate images

    F̂=F(θ;ξ)=(F₁(θ;ξ),…,Fₙ(θ;ξ)), ξ∼p(ξ),

    where ξ denotes the random numbers consumed by the operators, drawn independently of the scene θ. Unlike R, each Fₖ is a computationally efficient transport projection derived from θ, encoding structured quantities such as transmittance, scattering integrals, or low-order illumination terms rather than approximations of full radiance.

    We make the following assumptions:

    (A1) Sufficiency. The rendered image depends on the scene only through the distribution of its features:

    F(θ;ξ)\oversetd=F(θ^′;ξ) ⇒ R(θ)=R(θ^′),

    where \oversetd= denotes equality in distribution with respect to ξ∼p(ξ). Hence, the scene parameters θ are not required to infer the image. Notably, (A1) does not require θ itself to be recoverable from the features: different scenes, e.g., different density fields, may share the same feature distribution, as long as they also share the same rendered image.

    (A2) Noise-invariant decoding. There exists a deterministic mapping S that is insensitive to the stochastic estimation of the features, i.e., all realizations of the features of a scene decode to the same image:

    S(F(θ;ξ))=S(F(θ;ξ^′))=R(θ) almost surely.

    Under (A1) and (A2), rendering reduces to a deterministic mapping from noisy auxiliary features to radiance. Both assumptions can be tested separately: violations of (A1) appear as a systematic bias that persists even when the decoder observes arbitrarily many realizations F(θ;ξ₁),F(θ;ξ₂),… of the features, i.e., when their distribution is fully known, while violations of (A2) appear as a non-zero variance Var_ξ[S(F(θ;ξ))] across single realizations.

    This formulation generalizes MC denoising, where a single operator F_MC(θ;ξ) provides an unbiased radiance estimate. Its distribution determines R(θ)=𝔼_ξ[F_MC(θ;ξ)], so (A1) holds trivially, and the entire difficulty lies in (A2). Our operators shift this balance: most features are deterministic and the remaining ones have low variance, making (A2) easy to satisfy, while none of them is a degraded version of I. Instead, each Fₖ provides a complementary, physically meaningful projection of light transport, and S performs radiance reconstruction from heterogeneous transport measurements rather than denoising of a single stochastic estimator.

    3.3 Features

    We now define the operators {Fₖ} for volume rendering in optically thick media. All of them are evaluated along primary rays and describe attenuation, visibility, illumination, and local scattering properties (Fig. 2 Left).

    Optical depth F_τ. We consider the accumulated extinction for each ray

    τ(d)=∫₀ᵈσₜ(xₜ) dt,

    which governs transmittance, expected free-flight distance, and scattering density. Rather than using transmittance directly, we employ a normalized encoding of a medium with reduced extinction

    τ̂(d)=1-(1)/(1+0.5 τ(d)).

    This transformation suppresses the exponential saturation of T in high-opacity regions, yielding a smoother signal that preserves relative variations in dense media and improves numerical conditioning during reconstruction.

    Interaction depth F_d. We estimate the depth of the first scattering event, conditioned on an interaction occurring along the ray. Let τ=τ(d), then

    τ_c=1-τe^-τ/1-e^-τ

    is the expected optical depth of the first interaction, given that it occurs before d. We define the interaction depth as the minimum distance t₁ at which this optical depth is reached,

    τ(t₁)=τ_c.

    Unlike the expected distance, which may fall into empty space between separated structures, t₁ always lies inside the medium. It removes the noise and discontinuities of the free-flight estimator and is always defined for τ>0.

    Crossing layers F_c. To capture volumetric structure across scales, we compute multiple interaction-depth fields using progressively reduced extinction levels. Each layer represents the first conditioned interaction in a progressively more transparent version of the medium, producing a continuous multi-scale profile of volumetric occupancy. Instead of using the depth sequence, we use the distance between two consecutive crossings. This value remains more stable to camera variations.

    Transmittance for the next-event estimation Fₙ. For the first interaction point x_t₁, we estimate the transmittance towards a directional light source T(x_t₁↔xₗ).

    Environment illumination Fₑ. We additionally compute incident illumination from the environment map convolved through transmittance and phase function:

    ∫_S²T(x_t₁↔xᵢ) ρ(x_t₁,ω,ωᵢ)L(xᵢ,ωᵢ) dωᵢ.

    We estimate this integral using a low-sample-count Monte Carlo estimator, with 8 samples as a practical trade-off between computational cost and stability; this number can be adjusted as needed (see Section 4).

    Medium properties Fₘ. At the first interaction point, we extract local scattering parameters including the Henyey–Greenstein anisotropy parameter g and the single-scattering albedo φ(x_t₁).

    Together, these auxiliary quantities define a structured representation of the medium that captures partial yet informative constraints on global light transport.

    3.4 Learning the Decoder

    Assumptions (A1) and (A2) postulate the existence of the decoder S, but provide no closed form for it. We therefore approximate S by a parameterized model

    S_Ψ:ℝ^H×W×n→ℝ^H×W×3,

    an image-to-image neural network with weights Ψ that maps the n feature images of resolution H×W to the rendered image. The parameters are obtained by minimizing the expected reconstruction error over both the distribution of scenes and the stochastic source of the features:

    Ψ^⋆=\arg\min_Ψ 𝔼_θ∼p(θ) 𝔼_ξ∼p(ξ)[ℓ(S_Ψ(F(θ;ξ)), R(θ))],

    where ℓ is a reconstruction loss. In practice, the outer expectation is approximated by a finite set of training scenes θᵢ with converged reference renderings R(θᵢ), and the inner expectation by drawing several realizations ξ for each scene during training.

    Both expectations relate directly to our assumptions. The inner expectation pairs all realizations F(θ;ξ) of a scene with the same target R(θ), and thus rewards outputs that are invariant to ξ, as required by (A2). The outer expectation restricts the sufficiency assumption (A1) to the scene distribution p(θ): S_Ψ only needs to be accurate for plausible scenes, and may exploit regularities of p(θ), e.g., typical cloud structures, to resolve ambiguities left open by the features.

    3.5 Structured Decoder

    The formulation above holds for any decoder. In practice, we exploit exact properties of the rendering operator R to reduce the complexity of the learning problem. Since these properties are satisfied by R itself, the true decoder S shares them, and imposing them on S_Ψ restricts the hypothesis space without excluding the solution.

    Linearity in the illumination. We split the distant illumination into a smooth environment map Lₑₙᵥ and a dominant directional light ωₗ with intensities e and l. Since light transport is linear in the incident radiance,

    I=e (T B+Iₑ)+l Iₗ,

    where T B is the environment transmitted along the primary ray, and Iₑ, Iₗ are the radiance scattered towards the camera for a normalized environment and a unit directional light. T and B are known from the primary-ray traversal, so only Iₑ and Iₗ need to be inferred. We learn them with two decoders, Sₑ and Sₗ, each receiving the shared primary-ray features and the illumination feature of its component (Fₑ resp. Fₙ). Factoring out e and l also removes the illumination scale from the inputs, and a single prediction covers arbitrary intensity ratios (Fig. 2 Right).

    Independence across color channels. Without spectral coupling, each color channel is the solution of an independent transport problem. We therefore apply the same single-channel decoder to each channel, with the features of that channel as input. This shares weights across channels and reduces the output to a single channel. The decoder is agnostic to which medium properties vary across channels, since each channel is decoded from its own features. Which properties vary only affects the cost of feature extraction: a channel-dependent extinction requires a separate traversal of the volume per channel. In our experiments, we use a shared extinction and vary only the albedo and illumination per channel, so the density-dependent features are computed once and shared.

    Decoupling by construction. A single model that jointly predicts all components and channels would have to learn these independences from data. This requires training cases that cover the combinations of illumination and channel-dependent medium properties, and additional losses that penalize the influence of one channel or component on the others. In our experiments, such joint models did not achieve the required independence. In addition, they required considerably more capacity, which reduced performance substantially. Separate single-channel decoders satisfy both properties by construction and keep each decoder small.

    The specific architecture of the decoders, the loss ℓ, and the training procedure are described in Sec. 4.

    4 Implementation

    The rendering pipeline is implemented in Vulkan, with CUDA-exported device memory used to directly use rendered buffers in the neural network inference stage, avoiding host-side synchronization overhead and ensuring a tightly coupled rendering–inference loop.

    4.1 Feature Rendering

    Our scenes consist of volumes scaled to fit in a [-1,1]³ cube. We employ exhaustive ray-marching (step size 0.001u) to remove stochasticity for the primary ray features. We do a DDA on the coarse grid of majorants to skip empty regions when traversing the volume, and ray-march only non-zero voxels. A first traversal computes the optical depth τ. A second traversal starts from the first position with non-zero density, starting to determine the crossings, with scales ×4,×1,×0.25,×0.1. Because density scales are sorted, we can handle all crossings with just a second traversal. Early termination is possible when all crossings have been determined.

    For the first crossing depth, values are estimated for the transmittance towards the directional light, the environment samples, the anisotropy factor, and the single-scattering albedo.

    To reduce variance in the transmitted direct-lighting estimate, we use deterministic ray marching over a short initial segment of radius 0.1u, followed by stochastic ratio tracking. For environment lighting, we importance-sample directions using a quadtree over the equirectangular environment map, with sampling densities proportional to luminance.

    4.2 Network Architecture

    The reconstruction operator S is parametrized using a U-Net backbone composed of residual blocks and attention-based feature mixing. Following HaloNet [VRS∗21], we incorporate local spatial self-attention at intermediate resolutions and at the bottleneck. We call our model HaloRT—Halo-attention-based Radiative Transfer model (see Fig. 3).

    Since multiple scattering couples distant regions of the medium, a pixel’s radiance can depend on features at other image locations whose relevance varies with the scene, e.g., thin regions through which light enters the volume. Thus, we complement the convolutional backbone with local attention that relates features through content-dependent weights rather than fixed kernels (see Table 1).

    Restricting attention to local spatial blocks achieves similar scalability with image resolution as CNN-based models used in classical denoisers (4th row in Table 1) and avoids the quadratic computational and memory costs of full spatial self-attention (3rd row of Table 1). At the bottleneck, the reduced spatial resolution still allows each local attention block to operate on features whose receptive fields span the entire input image, enabling image-wide information exchange at a small additional cost compared to attention-free inference (2nd row in Table 1).

    Notably, the network is never explicitly provided with the light direction. Nevertheless, it can reconstruct backlit regions effectively by relating the directional light transmittance to the other extracted features, exploiting the spatially coherent visibility pattern of the light source across the image.

    4.3 Rendering and Dataset Generation

    We render volumetric scenes using delta-tracking combined with next-event estimation (NEE). Light transport is simulated through stochastic free-flight sampling and a single scattering evaluation along the ray. At each scattering event, direct illumination is estimated via explicit light sampling of the environment, while indirect contribution is accumulated through MC integration with a single sample over the phase function that continues estimating higher-order scattered light. Only for the primary rays, the case with no interaction accumulates the environment light (transmitted background).

    We further use ratio-tracking to estimate the transmittance, in combination with a coarse grid of majorants to accelerate delta-/ratio-tracking estimators.

    We generate a synthetic dataset composed of volumetric cloud scenes rendered under diverse lighting and medium configurations. Environment illumination is generated using 1000 HDR-like maps synthesized with Stable Diffusion [RBL∗22], covering a wide range of natural and stylized lighting conditions. In addition, we consider 500 volumes of cloud formations from the Cloudy Project dataset [LTW25]. In total we synthesize 22000 instances with 4096 samples per pixel (spp) for the images.

    Scenes are rendered with randomized camera poses, light directions, phase function anisotropy parameters, and scattering albedos. The latter are sampled in the high-scattering regime and may vary per color channel, enabling colored volumetric effects. For each instance we generate the scattered radiance from the environment, the scattered radiance from the light direction, the transmittance, and background. We render the images for a normalized (mean = 1.0) environment and a unitary light intensity since we can combine them with different scalings to cover a wider range of options.

    4.4 Training

    All models are trained using AdamW with identical hyperparameters for fair comparison between the CNN [HHCM21] and HaloRT. We use a learning rate exponentially decaying over 240K optimization steps from 10⁻³ to 10⁻⁶, then held constant for 120K extra steps to let the network fully converge at a low, stable rate.

    The optimization objective combines an ℓ₁ reconstruction loss with a ℓ₁ of a logarithmic compression variant to better balance low- and high-intensity regions:

    c(x)=sgn(x) \log(1+(100-1)|x|)/\log100
    L=0.6∥Î-I∥₁+0.4∥c(Î)-c(I)∥₁

    Each step draws a batch of 16 instances from an in-memory, periodically refreshed training pool, split into micro-batches of 4 for the forward pass. For every micro-batch we accumulate gradients over a horizontal flip augmentation and, independently, over all three color channels of the spectral-independent network, backpropagating each of the resulting six passes separately with the loss rescaled accordingly. Each training instance stores several independently sampled noisy realizations of its stochastic conditioning feature (next-event-estimation sample for the direct branch, environment sample for the environment branch); one realization is drawn at random per instance at every step, so the same deterministic target is seen under different noise draws across training. The number of environment samples varies uniformly between 1 and 16 to make the model agnostic to different noise levels.

    5 Results

    We evaluate three reconstruction approaches under identical rendering and evaluation conditions. The first baseline (Denoiser) is the CNN-based denoiser with 4-spp Monte Carlo radiance buffer proposed by Hofmann et al. [HMES20, HHCM21], which operates on noisy radiance estimates and statistical features. The second variant (DenoiserX) uses the same architecture but replaces the noisy features with our deterministic features, while retaining the 4-spp radiance buffer. Finally, our attention-based U-Net (HaloRT) operates exclusively on auxiliary transport features, without requiring path-traced radiance samples.

    Experiment Setup. All experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU. We evaluate all methods on a held-out set of 200 test images (512×512) rendered for 15 left-out clouds never used for training. We expand the evaluation dataset by including additional environment illumination scales (×0.2) and directional light intensities (×3), as well as five distinct directional light colors.

    Quantitative Results. We use Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) [WBSS04], Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Square of the pixel-wise predictive Standard Deviation (RMS-SD) as a measure of stability, and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [ZIE∗18] for quantitative results (Table 2). Our method surpasses denoisers in all metrics except PSNR, more notably in stability and time.

    We further organize the evaluation dataset according to lighting conditions and volume settings to examine how these parameters affect the performance of the three methods. Fig. 4 presents the corresponding metrics across the different configurations, allowing performance trends and sensitivities to be compared. While DenoiserX consistently achieves higher PSNR values than our method, both methods exhibit similar trends as the scene parameters vary. In contrast, HaloRT consistently achieves lower LPIPS scores, indicating better perceptual similarity to the reference images across all evaluated configurations. This suggests that, despite the lower pixel-wise fidelity measured by PSNR, our method better preserves perceptually relevant details and light transport characteristics across a wide range of scene conditions.

    Stability. One of the key properties of our method is that the decoder is largely invariant to feature noise, meaning that stochasticity in the features does not propagate through the model. To demonstrate this, we measure the model’s stability as the standard deviation of the inferred image over a given number of realizations (Fig. 5). In particular, we show that only a few environment samples are needed to make the variation imperceptible, with additional samples providing negligible benefits (Fig. 6).

    Performance analysis. Although the CNN used for classical denoising is computationally inexpensive, the radiance estimate it requires – computed using a few path traces through the volume – scales poorly with increasing cloud density (Fig. 7), as scattering events become more likely and require spawning additional rays. In contrast, since no paths are computed our runtime remains stable. Along primary rays and environment samples the workload is kept low, due to optimizations like empty-space skipping and fast ratio tracking in sparse volumes, and early termination once the optical depth saturates, along with Russian roulette in ratio tracking, in dense volumes.

    As the camera approaches the cloud, denoiser runtimes increase with screen coverage and, thus, with the number of paths to be evaluated. Our inexpensive auxiliary features in combination with the constant computational complexity of the inference step maintain stable runtimes and nearly constant FPS (Fig. 7).

    Qualitative Results. Fig. 8 compares all three different variants qualitatively.

    Fig. 9 compares our reconstructions with the path-traced references for a cloud lit from the front, the side, and the back. Starting from a base configuration, each row varies a single medium parameter: density, single-scattering albedo, and phase-function anisotropy. Our method reproduces the brightness and color of the multiply scattered light in all configurations, including the darker appearance of low-albedo media and the bright rim of strongly forward-scattering media under back lighting.

    Directional Light Inference. In a final experiment, we compare our approach to MRPNN [HYL∗23] using a single directional light. The experiment is carried out on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090, since the MRPPN code does not execute on the RTX 5090. MRPNN is not designed to efficiently infer the radiance transport in an ambient light environment (see Fig. 1), but it also requires multiple, yet significantly less samples to generate a noise-free image in the presence of a single directional light (Fig. 10). Ours infers directional light transport with a single pass, producing an accurate, noise-free estimation that runs faster than a single pass of MRPNN.

    6 Discussion and Limitations

    Feature sufficiency. Our results support the view that, for clouds, inexpensive primary-ray features with additional environment samples carry most of the information needed to infer the full transport solution. HaloRT, which never observes a path-traced radiance sample, achieves better perceptual quality and stability than volumetric denoisers at a slightly lower PSNR (Table 2).
