DynOLAT: OLAT Video Prediction for Controllable Dynamic Full-Body Relighting

2026

Abstract.

Accurate lighting response is essential for realistic dynamic human relighting, because shadows, highlights, and color changes should follow the target illumination in both direction and relative strength. Current learning-based relighting methods can generate visually plausible videos, but they often exhibit imprecise lighting responses: shadows and highlights may drift away from the target direction, and the output brightness may not faithfully follow the relative intensities in the target environment, making the result closer to appearance harmonization than controllable relighting. To address this issue, we propose DynOLAT, a generalizable OLAT video prediction framework for dynamic full-body humans. Instead of directly synthesizing a single relit appearance, our method predicts temporally consistent One-Light-At-a-Time (OLAT) basis videos from flat-lit inputs, and then linearly combines the predicted bases according to the target environment map. This OLAT-based formulation makes the directional response explicit in the predicted bases, while the relative lighting strength is determined by the linear weights derived from the environment map. We further introduce a dynamic capture pipeline and the first large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset, comprising over 24 million frames from 224 identity-outfit combinations, where different outfits of the same person define separate combinations. Experiments show that DynOLAT responds more faithfully to variations in target lighting direction and relative intensity than the tested baselines, enabling controllable video relighting while preserving fine appearance details and temporal coherence. The dataset and processing tools will be publicly released to foster future research.

Keywords:

Controllable relighting, full-body OLATs, latent bridge matching, video-to-video translation, HD full-body capture ††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

Realistic dynamic human relighting requires the synthesized subject to respond accurately to the specified illumination in addition to appearing visually plausible. In practical VR/AR, film production, immersive telepresence, and game-content workflows, artists expect a relighting method to place shadows, highlights, and color changes according to the target light direction and relative intensity. This paper studies this controllability-oriented setting: given a monocular flat-lit video of a full-body human captured from an arbitrary viewpoint, we aim to synthesize a temporally coherent video of the same performance under a new lighting environment.

Existing general relighting methods still struggle with two forms of lighting-response accuracy that are critical for production use. First, their directional response is often imprecise: even when the target light direction is specified, the synthesized shading may exhibit a noticeable angular offset. Second, their intensity response is often unreliable: the output brightness may not faithfully follow the relative intensities in the target environment, making the result behave more like appearance harmonization than physically controlled relighting. These failure modes, highlighted in Fig. 1 and Fig. 6, are not only local visual artifacts; they directly weaken control over the target light direction and relative strength.

The difficulty arises because monocular human relighting requires both appearance realism and disentangled light control. Traditional inverse-rendering methods [(Barron and Malik, 2015)] attempt to estimate geometry, material, and illumination explicitly, but the problem is severely under-constrained for dynamic humans with spatially varying skin, hair, and clothing reflectance. Strong priors are therefore needed to resolve the ambiguity, often suppressing high-frequency details and producing overly smooth or artificial human appearance. Recent diffusion-based relighting methods [(Liang et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2025)] reduce the need for explicit decomposition by learning direct image or video mappings from large-scale data. While these models can produce visually plausible results, their lighting conditions are often encoded as holistic environment images or prompts, making it difficult to guarantee that output shadows and intensities follow the target illumination in a directionally and radiometrically faithful way.

OLAT representations provide a natural route to controllable relighting because they separate light transport into directional basis responses. A one-light-at-a-time (OLAT) image records the subject response to a single lighting direction; arbitrary environment illumination can then be formed by linearly combining the corresponding bases. DifFRelight [(He et al., 2024)] demonstrates that predicting OLAT representations can yield highly realistic and controllable facial relighting. Extending this idea from single facial images to dynamic full-body videos is non-trivial, because full-body motion introduces loose clothing deformation, self-occlusion, larger pose variation, and a lack of large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT supervision.

To address this gap, we propose DynOLAT, an OLAT video prediction framework for controllable dynamic full-body relighting. Given a flat-lit human video and a target lighting direction, our model predicts the corresponding OLAT basis video; the predicted bases are then combined in linear color space according to any target environment map. This formulation makes the target lighting explicit at two levels: the network learns directional basis responses, and the final relit video is assembled with environment-dependent intensity weights. As a result, the method is designed to preserve directional alignment and support explicit relative-intensity control, rather than relying on an unconstrained end-to-end generation of a single relit appearance.

Our technical design adapts a pretrained video model [(Wan et al., 2025)] to this OLAT prediction task while preserving source identity, details, and temporal coherence. We adopt Latent Bridge Matching (LBM) [(Chadebec et al., 2025)] to transport flat-lit video latents directly toward OLAT latents, avoiding the source-detail loss introduced by sampling from independent Gaussian noise. We further inject the target lighting direction through block-specific AdaLN modulation, enabling fine-grained directional control across the video transformer. For long sequences, a recurrent bridge context reuses previously generated OLAT frames as analytic overlap constraints, maintaining coherence beyond the training window.

To train this data-driven model, we build a dedicated dynamic OLAT acquisition pipeline. The system rapidly alternates flat and directional illumination and then aligns the resulting frames to form paired flat-lit/OLAT videos. Using this pipeline, we collect a large-scale, multi-view, dynamic full-body OLAT dataset containing diverse subjects, clothing, motions, and viewpoints. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first dataset of comparable scale that provides dynamic full-body OLAT supervision for learning temporally consistent lighting responses. We will publicly release the dataset and processing tools to support future research.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that DynOLAT improves controllable full-body relighting in dynamic sequences. Qualitative comparisons show that our method better follows the target light direction and relative illumination strength, while preserving fine body details and temporal consistency. Quantitative comparisons and ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our design.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

  • (1)

    An OLAT video prediction framework that formulates dynamic full-body relighting as directionally decomposed light-response synthesis, enabling more faithful responses to target light direction and environment-map intensity.

  • (2)

    Tailored model designs that adapt Latent Bridge Matching for source-detail preservation, use block-specific lighting modulation for directional control, and employ recurrent bridge context for long-sequence temporal coherence.

  • (3)

    The first large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset with sufficient subject, clothing, motion, and viewpoint diversity for learning temporally consistent human light transport.

    • 2. Related Work

    2.1. Human-centric Relighting

    Relighting human performances from monocular video remains a fundamental challenge in computer graphics and vision. Existing methodologies can be broadly categorized into three paradigms: optimization-based inverse rendering, learning-based image relighting and learning-based video relighting.

    Optimization-Based Inverse Rendering

    Leveraging recent advances in 3D neural representations like NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)] and 3DGS [(Kerbl et al., 2023)], numerous works attempt to reconstruct human avatars and decompose intrinsic properties from multi-view images [(Li et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024; Zhan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2024a; Gao et al., 2024; Chen and Liu, 2022; Chen et al., 2024a; Singh et al., 2025)]. By explicitly estimating geometry, material, and illumination, these methods provide a physically interpretable route to relighting control. However, standard physically-based rendering (PBR) approximations often fail to capture complex surface effects, such as subsurface scattering and intricate self-shadowing, which affect both appearance realism and the accuracy of the predicted lighting response. To circumvent these limitations, recent approaches utilize ground-truth OLAT scans to learn neural reflectance fields directly [(Li et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b; Guo et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2025)]. While these approaches have achieved photorealistic results for both upper-body [(Saito et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024)] and full-body avatars [(Zhou et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b; Guo et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2025; Teufel et al., 2026)], they rely heavily on subject-specific optimization. This requirement for dense capture setups and per-identity training limits direct application to in-the-wild images or videos and makes controllable direction and intensity responses difficult for novel dynamic subjects.

    Learning-Based Image Relighting

    To achieve generalization across subjects, a classical paradigm [(Nestmeyer et al., 2020; Pandey et al., 2021; Yeh et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2024; Daichi Tajima, 2025; Mei et al., 2025)] adapts the physics-based inverse rendering workflow into 2D feature space. These methods typically employ a cascaded pipeline that first decomposes the input image into intrinsic components (e.g., albedo and normals) and subsequently synthesizes the relit output via a neural renderer. While this strategy explicitly models light transport, the multi-stage process is prone to error accumulation: inaccurate geometry or albedo can blur source details and also shift the resulting shadows, highlights, and brightness away from the target illumination. Conversely, end-to-end approaches [(Sun et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2025b)] map inputs directly to relit outputs. Due to the scarcity of paired real-world data under varying illumination, many methods rely on synthetic data [(Ren et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a)] or auxiliary generation tasks [(Chaturvedi et al., 2025)], which can yield unrealistic shading or artifacts due to the domain gap. More importantly for controllable relighting, direct output synthesis often uses a target environment or background as a holistic condition, providing limited constraints that ensure the generated shadow direction and relative brightness follow the specified illumination. DifFRelight [(He et al., 2024)] and POLAR [(Chen et al., 2026)] fine-tune generative models on real OLAT data to predict OLATs for explicit lighting superposition, avoiding physical decomposition and synthetic-data domain gaps. In contrast, 3DPR [(Rao et al., 2025)] predicts portrait OLATs with a 3D head prior and linearly combines them for relighting. Nevertheless, applying these image-based solutions frame by frame to dynamic full-body sequences yields temporally unstable results, lacking the robustness required for video applications.

    Learning-Based Video Relighting

    To extend relighting to videos, earlier methods attempted to enforce temporal consistency via loss constraints [(Zhang et al., 2021)] or feature blending [(Wang et al., 2025a)]. However, given the geometric and textural complexity of dynamic full-body motion, independent frame processing can struggle to maintain coherence at high resolution. With the advent of video diffusion models [(Blattmann et al., 2023; Brooks et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025)], the mainstream paradigm has shifted toward fine-tuning video diffusion models [(Liang et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a)] or controlnets [(Zhang et al., 2025b)]. These methods typically inject condition frames by concatenating them with noisy latents, and represent lighting with environment maps, background images, or text-like conditions. However, this standard conditioning strategy poses a fundamental conflict: the stochastic denoising process, while excellent for diversity, introduces randomness that undermines the deterministic nature of relighting. This often leads to hallucinated details or identity drift, where the generated texture deviates from the source, and can also weaken the alignment between the output illumination and the target direction or intensity distribution. Instead of predicting a single relit video directly, our framework predicts OLAT basis videos and assembles the final illumination explicitly. To make this basis prediction source-aligned, we employ bridge matching [(Chadebec et al., 2025)] from the input video latents to the target OLAT latents, preserving fine source textures while learning a more deterministic light-response mapping. However, the success of such a data-driven video paradigm is heavily contingent on the availability of high-quality, temporally consistent training data.

    2.2. LightStage and OLAT Acquisition

    The LightStage architecture, pioneered by [Debevec et al. (2000)], revolutionized reflectance acquisition through precise, programmable lighting control. This setup inherently enables the capture of multi-view OLAT imagery. Fundamentally, relying on the linearity of light transport, the appearance of a subject under arbitrary environmental illumination can be synthesized via the linear superposition of these OLAT basis images. Consequently, LightStage data has become a "gold standard" benchmark for realistic relighting and has driven significant evolution in hardware design [(Debevec, 2008; Jones et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2019; He et al., 2024)].

    Despite its importance, the acquisition of such high-quality data remains heavily restricted by domain. While numerous works have explored OLAT-based frameworks, they predominantly focus on restricted domains such as facial appearance [(Li et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026)], hands [(Chen et al., 2024b)], or static objects [(Zhou et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023; Toschi et al., 2023)]. Research addressing full-body capture remains scarce [(Wang et al., 2025b; Teufel et al., 2025; Martinez et al., 2024)], and publicly available datasets are extremely limited. More critically, prior work on time-multiplexed dynamic OLAT capture has focused on faces and upper bodies [(Debevec, 2008; Zhang et al., 2021)].

    To the best of our knowledge, no existing public dataset provides dynamic full-body OLAT sequences at a comparable scale. This data scarcity becomes a bottleneck for training generalizable full-body relighting models, which require a substantial diversity of human materials and motions to avoid overfitting.

    To bridge this gap, we present our OLAT dataset, which includes a dedicated motion-rich subset. This component provides extensive dynamic OLAT data that covers diverse human materials and motions while supplying the directional light-response supervision needed to train controllable video relighting models.

    3. Method

    We decompose dynamic human relighting into explicit light-response prediction and linear environment assembly. In the first stage, we employ our OLAT video prediction model to synthesize a set of basis OLAT videos from a flat-lit input sequence, where each basis corresponds to a specific lighting direction. In the second stage, we reconstruct the final relit video under any complex environment map by linearly accumulating these predicted OLAT components in the linear color space. This decomposition is central to our controllability goal: the lighting direction is handled by the predicted basis index, while the lighting intensity is handled by the environment-map weights. An overview of our proposed framework is illustrated in Fig. 2.

    We first describe the architecture of our OLAT video prediction model in Sec. 3.1. We then explain how the flat-lit input frames (Sec. 3.2) and the target lighting direction (Sec. 3.3) are processed and injected into the network. Subsequently, we elaborate on our strategies for recovering high-frequency details (Sec. 3.4), which are necessary for producing reliable OLAT bases that retain the subject’s material and texture response. We then discuss our solution for inference on long video sequences (Sec. 3.5). Finally, we present the image-based relighting (IBR) formulation that renders the final output via a linear combination of the predicted OLAT bases (Sec. 3.6).

    3.1. Overview of OLAT Video Prediction Model

    Given a flat-lit video sequence and a target lighting direction, our goal is to synthesize the corresponding OLAT video. Concretely, we operate within the compressed latent space of a pre-trained video diffusion model [(Wan et al., 2025)]. Adopting the formulation of [Chadebec et al. (2025)], we train the model to learn a flow trajectory that directly transports the source flat-lit latents to the target OLAT latents (see Sec. 3.2 for details). During this process, the specific target lighting direction steers the generation by modulating the network features via Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN) [(Perez et al., 2018)] (see Sec. 3.3 for details). Ultimately, the network predicts a velocity field to drive the transport of the input latents, which are subsequently decoded to yield the final high-fidelity OLAT video.

    We explicitly model this process over video sequences rather than individual frames. While static image relighting is well-established, the straightforward frame-by-frame application of such methods to dynamic sequences inherently suffers from temporal flickering and inconsistent shadowing. By operating directly on video data, our model not only ensures temporal coherence and geometric consistency but also benefits from the diverse pose coverage naturally present in dynamic captures.

    3.2. Bridge Matching for Video Latents

    To predict a reliable OLAT basis video, it is crucial to feed the original video frames into the model in a way that preserves source appearance while supporting deterministic lighting edits. Prior diffusion-based relighting methods typically concatenate input frames with Gaussian noise along a specific axis, such as the channel dimension [(Chaturvedi et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2025)] or the frame dimension [(He et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2025)], to maintain the standard denoising process. While this strategy supports the generative workflow, the reliance on randomly sampled noise often leads to outputs that fail to preserve fine textures and details from the input. Such inconsistency is unacceptable for human-centric relighting: texture drift changes the subject appearance, and the same stochasticity can also perturb the predicted shadows and highlights that should correspond to a specific lighting direction. See Fig. 9 for comparative results.

    Since relighting is inherently a pixel-aligned editing task, we draw inspiration from LBM [(Chadebec et al., 2025)] and replace the input noise with latent tokens encoded from the flat-lit frames, allowing direct token-wise alignment between model inputs and outputs. This source-to-target bridge helps preserve fine source textures while constraining the model to learn the lighting-dependent residual response needed for OLAT prediction.

    Specifically, we implement this paradigm by constructing a stochastic bridge between the source and target distributions. We first encode the flat-lit video and the corresponding OLAT video into latent space via the encoder of a pretrained video variational autoencoder (VAE) [(Kingma and Welling, 2013)], producing latents z_flat and zₒₗₐₜ. We then define the bridge interpolant zₜ as:

    (1)

    zₜ=(1-t)zₒₗₐₜ+tz_flat+σ√t(1-t)ε ,

    where t∈[0,1] is randomly sampled from a set of timesteps, ε∼ℕ(0,I), and σ denotes the noise strength, which we set to 0.001 to enhance model robustness while keeping the input distribution within a reasonable range. To learn the trajectory of this bridge, we regress a vector field using a video DiT model v_Θ by minimizing the bridge matching objective:

    (2)

    L_LBM=𝔼[∥(zₜ-zₒₗₐₜ)/t-v_Θ(zₜ,t)∥²] .

    At inference time, we feed the encoded flat-lit latents into the model and iteratively update them from t=1 toward the distribution of the corresponding OLAT latents via:

    (3)

    ẑ_t+Δt=zₜ+v_Θ(zₜ,t)Δt ,

    where Δt<0, and the noise term is removed to maximally preserve information from the original input. When the iteration reaches t=0, we map the predicted ẑ₀ back to the pixel space using the decoder of the video VAE.

    3.3. Lighting Direction Conditioning

    To achieve precise directional control while maintaining a compact representation, we condition the model directly on the 3D lighting direction vector. This approach serves as a robust alternative to explicit spatial encodings (e.g., shading maps [(Pandey et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2024)] or light source maps [(Choi et al., 2024)]), avoiding their associated computational overhead and potential geometric ambiguity.

    Encoding

    To ensure geometric consistency with the visual content, we first rotate the world-space light vector into the camera coordinate system of the input video. Furthermore, to facilitate the learning of high-frequency illumination variations, we augment the raw direction vector d using Spherical Harmonics (SH) encoding Y(·)[(Tancik et al., 2023)]. The final conditioning vector c_d is constructed by concatenating the raw vector with its positional encoding:

    (4)

    c_d=d⊕Y(d) ,

    where ⊕ indicates concatenation along the channel dimension, and the SH degree is empirically set to 3.

    Injection

    We inject this lighting condition via an adaptive modulation mechanism. Within each transformer block, an individual linear projection layer maps the frequency-augmented vector c_d to the model’s hidden dimension. This projected vector is subsequently added to the timestep embedding to modulate the input tokens by driving the scale, shift, and gate parameters of AdaLN [(Perez et al., 2018)]. To ensure the input distribution remains unperturbed at the onset of training, the parameters of these newly introduced linear layers are initialized to zero.

    3.4. High-Frequency Details Enhancement

    Accurate OLAT prediction requires preserving high-frequency human appearance in addition to estimating the correct lighting response. Fine wrinkles, hair strands, fabric texture, and sharp shadow boundaries are part of the basis response that will later be linearly combined under environment illumination. On one hand, the iterative denoising process of diffusion models excels at producing visually realistic results [(Rombach et al., 2021; Nichol et al., 2021)], but the randomness introduced by noise can degrade high-frequency details present in the input. On the other hand, while a bridge matching approach in latent space naturally preserves much of the input pattern, it tends to excessively attenuate high-frequency details that should otherwise be preserved. To make the predicted OLAT bases both visually faithful and reliable for controllable linear assembly, we strengthen high-frequency details across four complementary dimensions: image-video joint training, dynamic resolution, pixel-space supervision, and sampling iterations.

    Image-Video Joint Training

    Although video data is essential for learning temporal dynamics, raw OLAT video captures frequently suffer from inherent quality degradations, such as motion blur, compression noise, and warping artifacts, which inevitably smooth out high-frequency details. In contrast, static OLAT imagery typically preserves superior textural fidelity and sharpness. To bridge this gap, we implement a joint training scheme that interleaves high-quality static images with video sequences. In this setup, static images guide the model to recover fine-grained structural and lighting details, while video data ensures temporal coherence.

    Dynamic Resolution

    We also observe that full-body human figures in videos tend to be much taller than typical 16:9 frames, meaning that a fixed training resolution often compresses the subject’s effective pixels while leaving excessive background. We therefore use no fixed training resolution: for each sequence, we crop all flat-lit and OLAT frames to the union of the flat-lit foreground masks predicted by [Zheng et al. (2024)]. We then pad the crop, rather than resize the foreground, until both dimensions are divisible by 16 as required by the VAE.

    Pixel-Space Supervision

    Supervision using only a latent-space regression loss is insufficient to achieve high visual quality, as it does not emphasize the preservation of high-frequency structures that are perceptually important, whereas a perceptual loss can better retain these visually salient patterns. This supervision also benefits controllable relighting because blurred basis predictions can smear shadow boundaries and weaken the directional cues used in the final composition. Following [Chadebec et al. (2025)], we therefore incorporate a pixel-space LPIPS loss [(Zhang et al., 2018)]: the model’s predicted OLAT latents ẑₒₗₐₜ are decoded via the VAE into x̂ₒₗₐₜ and an LPIPS loss is computed between x̂ₒₗₐₜ and the ground truth xₒₗₐₜ in pixel space. In practice, to avoid excessive memory usage on video data, we apply a random cropping strategy, computing the perceptual loss only on patches when the video resolution exceeds a predefined threshold. The overall training objective is then defined as:

    (5)

    L=L_LBM(𝔼(x_flat),𝔼(xₒₗₐₜ),t)+λ·L_perceptual(x̂ₒₗₐₜ,xₒₗₐₜ) ,

    where x_flat and xₒₗₐₜ denote videos in pixel space, and L_perceptual refers to the frame-wise LPIPS loss.

    Sampling Iterations

    We find that simply reusing the single-step inference schedule from [Chadebec et al. (2025)] leads to overly smooth outputs, where high-frequency details such as wrinkles on human skin and clothing are not well preserved. Performing iterative sampling with 4 steps, however, sufficiently mitigates this issue and yields sharper OLAT bases for subsequent intensity-weighted composition.

    3.5. Long Sequence Inference

    Video generative models are typically constrained to a fixed context length F during training due to GPU memory constraints. Direct extrapolation to longer sequences is non-trivial; a naive approach of partitioning the video into independent chunks inevitably results in temporal discontinuities and flickering at the boundaries. Existing sliding-window strategies [(Wu et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025)] achieve consistency by fusing latents across varying Gaussian denoising levels. These are incompatible with our framework, where the generative trajectory is governed by a structured source distribution rather than stochastic noise.

    To address this, we propose a recurrent bridge context, a strategy tailored for consistency in bridge-matching-based generation. We employ a sliding window with length W=F and stride S, leveraging previously generated OLAT frames to guide the inference process. Specifically, we define a "history context" corresponding to the overlapping region of length W-S. This context is populated by zₒₗₐₜᵖʳᵉᵛ∈ℝ^(W-S)×c×h×w, which denotes the finalized OLAT latents derived from the preceding window. During the iterative sampling process of the current window, we enforce temporal continuity by overriding the estimated latents ẑₜ in this overlap region with the ideal bridge state derived from the history context:

    (6)

    ẑₜ[i]=\begincases(1-t)zₒₗₐₜᵖʳᵉᵛ[i]+tz_flat[i],&ifi

    where z_flat∈ℝ^W×c×h×w represents the encoded flat-lit frames of the current window. At each timestep, we replace the overlapping latents with the noise-free mean interpolant of Eq. 1, thereby constraining the current window to match the previously generated frames in the overlap region and propagating temporal context forward. Finally, we concatenate the context latents zₒₗₐₜᵖʳᵉᵛ with the non-overlapping part of the predicted ẑ₀[W-S:W]∈ℝ^S×c×h×w and decode the combined sequence via the video VAE.

    This recursive strategy leverages the causal nature of the video VAE to extend bridge-matching inference beyond the training context while preserving consistent appearance and illumination responses without additional training. Results on sequences of up to 917 frames are provided in the supplementary material.

    3.6. Linear Space Combination

    To relight the dynamic performance under a target high dynamic range (HDR) environment map, we associate each predicted OLAT basis with a light direction in the camera coordinate system. We partition the environment map according to the nearest basis direction and integrate the linear HDR radiance within each region to obtain its weight. The final video is synthesized by performing a frame-by-frame linear combination of the predicted OLAT videos. Specifically, for each frame, the corresponding outputs from all basis videos are converted to linear space, multiplied by these weights, and accumulated to produce the relit result. This linear-space assembly is the key step for intensity controllability: the relative strength of each environment region is explicitly determined by its combination weight, rather than being implicitly inferred by the model from an unconstrained conditioning image. A single global scaling factor, typically set to 3, is applied per environment map to match the dynamic range of the target illumination to the captured lighting bases, while preserving the relative weights among basis directions.

    4. The Dataset

    4.1. Overview

    Training our controllable video relighting model requires large-scale paired video data consisting of a subject under flat lighting and the corresponding response to known OLAT illumination.

    However, acquiring such ground truth is physically non-trivial, as a subject cannot simultaneously experience two distinct lighting conditions at the exact same instant. To address this, we employ a time-multiplexed acquisition protocol, rapidly alternating between flat-lit frames and OLAT frames. Since inevitable subject motion occurs during the interval between light switches, raw frames are inherently misaligned. We mitigate this by estimating optical flow between consecutive flat-lit frames and warping the intermediate OLAT frames to align spatially with the flat-lit references, thereby yielding pixel-aligned training pairs.

    Crucially, to ensure the model learns robust representations, we devised a novel Light Switching Pattern. Our empirical findings suggest that training on a single fixed light direction leads to overfitting, where the model fails to disentangle illumination from motion features. To address this, we alternate between two distinct OLAT directions throughout a capture session. Specifically, we select the two lights with the greatest spatial distance within the LightStage to maximize illumination variance, while ensuring that all 101 distinct light sources are traversed exactly once across the full recording session of each subject, with no repetitions. Each OLAT direction is repeated for 9 consecutive cycles to ensure sufficient temporal sampling. Consequently, these two sets of OLAT frames, along with their interleaved flat-lit references, constitute a block of 18 pairs, which we define as a single sequence. The raw structure of such a sequence is visualized in Fig. 3(1), while the processed, aligned pairs are shown in Fig. 3(3). Across a full recording session for one subject, this process yields 51 such sequences for each camera view. Through this protocol, we acquired over 23 million valid frames across 189 identity-outfit combinations in the Dynamic-subset. We avoid alternating among too many directions (e.g., three or more) as it introduces excessive temporal gaps between frames of the same lighting condition, which degrades the temporal coherence of the video and hinders training.

    Additionally, we acquired complete OLAT sequences from 35 identity-outfit combinations in static poses. These dense captures support image-based relighting synthesis of ground-truth images under target environment maps, providing a controlled benchmark for image-level lighting evaluation.

    Consequently, we organize our dataset into two primary components: the Dynamic-subset (comprising the motion-rich paired video data) and the Static-subset (comprising the comprehensive full OLAT sequences). Tab. 1 compares the scale and capture properties of our dataset with existing benchmarks. The supplementary material reports aggregate statistics for the 224 identity-outfit combinations and provides detailed dataset overviews.

    All participants provided informed consent that explicitly permits research use and public release of their captured data. The release will exclude unnecessary personal metadata and will document the intended research use, privacy considerations, and potential misuse in synthetic-media pipelines. We plan to release the processed dataset upon publication under terms consistent with the participants’ consent.

    In the following subsections, we detail the technical implementation of our dataset construction. In Sec. 4.2, we describe the Capture Setup, detailing the unified LightStage hardware and the distinct camera array configurations tailored for each subset. In Sec. 4.3, we present the data-processing pipeline, focusing on motion-artifact mitigation and data-quality assessment.

    4.2. Capture Setup

    LightStage System.

    Our illumination system is shared across both subsets (Fig. 4(a)). It consists of over 800 LEDs grouped into 101 finite-area, individually addressable lighting units (referred to as One-Light units), driven by a custom microcontroller with microsecond precision. For dynamic acquisition, we configure the lighting clock cycle to 35 ms.

    Camera Systems and Settings.

    We deployed two synchronized camera systems, one for each subset. We prioritized storage efficiency and bandwidth for the Dynamic-subset to enable large-scale recording, while prioritizing dynamic range and raw quality for the Static-subset.

  • •

    Dynamic-subset: We used 68 custom-built PTZ cameras (Sony IMX678) to record 4K H.264 video at 60 fps (60 Mbps bitrate, I-frame interval of 2). The array comprises 48 short-lens cameras (approximately 9 mm) distributed spherically and 20 telephoto cameras (approximately 34 mm) placed primarily in frontal positions to capture upper-body details. Exposure is fixed at 1/125 s (f/4.8) to reduce motion blur.

  • •

    Static-subset: We utilized 70 Blackmagic Micro Studio Camera 4K G2 units arranged in a similar spherical layout: 54 units (14/15 mm lenses, including six zenith/nadir cameras) and 16 telephoto units (47 mm lenses). The raw footage is stored as Blackmagic RAW. While this format provides superior fidelity, its prohibitive bitrate prevents further scaling. We use a faster shutter speed of 1/500 s (f/4.4, ISO 3200) to reduce motion blur and transcode the footage to 100 Mbps for processing.

    • The spatial distributions are visualized in Fig. 4(c) and (d). Representative images from these camera arrays are provided in the supplementary material.

    Illumination Strategy.

    A major challenge in OLAT capture is the extreme dynamic range discrepancy between full-on lighting and single OLAT conditions. To address this discrepancy, we activate a uniformly sampled subset (1/6) of the lights to simulate ambient illumination (Fig. 4(b)). This preserves perceptual consistency within the camera’s limited dynamic range. Note that all references to "flat-lit" in this paper refer to this flat-lit configuration.

    Light Switching Patterns.

    The two subsets employ different switching patterns to serve their respective goals:

  • •

    Dynamic-subset Pattern: As introduced in Sec. 4.1, we repeat one OLAT direction for 9 cycles, interleaved with its spatially most distant counterpart for another 9 cycles (Fig. 3(3)). This variation encourages the model to decouple motion from lighting.

  • •

    Static-subset Pattern: We use 10 consecutive OLAT frames followed by 1 flat-lit frame. For each identity-outfit combination, we capture at least three static poses and several flat-lit dynamic sequences for relighting evaluation.

    • 4.3. Data Processing

    Given the complexity of massive-scale OLAT acquisition, especially for the Dynamic-subset, the raw data requires careful processing to achieve geometric alignment and photometric consistency. The overall pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 3. In the following sections, we detail the core algorithms for OLAT to flat-lit warping, followed by specific strategies for data quality assessment.

    OLAT to Flat-lit Warping.

    We use optical flow to compensate for subject motion, including rapid actions in the Dynamic-subset and involuntary sway in the Static-subset, that causes misalignment between flat-lit and OLAT frames. We compute bidirectional optical flow between consecutive flat-lit frames [(Harley et al., 2025)]. Assuming linear motion within the short interval, we derive the flow field for the intermediate OLAT frame via temporal linear interpolation. Alongside flow estimation, we generate foreground masks for the flat-lit frames using BiRefNet [(Zheng et al., 2024)] and compute a unified bounding box.

    Based on the computed flow, we apply different warping strategies tailored to the downstream application:

  • •

    Training Pairs (Dynamic & Static): To minimize warping artifacts, we warp each OLAT frame to its temporal nearest-neighbor flat-lit frame. This yields diverse, well-aligned pairs for learning-based models, preserving the original motion fidelity.

  • •

    Quality Assessment Stack (Static only): For quality evaluation, we warp all OLAT frames within a pose to the first flat-lit frame of the sequence, producing a geometrically aligned OLAT stack for the photometric analyses described below.

    • Quality Assessment.

    We utilize the geometrically aligned OLAT stack from the Static-subset to quantitatively assess the quality of our acquisition system. As illustrated in Fig. 5, our raw captures from both short-lens (a) and telephoto (b) cameras preserve high-frequency details. To assess geometric detail, we estimate surface normals via photometric stereo using gradient-descent optimization with outlier rejection. The resulting normal maps in Fig. 5(c) retain fine-scale skin texture and clothing wrinkles. To assess photometric linearity, we synthesize relit images by linearly combining the OLAT bases with environment-map weights after gamma correction. The synthesized results (d) preserve fine shading and self-shadowing details more faithfully than the evaluated neural relighting baselines.

    5. Experiments

    5.1. Implementation Details

    Training Configuration

    We perform full-parameter fine-tuning based on the Wan2.1 1.3B foundation model [(Wan et al., 2025)]. The model is trained for a total of 60,000 steps with a constant learning rate of 10⁻⁴ and a batch size of 8. During training, the target OLAT directions are randomly sampled from all available lighting directions. The probability of sampling static images for joint training follows a stepwise curriculum: it is set to 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 for each consecutive 20,000-step interval. We use the same few-timestep sampling during training as [Chadebec et al. (2025)], where the discrete timesteps are sampled uniformly from the set {i/16}ᵢ₌₁¹⁶. For the objective function, we utilize a VGG16-based LPIPS metric for the perceptual loss, setting the weight coefficient λ to 1.

    Fixed Text Prompt

    Throughout both training and inference, we utilize a fixed, descriptive text prompt to provide a consistent semantic context: "Given: a reference video of a person and a lighting direction representing a specific point light source. Generate: a realistic relit video of the same person under the target lighting defined by one light. Requirements: preserve identity and appearance, maintain consistent clothing and proportions, correct perspective, realistic lighting, shadows, and no artifacts."

    Inference Configuration

    During inference, we disable classifier-free guidance to rely primarily on our conditioning signals. To ensure temporal consistency, the recurrent bridge context is configured with a window length of W=9 frames and a stride of S=4, which is essential for stable video generation. We employ a uniform sampling strategy with 4 discrete timesteps, specifically {1,0.75,0.5,0.25}. For each input sequence, we typically generate a set of 201 distinct OLAT videos to serve as the bases for relighting. These 201 bases preserve the zenith direction of the original 101-light configuration while doubling the azimuthal sampling density at each elevation. Additional results in the supplementary material show comparable quality under static lighting but smoother responses to rotating high-frequency illumination with 201 bases; 101 bases reduce generation and storage cost when finer sampling is unnecessary.

    Hardware and Runtime

    The entire training process is conducted on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and takes approximately one week to complete. We additionally measure the inference cost of generating the OLAT basis set. For a 57-frame video at 1920×1088, generating one OLAT basis takes 119.45 seconds. When generation is distributed across eight A100 GPUs, producing 101 bases takes 26.89 minutes, while producing 201 bases takes 52.01 minutes. At 1280×720, generating one basis takes 61.08 seconds; with the same eight-GPU setup, producing 101 bases takes 14.53 minutes, while producing 201 bases takes 27.56 minutes. Because individual bases can be generated independently, they can be computed in parallel and cached for subsequent linear combinations without online network inference, although generation and storage costs scale approximately with their number.

    5.2. Datasets and Metrics

    We construct our training set by randomly selecting 100 identity-outfit combinations from the Dynamic-subset and 28 from the Static-subset. For evaluation, we hold out 54 and 7 identity-outfit combinations from the two subsets, respectively. For the Dynamic-subset, we use only views captured with short-lens cameras.

    To ensure alignment with the pre-training distribution of the foundation model, all data are represented in the sRGB color space. Additionally, to isolate the subjects and eliminate background interference, we apply a uniform mask to all input frames, setting the background to black.

    Following the evaluation protocol of [He et al. (2024)], we employ PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] (with an AlexNet backbone), and FLIP [(Andersson et al., 2020)] to quantitatively assess model performance.

    5.3. Comparisons with Existing Methods

    We compare our model with three video relighting approaches: the open-source RelightVid [(Fang et al., 2025)], the Cosmos-based DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)], and UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)]. To establish a comprehensive benchmark, we also include two recent single-image relighting methods: IC-Light [(Zhang et al., 2025a)] and LBM [(Chadebec et al., 2025)]. For the open-source baselines, we resize input videos or images to their recommended resolutions and adapt the lighting inputs to each method’s requirements. For DiffusionRenderer and UniRelight, we use the full HDR environment map as the condition. For RelightVid, IC-Light, and LBM, which rely on a background image, we sample the corresponding field of view from the HDR map and convert it to sRGB.

    We qualitatively evaluate video relighting on our OLAT dataset and in-the-wild sequences in Figs. 6 and 7. Reference images are generated via image-based relighting from captured OLAT images, together with material balls rendered under the target environment maps.

    Fig. 6 qualitatively compares responses to target direction (a), intensity distributions (b), and real-world lighting (c). Our results follow the target changes more closely than the evaluated baselines. The supplementary material further shows how our method responds to different intensity scalings of the same environment map.

    To reduce the domain gap between the required flat-lit input and in-the-wild videos, we apply the delighting model described in the supplementary material before OLAT prediction. Consequently, beyond controlled setups, Fig. 7 highlights our strong generalization capabilities to novel, in-the-wild scenarios. Our model robustly preserves fine details and subject identity far better than the baselines. This superiority is evident in the fine-grained environmental interactions it synthesizes, such as the physically precise shadows in (a) and the accurate reflected bounce light from the background red curtain in the first frame of (b). Overall, these results confirm that our method synthesizes more photorealistic appearances and physically plausible lighting effects compared to existing approaches.

    For quantitative lighting evaluation, we use the Static-subset, whose complete captured OLAT sequences allow us to synthesize ground-truth images under target environment maps via image-based relighting. In this setting, we focus our comparison on two representative image-based methods (IC-Light [(Zhang et al., 2025a)] and LBM [(Chadebec et al., 2025)]) and two video-based methods (DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)] and UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)]).

    Image-relighting results are reported in Tab. 2 and Fig. 8, with an additional qualitative HumanOLAT comparison provided in the supplementary material. We resize all outputs and ground truth to the minimum evaluated resolution and mask their backgrounds. Following [Jin et al. (2024)], each predicted color channel is rescaled to the ground-truth mean to resolve global illumination–surface-color scale ambiguity. This calibration is used in quantitative evaluation to ensure a consistent comparison across methods. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms the baselines across most metrics and preserves significantly richer fine-grained details.

    Following Lux Post Facto [(Mei et al., 2025)], we evaluate temporal consistency using LPIPS between adjacent frames and warping error (WE) computed with optical flow from RAFT [(Teed and Deng, 2020)] and AllTracker [(Harley et al., 2025)]. Tab. 3 shows that our method achieves excellent temporal consistency.

    5.4. Ablation Studies

    We conduct three ablation studies to investigate the effectiveness of key components in our proposed framework. All quantitative evaluations are performed on a representative subset of 200 test sequences randomly sampled from our Dynamic-subset. Specifically, these sequences consist of paired flat-lit inputs and ground-truth OLAT videos, and all reported results (both quantitative and qualitative) evaluate the quality of the synthesized OLAT videos. To ensure fair comparison while managing computational costs, all ablated versions are trained for 20,000 steps with a sampling ratio of 0.1 for images and 0.9 for videos. Consistent with the main experiments, since our model focuses exclusively on the foreground subject, all quantitative metrics are computed on background-masked images to prevent background noise from biasing the results.

    Latent Bridge Matching for Input Frames

    To validate the efficacy of the LBM paradigm [(Chadebec et al., 2025)], we compare it against standard diffusion conditioning strategies that rely on noise concatenation. Specifically, we implemented two baseline variants where the flat-lit input latents are concatenated with the noisy latents along either the channel dimension or the frame dimension. For the channel-wise concatenation baseline, we expanded the input channels of the first convolutional layer by a factor of two and initialized the weights of the newly added channels to zero for training stability. Quantitative results in Tab. 4 and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 9 reveal a significant performance gap. The noise concatenation methods tend to degrade source fidelity, often producing artifacts or losing fine-grained texture details due to the destructive nature of the initial Gaussian noise. In contrast, by establishing a direct transport trajectory from the source, bridge matching for video latents effectively preserves the structural integrity and high-frequency details of the input, yielding significantly higher fidelity in the final relit video.

    Lighting Conditioning

    We primarily evaluate our design against two alternative mechanisms: cross-attention and global AdaLN. The cross-attention method, following [He et al. (2024)], injects SH encodings by replacing the original text prompt embeddings, which risks disrupting the inherent input distribution of the backbone. The global AdaLN scheme employs a single shared projection layer for all blocks, offering only coarse, uniform control. In contrast, our block-specific AdaLN strategy preserves the integrity of the input features while enabling finer-grained, block-wise lighting modulation. Quantitative results in Tab. 4 and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 10 demonstrate that our proposed conditioning scheme achieves more precise directional control and yields more photorealistic predictions.

    Long Sequence Inference

    We compare our recurrent bridge context with Position Interpolation (PI) [(Chen et al., 2023)] and sliding iterative sampling [(Jin et al., 2025)] in Fig. 11. PI introduces out-of-distribution positional embeddings, while heterogeneous latent timesteps cause significant lighting drift in sliding iterative sampling.

    5.5. Additional Qualitative Results

    We further demonstrate the versatility and robustness of our model on unseen subjects. As illustrated in Fig. 12, our model synthesizes precise shading and self-shadowing effects under continuously rotating lighting directions, maintaining physical plausibility. Fig. 13 validates temporal stability, showcasing a dynamic performance coherently illuminated by a fixed directional light source across the sequence. Finally, Fig. 14 highlights the geometric consistency of our predictions, successfully generalizing to diverse camera viewpoints for a specified lighting direction. For more extensive visualization results and dynamic comparisons, please refer to our supplementary video.

    6. Conclusion

    In this work, we have presented a comprehensive framework for controllable dynamic full-body relighting from monocular flat-lit videos. By shifting the paradigm from direct relit-image generation to data-driven OLAT video prediction, our approach decomposes human light transport into directional basis responses and reconstructs the final appearance through linear-space intensity weighting. This formulation makes direction explicit in the OLAT bases and relative intensity explicit in the environment-map weights while preserving appearance details and temporal coherence. The accompanying large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset provides the directional supervision needed to learn these responses across diverse identities, outfits, motions, and views.

    Current limitations include the flat-lit input assumption, sensitivity of delighting to strong shadows or colored illumination, and the reconstruction ceiling of the pretrained video VAE. The explicit OLAT representation also incurs basis-dependent generation and storage costs, while cross-OLAT and cross-view consistency remains implicit rather than architecturally guaranteed. Finally, the finite-area capture lights limit directional resolution; missing dynamic relighting ground truth and reliable pixel-level lighting-angle annotations further constrain quantitative evaluation. Further discussion and failure analysis are provided in the supplementary material.

    These boundaries motivate more robust delighting, higher-fidelity video autoencoders, efficient basis prediction with explicit consistency, finer illumination capture, and dynamic lighting benchmarks. The dataset may further support neural rendering and controllable generative video editing.

    Acknowledgements.

    We thank Dongli Tan for LightStage camera calibration and Linxian Wu for providing paired outdoor environment panoramas and reference images captured under the same lighting conditions. This work was partially supported by National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2024YFB2809105), NSFC (No. U24B20154), Zhejiang Provincial Natural Science Foundation of China (No. LR25F020003), and Information Technology Center and State Key Lab of CAD&CG, Zhejiang University.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Supplementary Material

    Appendix A Dataset Statistics

    Participants were 18–30 years old. Tab. 5 summarizes the combined dataset composition.

    Appendix B Supplementary of Data Processing

    B.1. Rolling Shutter Detection and Sequence Segmentation

    The light-switch cycle is intentionally set slightly longer than two camera frame periods (approximately 33.3 ms at 60 fps), which facilitates rolling-shutter detection. In addition to the target flat-lit and OLAT frames, our raw footage inevitably contains frames affected by rolling-shutter (RS) artifacts. Both subsets rely on the precise identification of valid frames to correctly extract lighting sequences. However, identifying RS frames is non-trivial for the Dynamic-subset: due to H.264 compression, the distinct RS boundary is blurred by spatial artifacts (Fig. 15(b)), rendering traditional spatial stitching or gradient-based detection infeasible.

一句话：现有学习式重打光画面像，但阴影高光会「漂」离目标方向，强度也不对。

要点：

  • 要求写得很清楚：动态人体重打光需要阴影、高光与颜色变化在**方向与相对强度**上都跟随目标光照
  • 现有学习式方法能生成视觉上合理的视频，但光照响应不准——阴影与高光会偏离目标方向，输出的强度关系也不对
  • DynOLAT 改为直接预测 OLAT（one-light-at-a-time）视频，从而获得可控、可重打光的表示

为什么值得看：OLAT 是离线渲染里成熟的分解方式，把它搬到视频预测上，等于用「物理分解」的思路约束生成模型。对需要让同一个角色在不同光照环境下复用的管线，这是比端到端重打光更可控的路。

中文摘要：动态人体重打光的关键在于光照响应要准：阴影、高光与颜色变化必须在方向与相对强度上都跟随目标光照。现有基于学习的方法能生成视觉上合理的视频，却常常光照响应不精确——阴影和高光会偏离目标方向，输出中的强度关系也不对。DynOLAT 因此改为直接预测 OLAT（one-light-at-a-time）视频：把每个光源的贡献分开建模，再组合出可控的重打光结果。这种把离线渲染里成熟的分解方式搬到视频预测上的做法，让重打光从「看起来像」变成「响应得对」。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

DynOLAT: OLAT Video Prediction for Controllable Dynamic Full-Body Relighting

2026

Abstract.

Accurate lighting response is essential for realistic dynamic human relighting, because shadows, highlights, and color changes should follow the target illumination in both direction and relative strength. Current learning-based relighting methods can generate visually plausible videos, but they often exhibit imprecise lighting responses: shadows and highlights may drift away from the target direction, and the output brightness may not faithfully follow the relative intensities in the target environment, making the result closer to appearance harmonization than controllable relighting. To address this issue, we propose DynOLAT, a generalizable OLAT video prediction framework for dynamic full-body humans. Instead of directly synthesizing a single relit appearance, our method predicts temporally consistent One-Light-At-a-Time (OLAT) basis videos from flat-lit inputs, and then linearly combines the predicted bases according to the target environment map. This OLAT-based formulation makes the directional response explicit in the predicted bases, while the relative lighting strength is determined by the linear weights derived from the environment map. We further introduce a dynamic capture pipeline and the first large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset, comprising over 24 million frames from 224 identity-outfit combinations, where different outfits of the same person define separate combinations. Experiments show that DynOLAT responds more faithfully to variations in target lighting direction and relative intensity than the tested baselines, enabling controllable video relighting while preserving fine appearance details and temporal coherence. The dataset and processing tools will be publicly released to foster future research.

Keywords:

Controllable relighting, full-body OLATs, latent bridge matching, video-to-video translation, HD full-body capture ††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

Realistic dynamic human relighting requires the synthesized subject to respond accurately to the specified illumination in addition to appearing visually plausible. In practical VR/AR, film production, immersive telepresence, and game-content workflows, artists expect a relighting method to place shadows, highlights, and color changes according to the target light direction and relative intensity. This paper studies this controllability-oriented setting: given a monocular flat-lit video of a full-body human captured from an arbitrary viewpoint, we aim to synthesize a temporally coherent video of the same performance under a new lighting environment.

Existing general relighting methods still struggle with two forms of lighting-response accuracy that are critical for production use. First, their directional response is often imprecise: even when the target light direction is specified, the synthesized shading may exhibit a noticeable angular offset. Second, their intensity response is often unreliable: the output brightness may not faithfully follow the relative intensities in the target environment, making the result behave more like appearance harmonization than physically controlled relighting. These failure modes, highlighted in Fig. 1 and Fig. 6, are not only local visual artifacts; they directly weaken control over the target light direction and relative strength.

The difficulty arises because monocular human relighting requires both appearance realism and disentangled light control. Traditional inverse-rendering methods [(Barron and Malik, 2015)] attempt to estimate geometry, material, and illumination explicitly, but the problem is severely under-constrained for dynamic humans with spatially varying skin, hair, and clothing reflectance. Strong priors are therefore needed to resolve the ambiguity, often suppressing high-frequency details and producing overly smooth or artificial human appearance. Recent diffusion-based relighting methods [(Liang et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2025)] reduce the need for explicit decomposition by learning direct image or video mappings from large-scale data. While these models can produce visually plausible results, their lighting conditions are often encoded as holistic environment images or prompts, making it difficult to guarantee that output shadows and intensities follow the target illumination in a directionally and radiometrically faithful way.

OLAT representations provide a natural route to controllable relighting because they separate light transport into directional basis responses. A one-light-at-a-time (OLAT) image records the subject response to a single lighting direction; arbitrary environment illumination can then be formed by linearly combining the corresponding bases. DifFRelight [(He et al., 2024)] demonstrates that predicting OLAT representations can yield highly realistic and controllable facial relighting. Extending this idea from single facial images to dynamic full-body videos is non-trivial, because full-body motion introduces loose clothing deformation, self-occlusion, larger pose variation, and a lack of large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT supervision.

To address this gap, we propose DynOLAT, an OLAT video prediction framework for controllable dynamic full-body relighting. Given a flat-lit human video and a target lighting direction, our model predicts the corresponding OLAT basis video; the predicted bases are then combined in linear color space according to any target environment map. This formulation makes the target lighting explicit at two levels: the network learns directional basis responses, and the final relit video is assembled with environment-dependent intensity weights. As a result, the method is designed to preserve directional alignment and support explicit relative-intensity control, rather than relying on an unconstrained end-to-end generation of a single relit appearance.

Our technical design adapts a pretrained video model [(Wan et al., 2025)] to this OLAT prediction task while preserving source identity, details, and temporal coherence. We adopt Latent Bridge Matching (LBM) [(Chadebec et al., 2025)] to transport flat-lit video latents directly toward OLAT latents, avoiding the source-detail loss introduced by sampling from independent Gaussian noise. We further inject the target lighting direction through block-specific AdaLN modulation, enabling fine-grained directional control across the video transformer. For long sequences, a recurrent bridge context reuses previously generated OLAT frames as analytic overlap constraints, maintaining coherence beyond the training window.

To train this data-driven model, we build a dedicated dynamic OLAT acquisition pipeline. The system rapidly alternates flat and directional illumination and then aligns the resulting frames to form paired flat-lit/OLAT videos. Using this pipeline, we collect a large-scale, multi-view, dynamic full-body OLAT dataset containing diverse subjects, clothing, motions, and viewpoints. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first dataset of comparable scale that provides dynamic full-body OLAT supervision for learning temporally consistent lighting responses. We will publicly release the dataset and processing tools to support future research.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that DynOLAT improves controllable full-body relighting in dynamic sequences. Qualitative comparisons show that our method better follows the target light direction and relative illumination strength, while preserving fine body details and temporal consistency. Quantitative comparisons and ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our design.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

  • (1)

    An OLAT video prediction framework that formulates dynamic full-body relighting as directionally decomposed light-response synthesis, enabling more faithful responses to target light direction and environment-map intensity.

  • (2)

    Tailored model designs that adapt Latent Bridge Matching for source-detail preservation, use block-specific lighting modulation for directional control, and employ recurrent bridge context for long-sequence temporal coherence.

  • (3)

    The first large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset with sufficient subject, clothing, motion, and viewpoint diversity for learning temporally consistent human light transport.

    • 2. Related Work

    2.1. Human-centric Relighting

    Relighting human performances from monocular video remains a fundamental challenge in computer graphics and vision. Existing methodologies can be broadly categorized into three paradigms: optimization-based inverse rendering, learning-based image relighting and learning-based video relighting.

    Optimization-Based Inverse Rendering

    Leveraging recent advances in 3D neural representations like NeRF [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)] and 3DGS [(Kerbl et al., 2023)], numerous works attempt to reconstruct human avatars and decompose intrinsic properties from multi-view images [(Li et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024; Zhan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2024a; Gao et al., 2024; Chen and Liu, 2022; Chen et al., 2024a; Singh et al., 2025)]. By explicitly estimating geometry, material, and illumination, these methods provide a physically interpretable route to relighting control. However, standard physically-based rendering (PBR) approximations often fail to capture complex surface effects, such as subsurface scattering and intricate self-shadowing, which affect both appearance realism and the accuracy of the predicted lighting response. To circumvent these limitations, recent approaches utilize ground-truth OLAT scans to learn neural reflectance fields directly [(Li et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b; Guo et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2025)]. While these approaches have achieved photorealistic results for both upper-body [(Saito et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024)] and full-body avatars [(Zhou et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025b; Guo et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2025; Teufel et al., 2026)], they rely heavily on subject-specific optimization. This requirement for dense capture setups and per-identity training limits direct application to in-the-wild images or videos and makes controllable direction and intensity responses difficult for novel dynamic subjects.

    Learning-Based Image Relighting

    To achieve generalization across subjects, a classical paradigm [(Nestmeyer et al., 2020; Pandey et al., 2021; Yeh et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2024; Daichi Tajima, 2025; Mei et al., 2025)] adapts the physics-based inverse rendering workflow into 2D feature space. These methods typically employ a cascaded pipeline that first decomposes the input image into intrinsic components (e.g., albedo and normals) and subsequently synthesizes the relit output via a neural renderer. While this strategy explicitly models light transport, the multi-stage process is prone to error accumulation: inaccurate geometry or albedo can blur source details and also shift the resulting shadows, highlights, and brightness away from the target illumination. Conversely, end-to-end approaches [(Sun et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2025b)] map inputs directly to relit outputs. Due to the scarcity of paired real-world data under varying illumination, many methods rely on synthetic data [(Ren et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a)] or auxiliary generation tasks [(Chaturvedi et al., 2025)], which can yield unrealistic shading or artifacts due to the domain gap. More importantly for controllable relighting, direct output synthesis often uses a target environment or background as a holistic condition, providing limited constraints that ensure the generated shadow direction and relative brightness follow the specified illumination. DifFRelight [(He et al., 2024)] and POLAR [(Chen et al., 2026)] fine-tune generative models on real OLAT data to predict OLATs for explicit lighting superposition, avoiding physical decomposition and synthetic-data domain gaps. In contrast, 3DPR [(Rao et al., 2025)] predicts portrait OLATs with a 3D head prior and linearly combines them for relighting. Nevertheless, applying these image-based solutions frame by frame to dynamic full-body sequences yields temporally unstable results, lacking the robustness required for video applications.

    Learning-Based Video Relighting

    To extend relighting to videos, earlier methods attempted to enforce temporal consistency via loss constraints [(Zhang et al., 2021)] or feature blending [(Wang et al., 2025a)]. However, given the geometric and textural complexity of dynamic full-body motion, independent frame processing can struggle to maintain coherence at high resolution. With the advent of video diffusion models [(Blattmann et al., 2023; Brooks et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025)], the mainstream paradigm has shifted toward fine-tuning video diffusion models [(Liang et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2025; He et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a)] or controlnets [(Zhang et al., 2025b)]. These methods typically inject condition frames by concatenating them with noisy latents, and represent lighting with environment maps, background images, or text-like conditions. However, this standard conditioning strategy poses a fundamental conflict: the stochastic denoising process, while excellent for diversity, introduces randomness that undermines the deterministic nature of relighting. This often leads to hallucinated details or identity drift, where the generated texture deviates from the source, and can also weaken the alignment between the output illumination and the target direction or intensity distribution. Instead of predicting a single relit video directly, our framework predicts OLAT basis videos and assembles the final illumination explicitly. To make this basis prediction source-aligned, we employ bridge matching [(Chadebec et al., 2025)] from the input video latents to the target OLAT latents, preserving fine source textures while learning a more deterministic light-response mapping. However, the success of such a data-driven video paradigm is heavily contingent on the availability of high-quality, temporally consistent training data.

    2.2. LightStage and OLAT Acquisition

    The LightStage architecture, pioneered by [Debevec et al. (2000)], revolutionized reflectance acquisition through precise, programmable lighting control. This setup inherently enables the capture of multi-view OLAT imagery. Fundamentally, relying on the linearity of light transport, the appearance of a subject under arbitrary environmental illumination can be synthesized via the linear superposition of these OLAT basis images. Consequently, LightStage data has become a "gold standard" benchmark for realistic relighting and has driven significant evolution in hardware design [(Debevec, 2008; Jones et al., 2006; Guo et al., 2019; He et al., 2024)].

    Despite its importance, the acquisition of such high-quality data remains heavily restricted by domain. While numerous works have explored OLAT-based frameworks, they predominantly focus on restricted domains such as facial appearance [(Li et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026)], hands [(Chen et al., 2024b)], or static objects [(Zhou et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023; Toschi et al., 2023)]. Research addressing full-body capture remains scarce [(Wang et al., 2025b; Teufel et al., 2025; Martinez et al., 2024)], and publicly available datasets are extremely limited. More critically, prior work on time-multiplexed dynamic OLAT capture has focused on faces and upper bodies [(Debevec, 2008; Zhang et al., 2021)].

    To the best of our knowledge, no existing public dataset provides dynamic full-body OLAT sequences at a comparable scale. This data scarcity becomes a bottleneck for training generalizable full-body relighting models, which require a substantial diversity of human materials and motions to avoid overfitting.

    To bridge this gap, we present our OLAT dataset, which includes a dedicated motion-rich subset. This component provides extensive dynamic OLAT data that covers diverse human materials and motions while supplying the directional light-response supervision needed to train controllable video relighting models.

    3. Method

    We decompose dynamic human relighting into explicit light-response prediction and linear environment assembly. In the first stage, we employ our OLAT video prediction model to synthesize a set of basis OLAT videos from a flat-lit input sequence, where each basis corresponds to a specific lighting direction. In the second stage, we reconstruct the final relit video under any complex environment map by linearly accumulating these predicted OLAT components in the linear color space. This decomposition is central to our controllability goal: the lighting direction is handled by the predicted basis index, while the lighting intensity is handled by the environment-map weights. An overview of our proposed framework is illustrated in Fig. 2.

    We first describe the architecture of our OLAT video prediction model in Sec. 3.1. We then explain how the flat-lit input frames (Sec. 3.2) and the target lighting direction (Sec. 3.3) are processed and injected into the network. Subsequently, we elaborate on our strategies for recovering high-frequency details (Sec. 3.4), which are necessary for producing reliable OLAT bases that retain the subject’s material and texture response. We then discuss our solution for inference on long video sequences (Sec. 3.5). Finally, we present the image-based relighting (IBR) formulation that renders the final output via a linear combination of the predicted OLAT bases (Sec. 3.6).

    3.1. Overview of OLAT Video Prediction Model

    Given a flat-lit video sequence and a target lighting direction, our goal is to synthesize the corresponding OLAT video. Concretely, we operate within the compressed latent space of a pre-trained video diffusion model [(Wan et al., 2025)]. Adopting the formulation of [Chadebec et al. (2025)], we train the model to learn a flow trajectory that directly transports the source flat-lit latents to the target OLAT latents (see Sec. 3.2 for details). During this process, the specific target lighting direction steers the generation by modulating the network features via Adaptive Layer Normalization (AdaLN) [(Perez et al., 2018)] (see Sec. 3.3 for details). Ultimately, the network predicts a velocity field to drive the transport of the input latents, which are subsequently decoded to yield the final high-fidelity OLAT video.

    We explicitly model this process over video sequences rather than individual frames. While static image relighting is well-established, the straightforward frame-by-frame application of such methods to dynamic sequences inherently suffers from temporal flickering and inconsistent shadowing. By operating directly on video data, our model not only ensures temporal coherence and geometric consistency but also benefits from the diverse pose coverage naturally present in dynamic captures.

    3.2. Bridge Matching for Video Latents

    To predict a reliable OLAT basis video, it is crucial to feed the original video frames into the model in a way that preserves source appearance while supporting deterministic lighting edits. Prior diffusion-based relighting methods typically concatenate input frames with Gaussian noise along a specific axis, such as the channel dimension [(Chaturvedi et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2025)] or the frame dimension [(He et al., 2025; Bian et al., 2025)], to maintain the standard denoising process. While this strategy supports the generative workflow, the reliance on randomly sampled noise often leads to outputs that fail to preserve fine textures and details from the input. Such inconsistency is unacceptable for human-centric relighting: texture drift changes the subject appearance, and the same stochasticity can also perturb the predicted shadows and highlights that should correspond to a specific lighting direction. See Fig. 9 for comparative results.

    Since relighting is inherently a pixel-aligned editing task, we draw inspiration from LBM [(Chadebec et al., 2025)] and replace the input noise with latent tokens encoded from the flat-lit frames, allowing direct token-wise alignment between model inputs and outputs. This source-to-target bridge helps preserve fine source textures while constraining the model to learn the lighting-dependent residual response needed for OLAT prediction.

    Specifically, we implement this paradigm by constructing a stochastic bridge between the source and target distributions. We first encode the flat-lit video and the corresponding OLAT video into latent space via the encoder of a pretrained video variational autoencoder (VAE) [(Kingma and Welling, 2013)], producing latents z_flat and zₒₗₐₜ. We then define the bridge interpolant zₜ as:

    (1)

    zₜ=(1-t)zₒₗₐₜ+tz_flat+σ√t(1-t)ε ,

    where t∈[0,1] is randomly sampled from a set of timesteps, ε∼ℕ(0,I), and σ denotes the noise strength, which we set to 0.001 to enhance model robustness while keeping the input distribution within a reasonable range. To learn the trajectory of this bridge, we regress a vector field using a video DiT model v_Θ by minimizing the bridge matching objective:

    (2)

    L_LBM=𝔼[∥(zₜ-zₒₗₐₜ)/t-v_Θ(zₜ,t)∥²] .

    At inference time, we feed the encoded flat-lit latents into the model and iteratively update them from t=1 toward the distribution of the corresponding OLAT latents via:

    (3)

    ẑ_t+Δt=zₜ+v_Θ(zₜ,t)Δt ,

    where Δt<0, and the noise term is removed to maximally preserve information from the original input. When the iteration reaches t=0, we map the predicted ẑ₀ back to the pixel space using the decoder of the video VAE.

    3.3. Lighting Direction Conditioning

    To achieve precise directional control while maintaining a compact representation, we condition the model directly on the 3D lighting direction vector. This approach serves as a robust alternative to explicit spatial encodings (e.g., shading maps [(Pandey et al., 2021; Zeng et al., 2024)] or light source maps [(Choi et al., 2024)]), avoiding their associated computational overhead and potential geometric ambiguity.

    Encoding

    To ensure geometric consistency with the visual content, we first rotate the world-space light vector into the camera coordinate system of the input video. Furthermore, to facilitate the learning of high-frequency illumination variations, we augment the raw direction vector d using Spherical Harmonics (SH) encoding Y(·)[(Tancik et al., 2023)]. The final conditioning vector c_d is constructed by concatenating the raw vector with its positional encoding:

    (4)

    c_d=d⊕Y(d) ,

    where ⊕ indicates concatenation along the channel dimension, and the SH degree is empirically set to 3.

    Injection

    We inject this lighting condition via an adaptive modulation mechanism. Within each transformer block, an individual linear projection layer maps the frequency-augmented vector c_d to the model’s hidden dimension. This projected vector is subsequently added to the timestep embedding to modulate the input tokens by driving the scale, shift, and gate parameters of AdaLN [(Perez et al., 2018)]. To ensure the input distribution remains unperturbed at the onset of training, the parameters of these newly introduced linear layers are initialized to zero.

    3.4. High-Frequency Details Enhancement

    Accurate OLAT prediction requires preserving high-frequency human appearance in addition to estimating the correct lighting response. Fine wrinkles, hair strands, fabric texture, and sharp shadow boundaries are part of the basis response that will later be linearly combined under environment illumination.
