On one hand, the iterative denoising process of diffusion models excels at producing visually realistic results [(Rombach et al., 2021; Nichol et al., 2021)], but the randomness introduced by noise can degrade high-frequency details present in the input. On the other hand, while a bridge matching approach in latent space naturally preserves much of the input pattern, it tends to excessively attenuate high-frequency details that should otherwise be preserved. To make the predicted OLAT bases both visually faithful and reliable for controllable linear assembly, we strengthen high-frequency details across four complementary dimensions: image-video joint training, dynamic resolution, pixel-space supervision, and sampling iterations.

    Image-Video Joint Training

    Although video data is essential for learning temporal dynamics, raw OLAT video captures frequently suffer from inherent quality degradations, such as motion blur, compression noise, and warping artifacts, which inevitably smooth out high-frequency details. In contrast, static OLAT imagery typically preserves superior textural fidelity and sharpness. To bridge this gap, we implement a joint training scheme that interleaves high-quality static images with video sequences. In this setup, static images guide the model to recover fine-grained structural and lighting details, while video data ensures temporal coherence.

    Dynamic Resolution

    We also observe that full-body human figures in videos tend to be much taller than typical 16:9 frames, meaning that a fixed training resolution often compresses the subject’s effective pixels while leaving excessive background. We therefore use no fixed training resolution: for each sequence, we crop all flat-lit and OLAT frames to the union of the flat-lit foreground masks predicted by [Zheng et al. (2024)]. We then pad the crop, rather than resize the foreground, until both dimensions are divisible by 16 as required by the VAE.

    Pixel-Space Supervision

    Supervision using only a latent-space regression loss is insufficient to achieve high visual quality, as it does not emphasize the preservation of high-frequency structures that are perceptually important, whereas a perceptual loss can better retain these visually salient patterns. This supervision also benefits controllable relighting because blurred basis predictions can smear shadow boundaries and weaken the directional cues used in the final composition. Following [Chadebec et al. (2025)], we therefore incorporate a pixel-space LPIPS loss [(Zhang et al., 2018)]: the model’s predicted OLAT latents ẑₒₗₐₜ are decoded via the VAE into x̂ₒₗₐₜ and an LPIPS loss is computed between x̂ₒₗₐₜ and the ground truth xₒₗₐₜ in pixel space. In practice, to avoid excessive memory usage on video data, we apply a random cropping strategy, computing the perceptual loss only on patches when the video resolution exceeds a predefined threshold. The overall training objective is then defined as:

    (5)

    L=L_LBM(𝔼(x_flat),𝔼(xₒₗₐₜ),t)+λ·L_perceptual(x̂ₒₗₐₜ,xₒₗₐₜ) ,

    where x_flat and xₒₗₐₜ denote videos in pixel space, and L_perceptual refers to the frame-wise LPIPS loss.

    Sampling Iterations

    We find that simply reusing the single-step inference schedule from [Chadebec et al. (2025)] leads to overly smooth outputs, where high-frequency details such as wrinkles on human skin and clothing are not well preserved. Performing iterative sampling with 4 steps, however, sufficiently mitigates this issue and yields sharper OLAT bases for subsequent intensity-weighted composition.

    3.5. Long Sequence Inference

    Video generative models are typically constrained to a fixed context length F during training due to GPU memory constraints. Direct extrapolation to longer sequences is non-trivial; a naive approach of partitioning the video into independent chunks inevitably results in temporal discontinuities and flickering at the boundaries. Existing sliding-window strategies [(Wu et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025)] achieve consistency by fusing latents across varying Gaussian denoising levels. These are incompatible with our framework, where the generative trajectory is governed by a structured source distribution rather than stochastic noise.

    To address this, we propose a recurrent bridge context, a strategy tailored for consistency in bridge-matching-based generation. We employ a sliding window with length W=F and stride S, leveraging previously generated OLAT frames to guide the inference process. Specifically, we define a "history context" corresponding to the overlapping region of length W-S. This context is populated by zₒₗₐₜᵖʳᵉᵛ∈ℝ^(W-S)×c×h×w, which denotes the finalized OLAT latents derived from the preceding window. During the iterative sampling process of the current window, we enforce temporal continuity by overriding the estimated latents ẑₜ in this overlap region with the ideal bridge state derived from the history context:

    (6)

    ẑₜ[i]=\begincases(1-t)zₒₗₐₜᵖʳᵉᵛ[i]+tz_flat[i],&ifi

    where z_flat∈ℝ^W×c×h×w represents the encoded flat-lit frames of the current window. At each timestep, we replace the overlapping latents with the noise-free mean interpolant of Eq. 1, thereby constraining the current window to match the previously generated frames in the overlap region and propagating temporal context forward. Finally, we concatenate the context latents zₒₗₐₜᵖʳᵉᵛ with the non-overlapping part of the predicted ẑ₀[W-S:W]∈ℝ^S×c×h×w and decode the combined sequence via the video VAE.

    This recursive strategy leverages the causal nature of the video VAE to extend bridge-matching inference beyond the training context while preserving consistent appearance and illumination responses without additional training. Results on sequences of up to 917 frames are provided in the supplementary material.

    3.6. Linear Space Combination

    To relight the dynamic performance under a target high dynamic range (HDR) environment map, we associate each predicted OLAT basis with a light direction in the camera coordinate system. We partition the environment map according to the nearest basis direction and integrate the linear HDR radiance within each region to obtain its weight. The final video is synthesized by performing a frame-by-frame linear combination of the predicted OLAT videos. Specifically, for each frame, the corresponding outputs from all basis videos are converted to linear space, multiplied by these weights, and accumulated to produce the relit result. This linear-space assembly is the key step for intensity controllability: the relative strength of each environment region is explicitly determined by its combination weight, rather than being implicitly inferred by the model from an unconstrained conditioning image. A single global scaling factor, typically set to 3, is applied per environment map to match the dynamic range of the target illumination to the captured lighting bases, while preserving the relative weights among basis directions.

    4. The Dataset

    4.1. Overview

    Training our controllable video relighting model requires large-scale paired video data consisting of a subject under flat lighting and the corresponding response to known OLAT illumination.

    However, acquiring such ground truth is physically non-trivial, as a subject cannot simultaneously experience two distinct lighting conditions at the exact same instant. To address this, we employ a time-multiplexed acquisition protocol, rapidly alternating between flat-lit frames and OLAT frames. Since inevitable subject motion occurs during the interval between light switches, raw frames are inherently misaligned. We mitigate this by estimating optical flow between consecutive flat-lit frames and warping the intermediate OLAT frames to align spatially with the flat-lit references, thereby yielding pixel-aligned training pairs.

    Crucially, to ensure the model learns robust representations, we devised a novel Light Switching Pattern. Our empirical findings suggest that training on a single fixed light direction leads to overfitting, where the model fails to disentangle illumination from motion features. To address this, we alternate between two distinct OLAT directions throughout a capture session. Specifically, we select the two lights with the greatest spatial distance within the LightStage to maximize illumination variance, while ensuring that all 101 distinct light sources are traversed exactly once across the full recording session of each subject, with no repetitions. Each OLAT direction is repeated for 9 consecutive cycles to ensure sufficient temporal sampling. Consequently, these two sets of OLAT frames, along with their interleaved flat-lit references, constitute a block of 18 pairs, which we define as a single sequence. The raw structure of such a sequence is visualized in Fig. 3(1), while the processed, aligned pairs are shown in Fig. 3(3). Across a full recording session for one subject, this process yields 51 such sequences for each camera view. Through this protocol, we acquired over 23 million valid frames across 189 identity-outfit combinations in the Dynamic-subset. We avoid alternating among too many directions (e.g., three or more) as it introduces excessive temporal gaps between frames of the same lighting condition, which degrades the temporal coherence of the video and hinders training.

    Additionally, we acquired complete OLAT sequences from 35 identity-outfit combinations in static poses. These dense captures support image-based relighting synthesis of ground-truth images under target environment maps, providing a controlled benchmark for image-level lighting evaluation.

    Consequently, we organize our dataset into two primary components: the Dynamic-subset (comprising the motion-rich paired video data) and the Static-subset (comprising the comprehensive full OLAT sequences). Tab. 1 compares the scale and capture properties of our dataset with existing benchmarks. The supplementary material reports aggregate statistics for the 224 identity-outfit combinations and provides detailed dataset overviews.

    All participants provided informed consent that explicitly permits research use and public release of their captured data. The release will exclude unnecessary personal metadata and will document the intended research use, privacy considerations, and potential misuse in synthetic-media pipelines. We plan to release the processed dataset upon publication under terms consistent with the participants’ consent.

    In the following subsections, we detail the technical implementation of our dataset construction. In Sec. 4.2, we describe the Capture Setup, detailing the unified LightStage hardware and the distinct camera array configurations tailored for each subset. In Sec. 4.3, we present the data-processing pipeline, focusing on motion-artifact mitigation and data-quality assessment.

    4.2. Capture Setup

    LightStage System.

    Our illumination system is shared across both subsets (Fig. 4(a)). It consists of over 800 LEDs grouped into 101 finite-area, individually addressable lighting units (referred to as One-Light units), driven by a custom microcontroller with microsecond precision. For dynamic acquisition, we configure the lighting clock cycle to 35 ms.

    Camera Systems and Settings.

    We deployed two synchronized camera systems, one for each subset. We prioritized storage efficiency and bandwidth for the Dynamic-subset to enable large-scale recording, while prioritizing dynamic range and raw quality for the Static-subset.

  • •

    Dynamic-subset: We used 68 custom-built PTZ cameras (Sony IMX678) to record 4K H.264 video at 60 fps (60 Mbps bitrate, I-frame interval of 2). The array comprises 48 short-lens cameras (approximately 9 mm) distributed spherically and 20 telephoto cameras (approximately 34 mm) placed primarily in frontal positions to capture upper-body details. Exposure is fixed at 1/125 s (f/4.8) to reduce motion blur.

  • •

    Static-subset: We utilized 70 Blackmagic Micro Studio Camera 4K G2 units arranged in a similar spherical layout: 54 units (14/15 mm lenses, including six zenith/nadir cameras) and 16 telephoto units (47 mm lenses). The raw footage is stored as Blackmagic RAW. While this format provides superior fidelity, its prohibitive bitrate prevents further scaling. We use a faster shutter speed of 1/500 s (f/4.4, ISO 3200) to reduce motion blur and transcode the footage to 100 Mbps for processing.

    • The spatial distributions are visualized in Fig. 4(c) and (d). Representative images from these camera arrays are provided in the supplementary material.

    Illumination Strategy.

    A major challenge in OLAT capture is the extreme dynamic range discrepancy between full-on lighting and single OLAT conditions. To address this discrepancy, we activate a uniformly sampled subset (1/6) of the lights to simulate ambient illumination (Fig. 4(b)). This preserves perceptual consistency within the camera’s limited dynamic range. Note that all references to "flat-lit" in this paper refer to this flat-lit configuration.

    Light Switching Patterns.

    The two subsets employ different switching patterns to serve their respective goals:

  • •

    Dynamic-subset Pattern: As introduced in Sec. 4.1, we repeat one OLAT direction for 9 cycles, interleaved with its spatially most distant counterpart for another 9 cycles (Fig. 3(3)). This variation encourages the model to decouple motion from lighting.

  • •

    Static-subset Pattern: We use 10 consecutive OLAT frames followed by 1 flat-lit frame. For each identity-outfit combination, we capture at least three static poses and several flat-lit dynamic sequences for relighting evaluation.

    • 4.3. Data Processing

    Given the complexity of massive-scale OLAT acquisition, especially for the Dynamic-subset, the raw data requires careful processing to achieve geometric alignment and photometric consistency. The overall pipeline is illustrated in Fig. 3. In the following sections, we detail the core algorithms for OLAT to flat-lit warping, followed by specific strategies for data quality assessment.

    OLAT to Flat-lit Warping.

    We use optical flow to compensate for subject motion, including rapid actions in the Dynamic-subset and involuntary sway in the Static-subset, that causes misalignment between flat-lit and OLAT frames. We compute bidirectional optical flow between consecutive flat-lit frames [(Harley et al., 2025)]. Assuming linear motion within the short interval, we derive the flow field for the intermediate OLAT frame via temporal linear interpolation. Alongside flow estimation, we generate foreground masks for the flat-lit frames using BiRefNet [(Zheng et al., 2024)] and compute a unified bounding box.

    Based on the computed flow, we apply different warping strategies tailored to the downstream application:

  • •

    Training Pairs (Dynamic & Static): To minimize warping artifacts, we warp each OLAT frame to its temporal nearest-neighbor flat-lit frame. This yields diverse, well-aligned pairs for learning-based models, preserving the original motion fidelity.

  • •

    Quality Assessment Stack (Static only): For quality evaluation, we warp all OLAT frames within a pose to the first flat-lit frame of the sequence, producing a geometrically aligned OLAT stack for the photometric analyses described below.

    • Quality Assessment.

    We utilize the geometrically aligned OLAT stack from the Static-subset to quantitatively assess the quality of our acquisition system. As illustrated in Fig. 5, our raw captures from both short-lens (a) and telephoto (b) cameras preserve high-frequency details. To assess geometric detail, we estimate surface normals via photometric stereo using gradient-descent optimization with outlier rejection. The resulting normal maps in Fig. 5(c) retain fine-scale skin texture and clothing wrinkles. To assess photometric linearity, we synthesize relit images by linearly combining the OLAT bases with environment-map weights after gamma correction. The synthesized results (d) preserve fine shading and self-shadowing details more faithfully than the evaluated neural relighting baselines.

    5. Experiments

    5.1. Implementation Details

    Training Configuration

    We perform full-parameter fine-tuning based on the Wan2.1 1.3B foundation model [(Wan et al., 2025)]. The model is trained for a total of 60,000 steps with a constant learning rate of 10⁻⁴ and a batch size of 8. During training, the target OLAT directions are randomly sampled from all available lighting directions. The probability of sampling static images for joint training follows a stepwise curriculum: it is set to 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 for each consecutive 20,000-step interval. We use the same few-timestep sampling during training as [Chadebec et al. (2025)], where the discrete timesteps are sampled uniformly from the set {i/16}ᵢ₌₁¹⁶. For the objective function, we utilize a VGG16-based LPIPS metric for the perceptual loss, setting the weight coefficient λ to 1.

    Fixed Text Prompt

    Throughout both training and inference, we utilize a fixed, descriptive text prompt to provide a consistent semantic context: "Given: a reference video of a person and a lighting direction representing a specific point light source. Generate: a realistic relit video of the same person under the target lighting defined by one light. Requirements: preserve identity and appearance, maintain consistent clothing and proportions, correct perspective, realistic lighting, shadows, and no artifacts."

    Inference Configuration

    During inference, we disable classifier-free guidance to rely primarily on our conditioning signals. To ensure temporal consistency, the recurrent bridge context is configured with a window length of W=9 frames and a stride of S=4, which is essential for stable video generation. We employ a uniform sampling strategy with 4 discrete timesteps, specifically {1,0.75,0.5,0.25}. For each input sequence, we typically generate a set of 201 distinct OLAT videos to serve as the bases for relighting. These 201 bases preserve the zenith direction of the original 101-light configuration while doubling the azimuthal sampling density at each elevation. Additional results in the supplementary material show comparable quality under static lighting but smoother responses to rotating high-frequency illumination with 201 bases; 101 bases reduce generation and storage cost when finer sampling is unnecessary.

    Hardware and Runtime

    The entire training process is conducted on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and takes approximately one week to complete. We additionally measure the inference cost of generating the OLAT basis set. For a 57-frame video at 1920×1088, generating one OLAT basis takes 119.45 seconds. When generation is distributed across eight A100 GPUs, producing 101 bases takes 26.89 minutes, while producing 201 bases takes 52.01 minutes. At 1280×720, generating one basis takes 61.08 seconds; with the same eight-GPU setup, producing 101 bases takes 14.53 minutes, while producing 201 bases takes 27.56 minutes. Because individual bases can be generated independently, they can be computed in parallel and cached for subsequent linear combinations without online network inference, although generation and storage costs scale approximately with their number.

    5.2. Datasets and Metrics

    We construct our training set by randomly selecting 100 identity-outfit combinations from the Dynamic-subset and 28 from the Static-subset. For evaluation, we hold out 54 and 7 identity-outfit combinations from the two subsets, respectively. For the Dynamic-subset, we use only views captured with short-lens cameras.

    To ensure alignment with the pre-training distribution of the foundation model, all data are represented in the sRGB color space. Additionally, to isolate the subjects and eliminate background interference, we apply a uniform mask to all input frames, setting the background to black.

    Following the evaluation protocol of [He et al. (2024)], we employ PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] (with an AlexNet backbone), and FLIP [(Andersson et al., 2020)] to quantitatively assess model performance.

    5.3. Comparisons with Existing Methods

    We compare our model with three video relighting approaches: the open-source RelightVid [(Fang et al., 2025)], the Cosmos-based DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)], and UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)]. To establish a comprehensive benchmark, we also include two recent single-image relighting methods: IC-Light [(Zhang et al., 2025a)] and LBM [(Chadebec et al., 2025)]. For the open-source baselines, we resize input videos or images to their recommended resolutions and adapt the lighting inputs to each method’s requirements. For DiffusionRenderer and UniRelight, we use the full HDR environment map as the condition. For RelightVid, IC-Light, and LBM, which rely on a background image, we sample the corresponding field of view from the HDR map and convert it to sRGB.

    We qualitatively evaluate video relighting on our OLAT dataset and in-the-wild sequences in Figs. 6 and 7. Reference images are generated via image-based relighting from captured OLAT images, together with material balls rendered under the target environment maps.

    Fig. 6 qualitatively compares responses to target direction (a), intensity distributions (b), and real-world lighting (c). Our results follow the target changes more closely than the evaluated baselines. The supplementary material further shows how our method responds to different intensity scalings of the same environment map.

    To reduce the domain gap between the required flat-lit input and in-the-wild videos, we apply the delighting model described in the supplementary material before OLAT prediction. Consequently, beyond controlled setups, Fig. 7 highlights our strong generalization capabilities to novel, in-the-wild scenarios. Our model robustly preserves fine details and subject identity far better than the baselines. This superiority is evident in the fine-grained environmental interactions it synthesizes, such as the physically precise shadows in (a) and the accurate reflected bounce light from the background red curtain in the first frame of (b). Overall, these results confirm that our method synthesizes more photorealistic appearances and physically plausible lighting effects compared to existing approaches.

    For quantitative lighting evaluation, we use the Static-subset, whose complete captured OLAT sequences allow us to synthesize ground-truth images under target environment maps via image-based relighting. In this setting, we focus our comparison on two representative image-based methods (IC-Light [(Zhang et al., 2025a)] and LBM [(Chadebec et al., 2025)]) and two video-based methods (DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)] and UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)]).

    Image-relighting results are reported in Tab. 2 and Fig. 8, with an additional qualitative HumanOLAT comparison provided in the supplementary material. We resize all outputs and ground truth to the minimum evaluated resolution and mask their backgrounds. Following [Jin et al. (2024)], each predicted color channel is rescaled to the ground-truth mean to resolve global illumination–surface-color scale ambiguity. This calibration is used in quantitative evaluation to ensure a consistent comparison across methods. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms the baselines across most metrics and preserves significantly richer fine-grained details.

    Following Lux Post Facto [(Mei et al., 2025)], we evaluate temporal consistency using LPIPS between adjacent frames and warping error (WE) computed with optical flow from RAFT [(Teed and Deng, 2020)] and AllTracker [(Harley et al., 2025)]. Tab. 3 shows that our method achieves excellent temporal consistency.

    5.4. Ablation Studies

    We conduct three ablation studies to investigate the effectiveness of key components in our proposed framework. All quantitative evaluations are performed on a representative subset of 200 test sequences randomly sampled from our Dynamic-subset. Specifically, these sequences consist of paired flat-lit inputs and ground-truth OLAT videos, and all reported results (both quantitative and qualitative) evaluate the quality of the synthesized OLAT videos. To ensure fair comparison while managing computational costs, all ablated versions are trained for 20,000 steps with a sampling ratio of 0.1 for images and 0.9 for videos. Consistent with the main experiments, since our model focuses exclusively on the foreground subject, all quantitative metrics are computed on background-masked images to prevent background noise from biasing the results.

    Latent Bridge Matching for Input Frames

    To validate the efficacy of the LBM paradigm [(Chadebec et al., 2025)], we compare it against standard diffusion conditioning strategies that rely on noise concatenation. Specifically, we implemented two baseline variants where the flat-lit input latents are concatenated with the noisy latents along either the channel dimension or the frame dimension. For the channel-wise concatenation baseline, we expanded the input channels of the first convolutional layer by a factor of two and initialized the weights of the newly added channels to zero for training stability. Quantitative results in Tab. 4 and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 9 reveal a significant performance gap. The noise concatenation methods tend to degrade source fidelity, often producing artifacts or losing fine-grained texture details due to the destructive nature of the initial Gaussian noise. In contrast, by establishing a direct transport trajectory from the source, bridge matching for video latents effectively preserves the structural integrity and high-frequency details of the input, yielding significantly higher fidelity in the final relit video.

    Lighting Conditioning

    We primarily evaluate our design against two alternative mechanisms: cross-attention and global AdaLN. The cross-attention method, following [He et al. (2024)], injects SH encodings by replacing the original text prompt embeddings, which risks disrupting the inherent input distribution of the backbone. The global AdaLN scheme employs a single shared projection layer for all blocks, offering only coarse, uniform control. In contrast, our block-specific AdaLN strategy preserves the integrity of the input features while enabling finer-grained, block-wise lighting modulation. Quantitative results in Tab. 4 and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 10 demonstrate that our proposed conditioning scheme achieves more precise directional control and yields more photorealistic predictions.

    Long Sequence Inference

    We compare our recurrent bridge context with Position Interpolation (PI) [(Chen et al., 2023)] and sliding iterative sampling [(Jin et al., 2025)] in Fig. 11. PI introduces out-of-distribution positional embeddings, while heterogeneous latent timesteps cause significant lighting drift in sliding iterative sampling.

    5.5. Additional Qualitative Results

    We further demonstrate the versatility and robustness of our model on unseen subjects. As illustrated in Fig. 12, our model synthesizes precise shading and self-shadowing effects under continuously rotating lighting directions, maintaining physical plausibility. Fig. 13 validates temporal stability, showcasing a dynamic performance coherently illuminated by a fixed directional light source across the sequence. Finally, Fig. 14 highlights the geometric consistency of our predictions, successfully generalizing to diverse camera viewpoints for a specified lighting direction. For more extensive visualization results and dynamic comparisons, please refer to our supplementary video.

    6. Conclusion

    In this work, we have presented a comprehensive framework for controllable dynamic full-body relighting from monocular flat-lit videos. By shifting the paradigm from direct relit-image generation to data-driven OLAT video prediction, our approach decomposes human light transport into directional basis responses and reconstructs the final appearance through linear-space intensity weighting. This formulation makes direction explicit in the OLAT bases and relative intensity explicit in the environment-map weights while preserving appearance details and temporal coherence. The accompanying large-scale dynamic full-body OLAT dataset provides the directional supervision needed to learn these responses across diverse identities, outfits, motions, and views.

    Current limitations include the flat-lit input assumption, sensitivity of delighting to strong shadows or colored illumination, and the reconstruction ceiling of the pretrained video VAE. The explicit OLAT representation also incurs basis-dependent generation and storage costs, while cross-OLAT and cross-view consistency remains implicit rather than architecturally guaranteed. Finally, the finite-area capture lights limit directional resolution; missing dynamic relighting ground truth and reliable pixel-level lighting-angle annotations further constrain quantitative evaluation. Further discussion and failure analysis are provided in the supplementary material.

    These boundaries motivate more robust delighting, higher-fidelity video autoencoders, efficient basis prediction with explicit consistency, finer illumination capture, and dynamic lighting benchmarks. The dataset may further support neural rendering and controllable generative video editing.

    Acknowledgements.

    We thank Dongli Tan for LightStage camera calibration and Linxian Wu for providing paired outdoor environment panoramas and reference images captured under the same lighting conditions. This work was partially supported by National Key R&D Program of China (No. 2024YFB2809105), NSFC (No. U24B20154), Zhejiang Provincial Natural Science Foundation of China (No. LR25F020003), and Information Technology Center and State Key Lab of CAD&CG, Zhejiang University.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Supplementary Material

    Appendix A Dataset Statistics

    Participants were 18–30 years old. Tab. 5 summarizes the combined dataset composition.

    Appendix B Supplementary of Data Processing

    B.1. Rolling Shutter Detection and Sequence Segmentation

    The light-switch cycle is intentionally set slightly longer than two camera frame periods (approximately 33.3 ms at 60 fps), which facilitates rolling-shutter detection. In addition to the target flat-lit and OLAT frames, our raw footage inevitably contains frames affected by rolling-shutter (RS) artifacts. Both subsets rely on the precise identification of valid frames to correctly extract lighting sequences. However, identifying RS frames is non-trivial for the Dynamic-subset: due to H.264 compression, the distinct RS boundary is blurred by spatial artifacts (Fig. 15(b)), rendering traditional spatial stitching or gradient-based detection infeasible.

item.title: 建筑代理模型不该「先削几何、后贴图」：这篇让图像证据参与几何抽象，贴图不再错位 ｜ Architectural Textured Proxy Generation
item.description:
一句话：顺序式管线的「先几何后贴图」丢掉了图像证据，导致代理模型与照片对不上。

要点：

  • 带纹理的代理模型是建筑场景的基础表示：既保证渲染效率，又要保留视觉保真度
  • 现有做法是顺序管线——先从稠密重建里抽象出几何，再把输入图像投影成纹理。这种「只看几何」的建模在代理生成阶段就丢掉了图像证据
  • 这篇因此把图像证据引入代理生成阶段，而不是等几何定死之后再贴图

为什么值得看：数字孪生、建筑可视化里最烦的就是「代理模型贴图错位」。把图像证据前移到几何抽象阶段，是从流程顺序上解决错位，而不是事后修 UV。

中文摘要：带纹理的代理模型是建筑场景的基础表示，既要保证渲染效率，又要保留视觉保真度。现有方法采用顺序式管线：先从稠密重建中抽象出几何，再把输入图像投影上去形成纹理。问题在于这种只依赖几何的建模方式，在代理生成阶段就把图像证据丢掉了，等到贴图环节再补已经无法纠正几何与影像之间的偏差。这篇改为让图像证据参与代理的生成过程，从流程顺序上避免「几何定死、贴图只好将就」的结构性问题，对数字孪生与建筑可视化的资产管线更实用。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

Architectural Textured Proxy Generation

© cc

Abstract.

Textured proxy models are a fundamental representation for architectural scenes, enabling efficient rendering while preserving visual fidelity. Existing approaches construct such proxies through a sequential pipeline in which geometry is first abstracted from a dense reconstruction and textures are later projected from input images. This geometry-only formulation neglects image evidence during proxy generation, leading to misalignment of structural features such as facades, edges, and their intersections across views. As a result, inconsistencies are deferred to a downstream correction stage during texturing, where the underlying geometric structure can no longer be reliably recovered. In this work, we introduce an image-guided proxy formulation in which proxy generation is jointly constrained by both the dense reconstruction and the input aerial images. By incorporating image derived structural cues directly into the construction process, the proxy is optimized to align with observed features across views from the outset, rather than relying on post hoc correction that may be infeasible. This shift from a geometry-only to an image-guided paradigm produces proxies that are inherently consistent with the input imagery, enabling more accurate geometry and more coherent texture mapping. We realize this formulation through a framework that extracts structural priors from images and dense geometry, and enforces their consistency during proxy optimization. The resulting proxies exhibit improved alignment of structural features, reducing artifacts such as edge duplication, texture drift, and cross view inconsistencies. Experiments on diverse architectural scenes demonstrate that our approach produces compact, geometry texture aligned proxies with substantially improved visual fidelity compared to existing methods.

Keywords:

Architectural Models, Proxy Generation, Geometry-Texture Alignment, Camera Pose Adjustment ††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

High-quality 3D reconstruction from images has become widely accessible, producing dense geometric models with detailed appearance [(Sinha et al., 2008; Musialski et al., 2013)]. However, such models remain impractical for downstream applications due to their complexity. Proxy representations address this limitation by abstracting geometry into compact, structured models that enable efficient rendering and manipulation. In architectural scenes, proxies are typically composed of piecewise planar elements, capturing the dominant structure of buildings while serving as the support for texture mapping [(Garland and Heckbert, 1997; Salinas et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024)].

Despite their utility, existing pipelines suffer from a fundamental limitation: geometry abstraction and texturing are treated as separate stages. A proxy is first constructed from a dense model, and textures are later projected from the input images [(Xiong et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2025a)]. This sequential design leads to inconsistencies in what we term structural features—planar facades, edges, and their intersections that define the geometry of buildings. These features should coincide across the proxy and all input views, yet in practice they drift. Errors from camera estimation, geometric abstraction, and projection accumulate, causing edges to misalign, planar regions to fragment, and textures from different views to disagree (Fig. 2). As a result, texturing becomes a corrective step that attempts to compensate for misaligned geometry, often with limited success [(Xiong et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2025a)]. Prior approaches either optimize textures without modifying geometry, rely on manual adjustments [(Sinha et al., 2008)], or employ learning-based generation that may deviate from the observed scene [(Chen et al., 2025)].

We replace this pipeline with a coupled formulation in which proxy geometry is directly constrained by image-derived structural features. Rather than constructing a proxy and then fitting textures, we build the proxy so that structural features are already aligned across views, prior to texturing. By enforcing this alignment at construction time, the proxy becomes a geometrically consistent support for all image observations, eliminating the need for downstream correction. To realize this formulation, we extract priors from the input images and use them to jointly guide camera refinement and proxy generation. Camera poses are optimized to align projected geometry with image-derived normal cues, while proxy geometry is iteratively adjusted under a guidance field that enforces piecewise planar structure consistent with these priors. This shared structural signal couples geometry and appearance throughout the pipeline. Given the resulting aligned proxy and refined cameras, texture mapping reduces to aggregating consistent observations rather than resolving inconsistencies.

Our approach produces textured proxies with significantly improved alignment of structural features, reducing artifacts such as ghosting, edge duplication, and texture drift. We demonstrate consistent gains in both geometric accuracy and visual fidelity over prior methods that decouple geometry and texturing. More broadly, our results suggest that enforcing structural alignment at the level of representation, rather than repairing it afterward, is key to reliable proxy reconstruction. Our contributions are summarized as:

  • •

    An automatic framework for generating texture-geometry-aligned proxy models given aerial images. Our novel framework can achieve not only high-fidelity textures but also high-quality proxy geometries;

  • •

    A building-oriented camera pose refinement method leveraging normal consistency between the input images and reconstructed dense geometries;

  • •

    A planar structure segmentation benchmark targeting urban aerial images and a fine-tuned segmentation model. We hope the benchmark can benefit the community;

  • •

    The first proxy generation method targeting texture-geometry alignment, from a textureless dense building reconstruction.

    • 2. Related Works

    Texture Remapping

    Existing texture remapping methods for reconstructed dense geometry can be classified into two categories: i) Image-only remapping methods associate each face or vertex with one or multiple appropriate input images, then create textures via seam/weights optimization to avoid visible seams between adjacent patches [(Wang et al., 2018; Waechter et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2018; Bernardini et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2020; Bi et al., 2017)], ii) Joint optimization methods jointly rectify the camera poses and geometric errors, to avoid texture misalignment caused by geometric error and camera drifting [(Lempitsky and Ivanov, 2007; Gal et al., 2010; Zhou and Koltun, 2014; Fu et al., 2020)].

    In recent years, texturing architectural proxy models has emerged as a topic of growing interest. [Xiong et al. (2023); Xiong et al. (2025a)] generate a texture map for each planar polygon of an architectural proxy, minimizing the intra-misalignment via image warping or weights optimization. However, these methods focus only on texture improvement, which subjectively decouples the inter-relationship between camera pose, geometry and texture. These image-only methods still struggle in tackling inter-misalignment and structure misalignment.

    In this paper, we focus on generating a texture-geometry aligned proxy model given aerial images. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first textured proxy generation method that jointly optimizes camera poses, proxy model, and texture maps.

    Camera Calibration

    Camera calibration methods can be categorized by optimization granularity. Pixel-based methods [(Schonberger and Frahm, 2016; Triggs et al., 1999)] minimize per-pixel reprojection errors and achieve high accuracy, but are sensitive to textureless regions and image noise. Primitive-based methods [(Hu et al., 2024; Shu et al., 2023)] exploit geometric primitives such as feature points, lines, and planes to formulate more robust alignment objectives, yet their effectiveness depends on reliable primitive detection and association. In large-scale urban reconstruction, building facades are dominated by weak/repetitive textures and convex/concave structures varying with viewing angles, which yield sparse and unreliable feature correspondences. Furthermore, current methods minimize average error over all matched feature points rather than enforcing local geometric alignment on individual building structures. As a result, the camera poses may be globally plausible but locally inaccurate for every single building.

    Per-image calibration can be further improved using object silhouettes [(Lensch et al., 2001)] or image matching. We introduce a building-oriented camera refinement method that incorporates geometric priors estimated by a foundation model.

    Proxy Model Generation

    Early methods used geometric error metrics or structure-aware decimation techniques [(Yan et al., 2006; Garland and Heckbert, 1997; Cohen-Steiner et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2022; Khan et al., 2020)]. Appearance-preserving simplification approaches seek to approximate the rendered appearance of an existing textured model [(Garland and Heckbert, 1998; Cohen et al., 1998; Choi et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b; Bo et al., 2026)]. Another important family follows a detect-then-assemble paradigm, where planar primitives are first extracted and subsequently assembled into polygonal or polyhedral meshes through optimization [(Chauve et al., 2010; Nan and Wonka, 2017; Bauchet and Lafarge, 2020; Fang and Lafarge, 2020; Fang et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2017)]. Representative methods such as PolyFit [(Nan and Wonka, 2017)] and KSR [(Bauchet and Lafarge, 2020)] produce compact and structured models, but their performance heavily depends on the completeness and accuracy of primitive detection. Missing or noisy planar hypotheses often lead to structural misalignment. More recently, BLOD [(Pan et al., 2025)] extends this paradigm to multi-scale LOD generation by introducing an Inside/Outside-view analysis and organizing reconstructed structures into a hierarchical LOD-Tree representation. Despite their effectiveness in geometric abstraction, these approaches largely rely on geometry-only formulations and do not explicitly enforce consistency with image observations during proxy construction.

    In contrast to prior geometry-only pipelines, our method incorporates image-derived structural cues directly into proxy optimization. By jointly enforcing geometric abstraction and cross-view image consistency during proxy generation, our approach produces texture-geometry aligned architectural proxies.

    Monocular-Plane Extraction

    Estimating planar structures from images has been studied extensively. Existing monocular plane extraction methods have achieved notable progress in recovering local planar regions from single images. CNN-based methods [(Liu et al., 2018; Yang and Zhou, 2018)] formulate plane extraction as pixel-wise prediction with a predefined set of planar hypotheses, while instance-level approaches [(Liu et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2019)] identify multiple plane instances in a scene. More recent Transformer-based and foundation-model-based methods [(Tan et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2024a; Deng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a)] further improve robustness through stronger global reasoning, multiscale context, and large-scale data. However, these methods are mainly developed for indoor scenes or street-level imagery, where planes are typically observed as local surfaces from close-range viewpoints. In contrast, our goal is building-plane extraction from low-altitude UAV images, which requires globally coherent reasoning over large facade and roof structures under oblique aerial views. The scarcity of fine-grained aerial facade annotations further limits the direct applicability of existing supervised plane extraction pipelines.

    3. Overview

    Given a set of RGB aerial images {Iₖ}, we aim at generating an architectural proxy model M capturing dominant and salient planar structures, along with high-quality texture maps U aligned with the proxy geometry.

    Our framework is illustrated in Fig. 3. Firstly, we calibrate the images and generate a dense reconstruction. To reduce the geometry-image misalignment, the generated camera poses are then refined to minimize the differences between the normal priors estimated from input photos and the normal maps rendered via a differential renderer. Next, we construct local/global guidance of dense mesh from planar priors estimated from the input photos via our planar structure segmentation model, called ProxySAM. Guided by such priors, we optimize the mesh vertices to generate a piece-wise planar building proxy M, via balancing the geometric planarity, preservation of distinct structures, and mesh quality. Finally, given the refined camera poses and image-guided proxy, we perform texture remapping to generate the texture maps, U.

    4. Method

    4.1. Initialization

    Given the input images {Iₖ}, we first obtain the initial camera pose {ℂₖ}⁰ and a 3D dense model D=(F,V) using ContextCapture 111 https://www.soarscape.com/, following the standard 3D reconstruction pipeline includes: feature mapping, structure from motion (SfM), multi-view stereo (MVS), and surface reconstruction. The generated camera pose ℂₖ of Iₖ consists of a rotation matrix Rₖ and a translation vector tₖ. We create a set of binary activation masks {Aₖ}, each with the same size as Iₖ, to indicate the target building regions of D.

    Building-oriented Camera Error

    Since the calibration method aims to achieve consistency among the observed image features throughout the scene, the initial camera poses {ℂₖ}⁰ may be globally plausible, but locally inaccurate for a single building. Such camera errors bring obvious misalignments between the reconstructed building model D and the calibrated image views (see the difference between the green image-based building silhouettes and the red building silhouette of reconstructed D projected to the image in Fig. 4). The misalignment often led to distinct visual artifacts in the final texture maps and building proxy.

    Normal-based Camera Pose Refinement

    To mitigate such an issue, we propose to refine the camera poses such that each of the input images is geometrically consistent with D. As normal maps provide strong geometric cues compared to RGB images [(Yu et al., 2022; Binninger et al., 2025)], we use the normal maps to guide the refinement of camera poses.

    We first estimated the set of normal maps {ℕ̂ₖ} of all the input images to serve as normal priors, via a monocular normal estimation model, called MoGe [(Wang et al., 2025)]. Next, for an image Iₖ with camera pose Cₖ=(Rₖ,tₖ), we render D to produce a normal map ℕₖ under the identical viewing pose using a differentiable renderer. In this way, the differential renderer renders ℕₖ of each view to compute a loss measuring its distance to the related normal prior ℕ̂ₖ, which propagates back to optimize the camera pose Cₖ. The pipeline of our iterative camera refinement method is illustrated in Fig. 5.

    Objective Function

    For image Iₖ, we define the objective function as the weighted sum of a normal loss and a regularization term:

    (1)

    L_Camera=L_Normal+L_Reg.

    To minimize the angular discrepancy between the rendered and estimated normals, we introduce the normal loss, L_Normal, computed as the sum of pixel-wise distances between the rendered and estimated normals over the target building region:

    (2)

    L_Normal=(1)/(|Aₖ|)∥Aₖ⊙(ℕ̂ₖ-ℕₖ)∥₂²,

    where ⊙ is the element-wise product.

    To ensure numerical stability, we introduce a regularization term [(Carlone et al., 2015)] that penalizes excessive deviations of the camera pose from the initial value, Cₖ⁰=(Rₖ⁰,tₖ⁰):

    (3)

    L_Reg=∥tₖ-tₖ⁰∥₂²+∥\log(Rₖ^⊤Rₖ⁰)∥₂².

    The camera pose of each image is optimized separately. We use Adam [(Kingma, 2014)] with an initial learning rate of 0.005, running for 1000 iterations per view, and decay the learning rate exponentially every 100 iterations with γ=0.995.

    4.2. Proxy Generation

    After obtaining accurate camera poses and dense geometry, our next goal is to transform the dense model D=(F,V) into a structured proxy M that aligns with the images.

    Previous approaches derive proxy models solely from the intermediate dense representation (i.e., dense mesh, point clouds) [(Nan and Wonka, 2017; Bauchet and Lafarge, 2020; Pan et al., 2025; Cohen-Steiner et al., 2004)]. These methods struggle to distinguish structural planes from the noisy dense model, generating inaccurate proxy geometry that heavily deviates from the building shape (see Fig. 2). We propose to generate proxy models by jointly leveraging the dense reconstruction and the aerial images. This new approach enforces the alignment of structural features (planar facades, etc) across views during proxy generation, leading to more accurate and consistent structural features.

    Our proxy generation method consists mainly of three stages. Firstly, we extract 2D planar priors and then compute 3D aerial planar priors accordingly (Sec. 4.2.1). Next, we compute local and global normal guidance based on planar priors (Sec. 4.2.2). The mesh vertices of dense model D are optimized based on the normal guidance to generate a piece-wise planar mesh D^* (Sec. 4.2.3). Finally, we extract planar polygons from D^* to generate a proxy model ℙ (Sec. 4.2.4). In this section, we will elaborate on each step in detail.

    4.2.1. Planar Priors Extraction

    Conventional geometry-only methods are sensitive to local noise, whereas the rich structural cues in the images can compensate for this limitation. Hence, we extract 2D planar structure from images as priors, then map them onto D to generate 3D planar priors.

    2D Planar Priors.

    Existing planar structure segmentation methods and benchmarks target indoor scenes[(Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2024a; Deng et al., 2025)], or street view images[(Zhou et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022)], which failed in aerial images of buildings. Successful cases demonstrate the strong semantic understanding ability of Modern fundamental models given sufficient and high-quality training data [(Carion et al., 2025)]. Hence, we constructed PlaneSet, a building planar structure benchmark leveraging the Tokyo Dataset [(Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism , Japan(2023), MLIT)] (covering approximately 3.62km²). We render approximately 1000 aerial views of the Tokyo Dataset using the provided plain proxies. Next, we apply the region-growing algorithm  [(Rabbani et al., 2006)] to aggregate faces with similar face normals into the same planar structure. After that, we employ Stable Diffusion 3.5 [(Esser et al., 2024)] conditioned on the rendered plain geometry views via dual ControlNets (Depth and Canny)  [(Zhang et al., 2023)], to yield realistic rendering. Thus, each view has a planar structure mask (see Fig. 6). We then fine-tuned SAM 3 [(Carion et al., 2025)] using PlaneSet via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [(KMUTT, 2025)], to obtain a variant called ProxySAM (see supplementary material for details).

    Formally, given an aerial image Iₖ and a text prompt “facade plane", ProxySAM predicts corresponding masks of all the distinct planar structures (see Fig. 6). These masks remain fixed in the subsequent stages.

    3D Planar Priors.

    For each 2D planar instance mask, we project it onto the dense mesh and obtain a set of triangular faces {f}ₘ. We measure the quality, Q, of each 2D planar instance mask based on {f}ₘ, considering three aspects: face normal consistency, face planarity, and connectivity. Next, for each frequently observed triangular face, we find the set of instance masks that observe it. We greedily aggregate adjacent faces into coherent 3D planar regions via region growing [(Marshall et al., 2001; Rabbani et al., 2006)]. The similarity of two faces is measured by the Jaccard similarity [(Manning, 2008)] considering their instance mask set and relative qualities. Finally, we obtain a partition of F into planar faces {f}ₚ and non-planar faces {f}ₙₚ (see supplementary material for more details).

    4.2.2. Guidance Computation

    Next, we compute and assign a guidance normal G to each triangular face that jointly leverages planar priors and geometric cues from the mesh. For planar faces, we use global guidance to enforce their smoothness over their planar instance. We first estimate the K dominant principal directions by clustering the normals of {f}ₚ using spherical K-means (K=3) [(Hornik et al., 2012)]. These principal directions and their reverse directions together serve as a set of principal normals {u}. Experimentally, we found that not enforcing orthogonal principal directions yields proxy models that more accurately align with the reconstructed building shapes and texture maps. For face fᵢ∈{f}ₚ, its guidance normal Gᵢ is initialized as the average normal n̄ of its planar instance. We then replace Gᵢ with the closest u, if their cosine similarity is larger than τ=0.95. For non-planar faces, we use local guidance to enhance planar structures while preserving sharp structural details. For non-planar face fᵢ∈{f}ₙₚ, inspired by [(Zhang et al., 2015)], we select the most coherent one-ring patch pᵢ containing fᵢ. We simplify the patch refinement strategy in [Zhong et al. (2021)], by eliminating the faces whose normal distance from nᵢ is smaller than a predefined threshold τₙ=0.95 from the patch. The normal-wise distance is measured using the dot product. We then compute the area-weighted average face normal over the refined patch to obtain a representative normal gᵢ for fᵢ[(Zhang et al., 2015)] (see supplementary material for details). The final local guidance Gᵢ is computed by aggregating its neighboring normals via joint bilateral weights [(Petschnigg et al., 2004)] anchored by representative normals g. Thus, we obtain a per-face guidance normal field {G}.

    4.2.3. Normal Guided Model Optimization

    To obtain a piece-wise planar mesh that adheres to the computed guidance field {G}, we iteratively optimize the vertex positions V={vⱼ} of D by minimizing a loss function L_Proxy:

    (4)

    L_Proxy=L_Planar+λₗL_Lap+λᵣL_PReg,

    where λₗ and λᵣ are the balancing coefficient. We let λₗ=1 and λᵣ=100. The pipeline of optimization is shown in Fig. 7.

    We introduce a planar loss term, L_Planar, to align the face normal nᵢ of face fᵢ with its guidance normal Gᵢ:

    (5)

    L_Planar=(1)/(|F|)∑ᵢ∥nᵢ-Gᵢ∥₂²,

    where |F| denotes the face number of Dᵗ in iteration t.

    Meanwhile, we make use of a Laplacian loss term, L_Lap, to prevent degenerate configurations [(Nicolet et al., 2021)]:

    (6)L_Lap=(1)/(|V|)∑_vⱼ∈V∥vⱼ-(∑_m∈Hⱼvₘ)/(|Hⱼ|)∥₂²,

    where |V| denotes the vertex number of Dᵗ in iteration t, Hⱼ denotes the one-ring neighbors of vertex vⱼ, |Hⱼ| denoted the number of adjacent vertices of vⱼ.

    Furthermore, we use a regularization term, L_PReg, to prevent excessive vertex drift comparing to previous iteration:

    (7)L_PReg=(1)/(|V|)∑_vⱼ∈V∥vⱼᵗ-vⱼᵗ⁻¹∥₂²,

    where vᵗ⁻¹ⱼ denotes the position of vⱼ in the previous iteration. See supplementary material for the ablation study on L_PReg.

    The L_Proxy is minimized using Adam [(Kingma, 2014)], with an initial learning rate set to 10⁻⁵. We employ exponential decay with γ=0.995. The 3D priors and guidance field will be updated after each iteration. The optimization converges when the number of iterations reaches the maximum value, or the maximum vertex displacement is negligible.

    Remeshing.

    To simplify the dense mesh, we apply adaptive isotropic remeshing [(Pietroni et al., 2009)] every 10 iterations, while setting the target edge length to 110% of the average edge length of the current mesh.

    4.2.4. Model Approximation

    Finally, we merge adjacent triangles whose normal difference is less than a threshold into a proxy polygon p, using the region growing algorithm [(Rabbani et al., 2006)]. The set of proxy polygons {p} is subsequently triangulated [(Botsch et al., 2010)] to generate a compact, piecewise-planar proxy mesh model , ℙ, as shown in Fig. 8. The representation of {p} adheres to the existing proxy texturing frameworks. Hence, we can directly send ℙ={p} to later texturing methods, without further processing.

    4.3. Texture Remapping

    Given the refined camera poses and the optimized proxy mesh ℙ={p}, we adopt the plane-based texture remapping method, DiffTex [(Xiong et al., 2025a)], to generate a texture map for each proxy polygon p. With our framework, the calibrated photos and proxy model are aligned within the same coordinate system. This allows users to generate a high-quality textured building proxy in a single workflow, without manual alignment between different coordinate systems (such as BLOD [(Pan et al., 2025)]).

    5. Experimental Results

    Implementation

    We calibrate the input aerial images with the commercial software, called ContextCapture (CC). The target building is reconstructed as a mesh manifold D (no self-intersection, etc.). Our camera refinement is implemented with Nvdiffrast [(Laine et al., 2020)], and proxy generation is implemented with Nvdiffrast and CGAL. All the presented experimental results are obtained on a desktop computer equipped with an Intel i9-14900k processor with 3.0 GHz, 128 GB RAM and an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

    Dataset

    We evaluate the quality of textured proxies using synthetic models and real-world buildings. We construct a synthetic dataset, containing six models with various layouts and complexity [(Xiong et al., 2025b)]. The real-world buildings come from public sources [(Xiong et al., 2023)].

    5.1. Stage Results

    In this section, we provide the stage results of the Hall example in Fig. 10. Our input is a set of aerial RGB images. We first obtain the initial poses (visualized as a sphere and a cylinder) of aerial images with ContexCapture, reconstruct a dense model, and estimate normal maps by MoGe. We then refine the initial camera pose through translation and rotation. In Fig. 10, we visualize the refinement respectively: for translation, the camera spheres are colored by the magnitude of the translation update, while the viewing-direction cylinders are shown in blue; for rotation, the cylinders are colored by the relative rotation angle in degrees between the initial and refined poses, and the camera spheres are shown in blue. Each color map spans the range from zero to the maximum update over all camera poses. Next, the aerial images are segmented by our ProxySAM to obtain 2D planar segmentation. The 3D planar segmentation is then obtained by lifting the 2D predictions through multi-view voting. Finally, we generate a proxy using our image-guided method and obtain the textured proxy based on refined camera parameters.

    5.2. Camera Refinement

    Firstly, we evaluate the textured proxy models generated by PolyFit, KSR and our method, given input aerial images with the initial camera poses and refined camera poses of a real scene called Hisense. As shown in Fig. 11, the textured proxy given initial poses exhibits distinct texture misalignment. After refinement, such misalignment is substantially reduced for the textured proxy of all methods, validating the effectiveness of our camera refinement.

    For the quantitative evaluation of the textured proxy, we adopt the evaluation scheme in [(Waechter et al., 2014)] to compare rendered images of the reconstructed scenes against the corresponding real images following a specific view from the input cameras. The statistics are provided in Table 1, across all three proxy generation methods, camera pose refinement consistently achieves superior SSIM and LPIPS scores compared to the initial camera baselines. See supplementary material for more comparisons.

    5.3. Proxy Generation

    Next, we estimate the effect of local and global guidance in mesh optimization, as shown in Fig. 9. If we construct the guidance field with only local guidance, the result is overall smooth while preserving sharp edges. However, the local guidance considers only local faces, which cannot distinguish planar structures. As a result, it blends small-scale planar structures and fails to encourage large-scale planarity (second column, Fig. 9). If we construct the guidance field with only global guidance, dominant planar structures and local structures are preserved, yet small-scale noise is retained (third column, Fig. 9). After incorporating local and global guidance into the guidance field, the generated mesh model is structurally faithful and piecewise-planar (fourth column, Fig. 9).

    5.4. Comparison of Proxy Model

    We compare our method on two challenging synthetic buildings against three proxy generation approaches: VSA [(Cohen-Steiner et al., 2004)] and BLOD [(Pan et al., 2025)], which take a dense triangle mesh as input; PolyFit [(Nan and Wonka, 2017)], which takes a point cloud as input. For a fair comparison, we tune the parameters of each method to obtain proxies with similar vertex counts. Due to the nature of different algorithms, we cannot guarantee an identical number of vertices.

    Following [Smith et al. (2018)] and [Xiong et al. (2025b)], we compute Error, which quantifies how closely ℙ approximates the ground-truth model. The results are visualized in Fig. 12. VSA produces compact approximations through variational surface clustering; however, its region boundaries often exhibit noticeable zigzag artifacts. PolyFit and BLOD recover more regular planar surfaces, but as geometry-only approaches, they rely solely on geometric evidence to determine the planar decomposition. Consequently, stepped or recessed structures with weak geometric cues may be oversimplified, with reconstructed planes spanning across distinct structural levels. Our method achieves the lowest Error among all methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of our image-guided method in preserving faithful structural details.

    5.5. Comparison of Textured Proxy

    Serving as geometric support, an accurate proxy model consistent with the input images is critical for the generation of coherent texture mapping. Finally, we compare our method with five proxy generation approaches on the textured proxy models: QEM [(Garland and Heckbert, 1997)], VSA and BLOD, which take a dense triangle mesh as input; KSR [(Bauchet and Lafarge, 2020)] and PolyFit, which take a point cloud as input. Here, we aim at comparing the visual quality of textured proxies. Instead of simply encouraging similar face/vertex count, for a fair comparison given such noisy dense models as input, we tune the parameters of each method to balance good visual quality with a small face count. The generated proxies are textured following the identical pipeline given the input aerial images. Statistics are provided in Table 2. See supplementary material for comparison based on similar face/vertex count.

    Qualitative Evaluation.

    The qualitative results are visualized in Fig. 13. The reconstructed dense geometry and vertex colors (assigned by CC) are provided as the reference for ground truth structure and colors. The QEM progressively simplifies the mesh geometry without considering architectural regularity or planar coherence. The generated models exhibit zigzag planar boundaries and irregular structures in all examples. Meanwhile, VSA approximates the input surface through variational clustering and produces piecewise-smooth regions, but it does not explicitly enforce architectural planarity, leading to locally uneven surfaces on building structures. In contrast, PolyFit, KSR, and BLOD approximate the dense model using planar structures, generating models consisting of smooth surfaces and sharp edges. However, without considering image evidence, they generate fragmented planar patches or spurious planes that span multiple distinct structural surfaces. These geometry-only proxy generation methods fail to accurately preserve structural details that align with the ground truth shape (first, fourth, sixth and twelfth rows in Fig. 13). Among all the results, our image-guided proxies achieve the best balance between simplicity and structural accuracy.

    Moreover, due to the errors that existed in the initial camera poses, there are obvious inter-misalignment (seventh, ninth rows in Fig. 13) and intra-misalignment (seventh and eleventh rows in Fig. 13) in the textured geometry-only proxies, whereas our camera refinement effectively mitigates them. Need to mention that texturing the geometry-only proxies with refined camera poses can achieve a significant improvement over both intra-misalignment and inter-misalignment. Please refer to the supplemental material for more results.

    Quantitative Evaluation.

    Following [Smith et al. (2018)] and [Xiong et al. (2025b)], we compute two metrics to assess the quality of the reconstructed geometry ℙ: i) Error, which quantifies how closely ℙ approximates the dense model D; and ii) Completeness, which measures the coverage of ℙ relative to D. These metrics are computed for all mesh vertices. We further analyze the distributions of these values and report the percentage of vertices with values smaller than 95% in Table 2. QEM and our method achieve the best or second-best Completeness in all scenes. While VSA, PolyFit and BLOD produce a compact proxy, they deliver noticeably higher Error and lower Completeness. KSR achieves reasonable Error and Completeness, but with a comparable or larger number of faces.

    Following [Shen et al. (2023)] and [Chen et al. (2022)], we use Edge Chamfer Distance (ECD) and Edge F1-score (EF1) to evaluate the preservation of sharp features. In most cases, our proxies achieve the best ECD and EF1 scores, demonstrating superior preservation of sharp geometric features, such as facade boundaries.

    For the evaluation of textured proxies, we compare the rendered images of the reconstructed scenes against the corresponding real images following a specific view from the input cameras [(Waechter et al., 2014)]. The comparison results are reported in Table 2. The rendered views of our textured models achieve the best SSIM and LPIPS scores all the time.

    6. Conclusion

    Current textured proxy generation methods treat geometry processing and texturing as independent steps, which struggle with texture and geometry misalignment. In this paper, we propose: i) a framework for generating texture-geometry aligned proxy models given aerial images; ii) A planar structure segmentation benchmark, PlaneSet, targeting urban aerial images, and a fine-tuned segmentation model, ProxySAM. We hope the benchmark can benefit the community; iii) A building-oriented camera pose refinement method leveraging monocular normal consistency; iv) The first image-guided proxy generation method, targeting texture-geometry alignment. With our novel framework, we can achieve not only high-fidelity textures but also high-quality geometries.

    Limitations and Future Work

    First, our algorithm will preserve unrecognized objects, such as foliage. We plan to incorporate more semantic information to allow the removal of user-specific objects. Second, we regard the creation of hierarchical planar structures that enable the generation of LODs as future work. Moreover, unlike performing sequential optimization on geometry and images in our proposed framework, a challenging direction is to jointly optimize the geometry and images for the generation of textured proxy in a single step.

    Acknowledgements.

    This work was supported in part by National Key R&D Program of China (2024YFB3908500, 2024YFB3908502), NSFC (62302313), ICFCRT (W2441020), Guangdong Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation (2023B1515120026), Shenzhen Science and Technology Program (KJZD20240903100022028, KQTD20210811090044003), and Scientific Development Fund from Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Visual Media and Multidimensional Intelligence.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：顺序式管线的「先几何后贴图」丢掉了图像证据，导致代理模型与照片对不上。

要点：

  • 带纹理的代理模型是建筑场景的基础表示：既保证渲染效率，又要保留视觉保真度
  • 现有做法是顺序管线——先从稠密重建里抽象出几何，再把输入图像投影成纹理。这种「只看几何」的建模在代理生成阶段就丢掉了图像证据
  • 这篇因此把图像证据引入代理生成阶段，而不是等几何定死之后再贴图

为什么值得看：数字孪生、建筑可视化里最烦的就是「代理模型贴图错位」。把图像证据前移到几何抽象阶段，是从流程顺序上解决错位，而不是事后修 UV。

中文摘要：带纹理的代理模型是建筑场景的基础表示，既要保证渲染效率，又要保留视觉保真度。现有方法采用顺序式管线：先从稠密重建中抽象出几何，再把输入图像投影上去形成纹理。问题在于这种只依赖几何的建模方式，在代理生成阶段就把图像证据丢掉了，等到贴图环节再补已经无法纠正几何与影像之间的偏差。这篇改为让图像证据参与代理的生成过程，从流程顺序上避免「几何定死、贴图只好将就」的结构性问题，对数字孪生与建筑可视化的资产管线更实用。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-10

本期推送：2026-11-11

Architectural Textured Proxy Generation

© cc

Abstract.

Textured proxy models are a fundamental representation for architectural scenes, enabling efficient rendering while preserving visual fidelity. Existing approaches construct such proxies through a sequential pipeline in which geometry is first abstracted from a dense reconstruction and textures are later projected from input images. This geometry-only formulation neglects image evidence during proxy generation, leading to misalignment of structural features such as facades, edges, and their intersections across views. As a result, inconsistencies are deferred to a downstream correction stage during texturing, where the underlying geometric structure can no longer be reliably recovered. In this work, we introduce an image-guided proxy formulation in which proxy generation is jointly constrained by both the dense reconstruction and the input aerial images. By incorporating image derived structural cues directly into the construction process, the proxy is optimized to align with observed features across views from the outset, rather than relying on post hoc correction that may be infeasible. This shift from a geometry-only to an image-guided paradigm produces proxies that are inherently consistent with the input imagery, enabling more accurate geometry and more coherent texture mapping. We realize this formulation through a framework that extracts structural priors from images and dense geometry, and enforces their consistency during proxy optimization. The resulting proxies exhibit improved alignment of structural features, reducing artifacts such as edge duplication, texture drift, and cross view inconsistencies. Experiments on diverse architectural scenes demonstrate that our approach produces compact, geometry texture aligned proxies with substantially improved visual fidelity compared to existing methods.

Keywords:

Architectural Models, Proxy Generation, Geometry-Texture Alignment, Camera Pose Adjustment ††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

High-quality 3D reconstruction from images has become widely accessible, producing dense geometric models with detailed appearance [(Sinha et al., 2008; Musialski et al., 2013)]. However, such models remain impractical for downstream applications due to their complexity. Proxy representations address this limitation by abstracting geometry into compact, structured models that enable efficient rendering and manipulation. In architectural scenes, proxies are typically composed of piecewise planar elements, capturing the dominant structure of buildings while serving as the support for texture mapping [(Garland and Heckbert, 1997; Salinas et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024)].

Despite their utility, existing pipelines suffer from a fundamental limitation: geometry abstraction and texturing are treated as separate stages. A proxy is first constructed from a dense model, and textures are later projected from the input images [(Xiong et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2025a)]. This sequential design leads to inconsistencies in what we term structural features—planar facades, edges, and their intersections that define the geometry of buildings. These features should coincide across the proxy and all input views, yet in practice they drift. Errors from camera estimation, geometric abstraction, and projection accumulate, causing edges to misalign, planar regions to fragment, and textures from different views to disagree (Fig. 2). As a result, texturing becomes a corrective step that attempts to compensate for misaligned geometry, often with limited success [(Xiong et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2025a)]. Prior approaches either optimize textures without modifying geometry, rely on manual adjustments [(Sinha et al., 2008)], or employ learning-based generation that may deviate from the observed scene [(Chen et al., 2025)].

We replace this pipeline with a coupled formulation in which proxy geometry is directly constrained by image-derived structural features. Rather than constructing a proxy and then fitting textures, we build the proxy so that structural features are already aligned across views, prior to texturing. By enforcing this alignment at construction time, the proxy becomes a geometrically consistent support for all image observations, eliminating the need for downstream correction. To realize this formulation, we extract priors from the input images and use them to jointly guide camera refinement and proxy generation. Camera poses are optimized to align projected geometry with image-derived normal cues, while proxy geometry is iteratively adjusted under a guidance field that enforces piecewise planar structure consistent with these priors. This shared structural signal couples geometry and appearance throughout the pipeline. Given the resulting aligned proxy and refined cameras, texture mapping reduces to aggregating consistent observations rather than resolving inconsistencies.

Our approach produces textured proxies with significantly improved alignment of structural features, reducing artifacts such as ghosting, edge duplication, and texture drift. We demonstrate consistent gains in both geometric accuracy and visual fidelity over prior methods that decouple geometry and texturing. More broadly, our results suggest that enforcing structural alignment at the level of representation, rather than repairing it afterward, is key to reliable proxy reconstruction. Our contributions are summarized as:

  • •

    An automatic framework for generating texture-geometry-aligned proxy models given aerial images. Our novel framework can achieve not only high-fidelity textures but also high-quality proxy geometries;

  • •

    A building-oriented camera pose refinement method leveraging normal consistency between the input images and reconstructed dense geometries;

  • •

    A planar structure segmentation benchmark targeting urban aerial images and a fine-tuned segmentation model. We hope the benchmark can benefit the community;

  • •

    The first proxy generation method targeting texture-geometry alignment, from a textureless dense building reconstruction.

    • 2. Related Works

    Texture Remapping

    Existing texture remapping methods for reconstructed dense geometry can be classified into two categories: i) Image-only remapping methods associate each face or vertex with one or multiple appropriate input images, then create textures via seam/weights optimization to avoid visible seams between adjacent patches [(Wang et al., 2018; Waechter et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2018; Bernardini et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2020; Bi et al., 2017)], ii) Joint optimization methods jointly rectify the camera poses and geometric errors, to avoid texture misalignment caused by geometric error and camera drifting [(Lempitsky and Ivanov, 2007; Gal et al., 2010; Zhou and Koltun, 2014; Fu et al., 2020)].

    In recent years, texturing architectural proxy models has emerged as a topic of growing interest. [Xiong et al. (2023); Xiong et al. (2025a)] generate a texture map for each planar polygon of an architectural proxy, minimizing the intra-misalignment via image warping or weights optimization. However, these methods focus only on texture improvement, which subjectively decouples the inter-relationship between camera pose, geometry and texture. These image-only methods still struggle in tackling inter-misalignment and structure misalignment.

    In this paper, we focus on generating a texture-geometry aligned proxy model given aerial images. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first textured proxy generation method that jointly optimizes camera poses, proxy model, and texture maps.

    Camera Calibration

    Camera calibration methods can be categorized by optimization granularity. Pixel-based methods [(Schonberger and Frahm, 2016; Triggs et al., 1999)] minimize per-pixel reprojection errors and achieve high accuracy, but are sensitive to textureless regions and image noise. Primitive-based methods [(Hu et al., 2024; Shu et al., 2023)] exploit geometric primitives such as feature points, lines, and planes to formulate more robust alignment objectives, yet their effectiveness depends on reliable primitive detection and association. In large-scale urban reconstruction, building facades are dominated by weak/repetitive textures and convex/concave structures varying with viewing angles, which yield sparse and unreliable feature correspondences. Furthermore, current methods minimize average error over all matched feature points rather than enforcing local geometric alignment on individual building structures. As a result, the camera poses may be globally plausible but locally inaccurate for every single building.

    Per-image calibration can be further improved using object silhouettes [(Lensch et al., 2001)] or image matching. We introduce a building-oriented camera refinement method that incorporates geometric priors estimated by a foundation model.

    Proxy Model Generation

    Early methods used geometric error metrics or structure-aware decimation techniques [(Yan et al., 2006; Garland and Heckbert, 1997; Cohen-Steiner et al., 2004; Gao et al., 2022; Khan et al., 2020)]. Appearance-preserving simplification approaches seek to approximate the rendered appearance of an existing textured model [(Garland and Heckbert, 1998; Cohen et al., 1998; Choi et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b; Bo et al., 2026)]. Another important family follows a detect-then-assemble paradigm, where planar primitives are first extracted and subsequently assembled into polygonal or polyhedral meshes through optimization [(Chauve et al., 2010; Nan and Wonka, 2017; Bauchet and Lafarge, 2020; Fang and Lafarge, 2020; Fang et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2017)]. Representative methods such as PolyFit [(Nan and Wonka, 2017)] and KSR [(Bauchet and Lafarge, 2020)] produce compact and structured models, but their performance heavily depends on the completeness and accuracy of primitive detection. Missing or noisy planar hypotheses often lead to structural misalignment. More recently, BLOD [(Pan et al., 2025)] extends this paradigm to multi-scale LOD generation by introducing an Inside/Outside-view analysis and organizing reconstructed structures into a hierarchical LOD-Tree representation. Despite their effectiveness in geometric abstraction, these approaches largely rely on geometry-only formulations and do not explicitly enforce consistency with image observations during proxy construction.

    In contrast to prior geometry-only pipelines, our method incorporates image-derived structural cues directly into proxy optimization. By jointly enforcing geometric abstraction and cross-view image consistency during proxy generation, our approach produces texture-geometry aligned architectural proxies.

    Monocular-Plane Extraction

    Estimating planar structures from images has been studied extensively. Existing monocular plane extraction methods have achieved notable progress in recovering local planar regions from single images.
